quote: as regards AI systems put into service or used by Union institutions, agencies, offices and bodies, references to national competent authorities or market surveillance authorities in this Regulation shall be construed as references to the European Data Protection Supervisor
note: Appoints the EDPS as supervisor for AI used by EU bodies. 'national competent authority' = notifying authority or MSA. See also Art. 3(47): references to the AI Office are references to the Commission.

quote: The following AI practices shall be prohibited:
if_not_met: Art. 99(3) (outside this part): administrative fines up to EUR 35 000 000 or 7% of worldwide turnover; Union bodies up to EUR 1 500 000 (Art. 100(2)); fines on national public authorities only as each Member State lays down (Art. 99(8)).
note: Bars use outright for anyone placing on the market, putting into service or using. Listed: (a) subliminal/manipulative techniques causing significant harm; (b) exploiting vulnerabilities (age, disability, social or economic situation); (c) social scoring; (d) criminal-offence risk prediction based solely on profiling; (e) untargeted scraping for facial recognition databases; (f) emotion inference in workplace and education (except medical/safety); (g) biometric categorisation inferring race, political opinions, trade union membership, religion, sex life or orientation; (h) real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces for law enforcement save listed objectives. (c), (d), (h) coded separately. Applies from 2 February 2025 (Recital 179).

quote: the placing on the market, the putting into service or the use of an AI system that deploys subliminal techniques beyond a person’s consciousness or purposefully manipulative or deceptive techniques
holder: not stated (applies to anyone placing on the market, putting into service or using)
if_not_met: not stated in Art. 5; Art. 99(3) (outside this part): administrative fines up to EUR 35 000 000 or up to 7% of worldwide annual turnover; Union bodies up to EUR 1 500 000 (Art. 100(2)); each Member State sets the extent to which fines may be imposed on its public authorities (Art. 99(8))
note: Ban (stop decision set in law). Condition: 'with the objective, or the effect of materially distorting the behaviour' and causing or being reasonably likely to cause 'significant harm'. Nearest named actors: providers and deployers.

quote: the use of an AI system that exploits any of the vulnerabilities of a natural person or a specific group of persons due to their age, disability or a specific social or economic situation
holder: not stated (applies to anyone placing on the market, putting into service or using)
if_not_met: not stated in Art. 5; Art. 99(3) (outside this part): fines up to EUR 35 000 000 or 7% of turnover; Union bodies up to EUR 1 500 000 (Art. 100(2)); Member States set extent for public authorities (Art. 99(8))
note: Ban where the objective or effect is materially distorting behaviour causing or reasonably likely to cause significant harm. [inference] Relevant to public services dealing with people in vulnerable social or economic situations.

quote: the use of AI systems for the evaluation or classification of natural persons or groups of persons over a certain period of time based on their social behaviour
if_not_met: Art. 99(3) (outside this part): fines up to EUR 35 000 000 or 7%; Union bodies up to EUR 1 500 000 (Art. 100(2)); national public authorities as each Member State lays down (Art. 99(8)).
note: Prohibited where the social score leads to detrimental treatment in unrelated social contexts, or treatment unjustified or disproportionate to the behaviour. Applies to public and private users alike.

quote: the use of an AI system for making risk assessments of natural persons in order to assess or predict the risk of a natural person committing a criminal offence, based solely on the profiling of a natural person
if_not_met: Art. 99(3) (outside this part): fines up to EUR 35 000 000 or 7%; Union bodies up to EUR 1 500 000 (Art. 100(2)); national public authorities as each Member State lays down (Art. 99(8)).
note: Also covers assessing personality traits and characteristics. Exception: systems supporting human assessment of involvement in crime 'already based on objective and verifiable facts directly linked to a criminal activity'.

quote: the use of AI systems that create or expand facial recognition databases through the untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV footage
holder: not stated (applies to anyone placing on the market, putting into service for this purpose or using)
if_not_met: not stated in Art. 5; Art. 99(3) (outside this part): fines up to EUR 35 000 000 or 7% of turnover; Union bodies up to EUR 1 500 000 (Art. 100(2)); Member States set extent for public authorities (Art. 99(8))
note: Ban on untargeted scraping to build facial recognition databases.

quote: the use of AI systems to infer emotions of a natural person in the areas of workplace and education institutions
holder: not stated (applies to anyone placing on the market, putting into service for this purpose or using)
if_not_met: not stated in Art. 5; Art. 99(3) (outside this part): fines up to EUR 35 000 000 or 7% of turnover; Union bodies up to EUR 1 500 000 (Art. 100(2)); Member States set extent for public authorities (Art. 99(8))
note: Exception: 'except where the use of the AI system is intended to be put in place or into the market for medical or safety reasons'. Covers public-sector workplaces and public schools/universities.

quote: the use of biometric categorisation systems that categorise individually natural persons based on their biometric data to deduce or infer their race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation
holder: not stated (applies to anyone placing on the market, putting into service for this purpose or using)
if_not_met: not stated in Art. 5; Art. 99(3) (outside this part): fines up to EUR 35 000 000 or 7% of turnover; Union bodies up to EUR 1 500 000 (Art. 100(2)); Member States set extent for public authorities (Art. 99(8))
note: Carve-out: does not cover 'any labelling or filtering of lawfully acquired biometric datasets, such as images, based on biometric data or categorizing of biometric data in the area of law enforcement'.

quote: the use of ‘real-time’ remote biometric identification systems in publicly accessible spaces for the purposes of law enforcement, unless and in so far as such use is strictly necessary for one of the following objectives
if_not_met: Art. 99(3) (outside this part): fines up to EUR 35 000 000 or 7%; national public authorities as each Member State lays down (Art. 99(8)).
note: Objectives: (i) targeted search for victims of abduction, trafficking, sexual exploitation, and missing persons; (ii) preventing a specific, substantial and imminent threat to life or a terrorist attack; (iii) locating or identifying suspects of Annex II offences punishable by at least four years. Further conditions in Art. 5(2)-(7).

quote: shall be deployed for the purposes set out in that point only to confirm the identity of the specifically targeted individual
if_not_met: Art. 99(3) (outside this part) for breach of Art. 5.
note: Must take into account (a) seriousness, probability and scale of harm if not used; (b) consequences for rights and freedoms of all persons concerned. Must comply with necessary and proportionate safeguards in the authorising national law (temporal, geographic, personal limits).

quote: No decision that produces an adverse legal effect on a person may be taken based solely on the output of the ‘real-time’ remote biometric identification system.
obligation: statutory prohibition (no solely automated adverse decision)
if_not_met: Art. 99(3) (outside this part) for breach of Art. 5.
note: Passive; nearest named actor: the law enforcement authority. Requires a human decision; output alone cannot ground an adverse legal decision.

quote: A Member State may decide to provide for the possibility to fully or partially authorise the use of ‘real-time’ remote biometric identification systems in publicly accessible spaces for the purposes of law enforcement
note: Within limits of Art. 5(1)(h), (2), (3). 'Member States may introduce, in accordance with Union law, more restrictive laws on the use of remote biometric identification systems.'

quote: Member States concerned shall lay down in their national law the necessary detailed rules for the request, issuance and exercise of, as well as supervision and reporting relating to, the authorisations referred to in paragraph 3
obligation: statutory duty (for Member States that opt in)
note: Rules must also specify the objectives and criminal offences for which competent authorities may be authorised. Also coded Coordination/Design (notify rules to Commission).

quote: In addition to the high-risk AI systems referred to in paragraph 1, AI systems referred to in Annex III shall be considered to be high-risk.
note: Decides which tools carry Chapter III obligations. Art. 6(1): AI that is, or is a safety component of, an Annex I product requiring third-party conformity assessment. Annex III (outside this part) lists areas incl. access to essential public services and benefits, law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control, and administration of justice.

quote: an AI system referred to in Annex III shall not be considered to be high-risk where it does not pose a significant risk of harm to the health, safety or fundamental rights of natural persons
note: Applies where the system is intended (a) to perform a narrow procedural task; (b) to improve a previously completed human activity; (c) to detect decision-making patterns without replacing or influencing prior human assessment without proper human review; or (d) to perform a preparatory task. Annex III systems that profile natural persons are always high-risk. The provider applies the derogation (Art. 6(4)).

quote: A provider who considers that an AI system referred to in Annex III is not high-risk shall document its assessment before that system is placed on the market or put into service.
holder: A provider who considers that an AI system referred to in Annex III is not high-risk
note: The provider itself decides whether the Art. 6(3) exemption applies; no prior approval by an authority is stated. Same passage also coded Delivery/Design (documenting the assessment); registration and disclosure coded Accountability/Design.

quote: The Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts in accordance with Article 97 in order to amend paragraph 3, second subparagraph, of this Article by adding new conditions to those laid down therein, or by modifying them
note: Trigger: 'concrete and reliable evidence' of Annex III systems not posing significant risk. Art. 6(7): Commission 'shall' delete conditions where necessary to maintain protection. Art. 6(8): amendments must not decrease overall protection.

quote: the relevant residual risk associated with each hazard, as well as the overall residual risk of the high-risk AI systems is judged to be acceptable
if_not_met: Not stated here. Breach of Art. 16(a) (Section 2 compliance): fines up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3% (Art. 99(4)(a), outside this part).
note: The document does not say who judges acceptability; nearest named actor: provider (Art. 9(9), 16(a)); no external approver named. Measures must first eliminate or reduce risks through design as far as technically feasible, then mitigate and control what remains.
basis: AI pass A; different cell in pass B

quote: The Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts in accordance with Article 97 in order to amend Annex IV, where necessary, to ensure that, in light of technical progress, the technical documentation provides all the information necessary
note: Sets what documentation must contain.

quote: this Regulation should not apply to public authorities of a third country and international organisations when acting in the framework of cooperation or international agreements concluded at Union or national level for law enforcement and judicial cooperation
holder: European Parliament and Council (legislator, through this Regulation)
obligation: non-binding interpretation (recital) of a scope exclusion; 'should not apply'
note: Scope exemption, conditional: 'provided that the relevant third country or international organisation provides adequate safeguards'. Same recital extends scope to third-country providers/deployers whose output is used in the Union.

quote: to decide, in any particular situation, not to use the high-risk AI system or to otherwise disregard, override or reverse the output of the high-risk AI system
holder: natural persons to whom human oversight is assigned (enabled by the provider's design)
if_not_met: Not stated here. Breach of Art. 16(a): fines up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3% (Art. 99(4)(a), outside this part).
note: Override authority at individual level. (e): intervene or interrupt via a 'stop' button or similar procedure. The provider designs for this; the deployer assigns the persons (Art. 26(2)).

quote: no action or decision is taken by the deployer on the basis of the identification resulting from the system unless that identification has been separately verified
if_not_met: not stated here; Art. 99(4)(a) (outside this part) via Art. 16(a)
note: Constrains decisions on biometric identification outputs. Exempted for law enforcement, migration, border control or asylum where Union or national law considers the requirement disproportionate. Also coded Delivery/Design.

quote: Each Member State shall determine conditions under which the documentation referred to in paragraph 1 remains at the disposal of the national competent authorities
note: Rule-setting for cases where a provider or its authorised representative 'goes bankrupt or ceases its activity' before the 10-year period ends. [inference] Bears on continuity of records for public-sector tools whose supplier fails.
basis: AI pass B; different cell in pass A

quote: shall immediately take the necessary corrective actions to bring that system into conformity, to withdraw it, to disable it, or to recall it, as appropriate
if_not_met: Not stated here. Art. 16(j) breach: fines up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3% (Art. 99(4)(a), outside this part).
note: Trigger: provider considers or has reason to consider the system not in conformity. Authority to stop the tool (withdraw, disable, recall). Also coded Coordination/Design.

quote: it shall not place the system on the market until it has been brought into conformity
if_not_met: Not stated here. Art. 99(4)(c) (outside this part).
note: Trigger: sufficient reason to consider non-conformity, falsification or falsified documentation. Where risk under Art. 79(1): inform provider, authorised representative and MSAs.

quote: it shall not make the high-risk AI system available on the market until the system has been brought into conformity with those requirements
if_not_met: Not stated here. Art. 99(4)(d) (outside this part).
note: Trigger: distributor considers or has reason to consider non-conformity. Where risk under Art. 79(1): inform provider or importer.

quote: shall take the corrective actions necessary to bring that system into conformity with those requirements, to withdraw it or recall it, or shall ensure that the provider, the importer or any relevant operator, as appropriate, takes those corrective actions
if_not_met: Not stated here. Art. 99(4)(d) (outside this part).
note: For systems already made available. Where risk under Art. 79(1): immediately inform provider or importer and competent authorities with details of non-compliance and corrective actions (accountability element).

quote: Deployers shall assign human oversight to natural persons who have the necessary competence, training and authority, as well as the necessary support.
if_not_met: Not stated here. Art. 99(4)(e) (outside this part): fines up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3%; national public authorities as each Member State lays down (Art. 99(8)); Union bodies up to EUR 750 000 (Art. 100(3)).
note: Appoints who oversees and may override outputs (Art. 14(4)(d)). Art. 26(3): without prejudice to 'the deployer’s freedom to organise its own resources and activities' to implement provider-indicated oversight measures. Also coded Delivery/Resources.

quote: they shall, without undue delay, inform the provider or distributor and the relevant market surveillance authority, and shall suspend the use of that system
if_not_met: Not stated here. Art. 99(4)(e) (outside this part).
note: Trigger: reason to consider that use per instructions may result in a risk within Art. 79(1). Deployer must pause the tool; also reports to the MSA (accountability element).

quote: has not been registered in the EU database referred to in Article 71, they shall not use that system and shall inform the provider or the distributor
holder: such deployers (public authorities, Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies)
if_not_met: Not stated here. Art. 99(4)(e) (outside this part).
note: Gate: public-sector deployers must not use a high-risk system the provider has not registered. Trigger: before use ('envisage using').

quote: It shall be ensured that no decision that produces an adverse legal effect on a person may be taken by the law enforcement authorities based solely on the output of such post-remote biometric identification systems.
obligation: statutory prohibition (no solely automated adverse decision)
if_not_met: Not stated here. Art. 99(4)(e) (outside this part).
note: Passive ('It shall be ensured'); nearest named actor: the law enforcement authorities. Requires a human decision.

quote: This Regulation should also apply to Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies when acting as a provider or deployer of an AI system.
obligation: non-binding interpretation (recital); describes scope set by the Regulation
note: Scope decision made by the Regulation itself (legislator: European Parliament and Council). Brings EU institutions, bodies, offices and agencies within provider and deployer obligations; nearest named actor: Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies. See Recital (156): EDPS as their market surveillance authority.

quote: those should be excluded from the scope of this Regulation regardless of which type of entity is carrying out those activities, such as whether it is a public or private entity.
obligation: non-binding interpretation (recital); describes scope exclusion set by the Regulation
note: Exclusion of AI systems placed on the market, put into service or used for military, defence or national security purposes, whether by public or private entities. Systems also used for civilian, humanitarian, law enforcement or public security purposes fall in scope. Scope set by the Regulation; nearest named actor: entities carrying out national security, defence and military activities. Also coded Delivery/Design (Recital 24).

quote: It is therefore necessary to exclude from its scope AI systems and models specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development.
holder: European Parliament and Council (legislator, through this Regulation)
obligation: non-binding interpretation (recital) of a scope exclusion
note: Also: product-oriented research, testing and development before placing on the market is out of scope, without prejudice to sandboxes and real-world testing; research 'should be carried out in accordance with recognised ethical and professional standards'.

quote: Each Member State shall designate or establish at least one notifying authority responsible for setting up and carrying out the necessary procedures for the assessment, designation and notification of conformity assessment bodies and for their monitoring.
note: Appoints who decides on designating the checkers (conformity assessment bodies). 28(2): Member States may have assessment and monitoring done by a national accreditation body under Regulation (EC) No 765/2008. Also coded Coordination/Design.

quote: Notifying authorities shall be organised in such a way that decisions relating to the notification of conformity assessment bodies are taken by competent persons different from those who carried out the assessment of those bodies.
note: Separation of assessor and decider. 28(3): no conflict of interest, objectivity and impartiality; 28(5): no CAB activities or consultancy on a commercial basis; 28(6): confidentiality (Art. 78).

quote: Notifying authorities may notify only conformity assessment bodies which have satisfied the requirements laid down in Article 31.
note: Approval decision on who may act as checker; standard = Art. 31 requirements.

quote: The conformity assessment body concerned may perform the activities of a notified body only where no objections are raised by the Commission or the other Member States within two weeks of a notification
holder: the Commission or the other Member States
note: Two weeks with accreditation certificate; two months with documentary evidence. If objections: Commission consults and 'shall decide whether the authorisation is justified' (30(5)).

quote: it shall be presumed to comply with the requirements set out in Article 31 in so far as the applicable harmonised standards cover those requirements
holder: not stated (the Regulation sets the presumption); applies to conformity assessment bodies
note: Standards-based route to meeting notified-body requirements: where a body 'demonstrates its conformity with the criteria laid down in the relevant harmonised standards' published in the Official Journal.

quote: Activities may be subcontracted or carried out by a subsidiary only with the agreement of the provider.
if_not_met: Not stated here. Art. 99(4)(f) (outside this part).
note: The assessed provider holds a veto over subcontracting of its assessment.

quote: require the notified body to suspend or withdraw, within a reasonable period of time determined by the authority, any certificates which were unduly issued
note: Following restriction, suspension or withdrawal of designation. Also: assess impact on certificates (a); inform Commission and Member States of required suspensions (d); inform NCAs of provider's Member State, which take measures to avoid risk to health, safety or fundamental rights (e).

quote: may extend the provisional validity of the certificates for additional periods of three months, which shall not exceed 12 months in total
holder: the national competent authority of the Member State in which the provider of the system covered by the certificate has its place of business
note: After withdrawal of designation, certificates remain valid nine months if the NCA confirms no risk and another notified body assumes responsibility and completes assessment within 12 months. 36(8): rules for suspension or restriction (notifying authority confirms no risk, or provider confirms another notified body within three months).

quote: the national competent authority of the Member State in which the provider of the system covered by the certificate has its place of business may extend the provisional validity of the certificates for additional periods of three months
holder: the national competent authority of the Member State in which the provider of the system covered by the certificate has its place of business; the notifying authority
note: Continuity of approvals after a designation changes. Suspension/restriction (36(8)): certificates stay valid if the notifying authority confirms within one month no risk to health, safety or fundamental rights and sets a remedy timeline, or confirms no certificates will be issued; otherwise the provider must confirm within three months that another notified body is temporarily responsible. Withdrawal (36(9)): valid nine months if the competent authority confirms no risk and another notified body assumes responsibility and completes assessment within 12 months; extensions 'shall not exceed 12 months in total'. Commission, Member States and other notified bodies informed.

quote: Where the Member State fails to take the necessary corrective measures, the Commission may, by means of an implementing act, suspend, restrict or withdraw the designation.
note: First the Commission requests the notifying Member State to take corrective measures, incl. suspension or withdrawal. Implementing act via examination procedure (Art. 98(2)).

quote: Conformity assessment bodies established under the law of a third country with which the Union has concluded an agreement may be authorised to carry out the activities of notified bodies under this Regulation
note: Passive; authorising body not named. Condition: meet Art. 31 or ensure an equivalent level of compliance.

quote: High-risk AI systems or general-purpose AI models which are in conformity with harmonised standards or parts thereof the references of which have been published in the Official Journal of the European Union
obligation: statutory presumption of conformity (standards are a voluntary route)
note: Such systems/models 'shall be presumed to be in conformity' with Section 2 or GPAI obligations to the extent covered. [inference] Whoever drafts the harmonised standard (European standardisation organisations, on Commission request, 40(2)) in effect sets what compliance means. Also coded Decision-making/Design (Commission requests).

quote: the Commission shall issue, without undue delay, standardisation requests covering all requirements set out in Section 2 of this Chapter
note: Also GPAI obligations and deliverables on energy and resource efficiency. Commission must specify standards be clear, consistent and aim to ensure requirements are met, and ask ESOs to evidence best efforts. Also coded Coordination/Design.

quote: to enhance multi-stakeholder governance ensuring a balanced representation of interests and the effective participation of all relevant stakeholders
holder: The participants in the standardisation process
note: Participants shall also seek to promote investment and innovation, legal certainty, competitiveness, global cooperation, and take into account international standards consistent with Union values and fundamental rights.

quote: High-risk AI systems that have been trained and tested on data reflecting the specific geographical, behavioural, contextual or functional setting within which they are intended to be used shall be presumed to comply
holder: not stated (the Regulation sets the presumption)
note: 42(2): systems certified or with a statement of conformity under an EU cybersecurity scheme (Regulation (EU) 2019/881) are presumed to meet Art. 15 cybersecurity requirements to the extent covered.

quote: For the purposes of the conformity assessment procedure referred to in Annex VII, the provider may choose any of the notified bodies.
note: The provider chooses its checker, except for systems intended for law enforcement, immigration, asylum authorities or EU bodies (MSA acts as notified body).

quote: in order to subject high-risk AI systems referred to in points 2 to 8 of Annex III to the conformity assessment procedure referred to in Annex VII or parts thereof
note: Could move public-sector Annex III systems from self-assessment to notified-body assessment, considering effectiveness of internal control and notified-body capacity. 43(5): power to amend Annexes VI and VII.

quote: Certificates shall be valid for the period they indicate, which shall not exceed five years for AI systems covered by Annex I, and four years for AI systems covered by Annex III.
holder: notified bodies (issue certificates); provider (may request extension)
note: Approval expires; extension 'At the request of the provider ... based on a re-assessment in accordance with the applicable conformity assessment procedures' (re-check trigger: expiry). Certificates in a language easily understood by authorities (44(1)).
basis: AI pass B; different cell in pass A

quote: Where a notified body finds that an AI system no longer meets the requirements set out in Section 2, it shall, taking account of the principle of proportionality, suspend or withdraw the certificate issued or impose restrictions on it
note: Unless the provider takes corrective action within a deadline set by the notified body; reasons must be given.

quote: All stakeholders, including industry, academia, civil society and standardisation organisations, are encouraged to take into account, as appropriate, the ethical principles for the development of voluntary best practices and standards.
holder: All stakeholders, including industry, academia, civil society and standardisation organisations
note: Standard-setting (voluntary best practices and standards) against the AI HLEG's seven non-binding ethical principles. The recital also says the principles 'should in any case serve as a basis for the drafting of codes of conduct under this Regulation'.

quote: The placing on the market, the putting into service or the use of certain AI systems with the objective to or the effect of materially distorting human behaviour
holder: European Parliament and Council (legislator, through this Regulation)
obligation: non-binding interpretation (recital) of a prohibition; 'should therefore be prohibited'
note: Prohibition of manipulative/deceptive techniques causing significant harm, and of exploiting vulnerabilities (age, disability, social or economic situation). Binds any provider or deployer, including public authorities. Intention to cause harm not needed.

quote: novel and powerful tools for manipulative, exploitative and social control practices. Such practices are particularly harmful and abusive and should be prohibited
obligation: non-binding interpretation (recital, 'should be prohibited'); describes a prohibition
note: Decides that certain tools may not be used at all. Recital (29) covers AI that materially distorts behaviour through subliminal, manipulative or deceptive techniques, or exploits vulnerabilities (age, disability, social or economic situation), causing significant harm; 'it is not necessary for the provider or the deployer to have the intention to cause significant harm'. Lawful medical practice is not affected. Nearest named actors: providers and deployers (placing on the market, putting into service or use). Operative rule appears to be Art. 5 [inference; not in this part].

quote: any market surveillance authority may authorise the placing on the market or the putting into service of specific high-risk AI systems within the territory of the Member State concerned, for exceptional reasons of public security
note: Also for protection of life and health, environment, key industrial and infrastructural assets. Limited period while conformity assessment proceeds. Only if the MSA concludes the system complies with Section 2 (46(3)). Deemed justified if no objection within 15 days (46(4)).

quote: law-enforcement authorities or civil protection authorities may put a specific high-risk AI system into service without the authorisation referred to in paragraph 1, provided that such authorisation is requested during or after the use without undue delay
holder: law-enforcement authorities or civil protection authorities
if_not_met: 'If the authorisation referred to in paragraph 1 is refused, the use of the high-risk AI system shall be stopped with immediate effect and all the results and outputs of such use shall be immediately discarded.'
note: Trigger: duly justified urgency for public security, or specific, substantial and imminent threat to life or physical safety.

quote: the Commission shall decide whether the authorisation is justified. The Commission shall address its decision to the Member State concerned and to the relevant operators.
if_not_met: Authorisation withdrawn by the MSA if the Commission considers it unjustified (Art. 46(6)).
note: Trigger: objection by a Member State within 15 days, or Commission considers authorisation contrary to Union law or unfounded; operators consulted. 46(7): for Annex I Section A products only sectoral derogations apply.

quote: Where the Commission considers the authorisation unjustified, it shall be withdrawn by the market surveillance authority of the Member State concerned.
holder: the Commission (decides); market surveillance authority of the Member State concerned (withdraws)
note: EU-level override of national derogations. 46(5): where a Member State objects within 15 days or the Commission considers the authorisation contrary to Union law or the compliance conclusion unfounded, the Commission consults the Member State; 'The operators concerned shall be consulted and have the possibility to present their views'; Commission decides. 46(7): Annex I Section A products use only their own legislation's derogations.

quote: The Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts in accordance with Article 97 in order to amend Annex V by updating the content of the EU declaration of conformity
note: Sets what the sign-off must contain.

quote: If it deems the code is not adequate, the Commission may adopt an implementing act specifying common rules for the implementation of those obligations
note: The Commission may also approve codes by implementing act (Art. 56(6) procedure).

quote: based on a decision of the Commission, ex officio or following a qualified alert from the scientific panel, it has capabilities or an impact equivalent to those set out in point (a)
note: Classification as GPAI model with systemic risk triggers Art. 55 duties. 51(1)(a): high impact capabilities evaluated by technical tools, indicators and benchmarks; (b) having regard to Annex XIII criteria.

quote: when the cumulative amount of computation used for its training measured in floating point operations is greater than 1025
note: Presumption of high impact capabilities. '1025' as extracted; [inference] the Official Journal reads 10^25 (superscript lost). 51(3): Commission 'shall adopt delegated acts' to amend thresholds and supplement benchmarks and indicators.

quote: The Commission may designate a general-purpose AI model as presenting systemic risks, ex officio or following a qualified alert from the scientific panel pursuant to Article 90(1), point (a), on the basis of criteria set out in Annex XIII.
note: Commission also empowered to amend Annex XIII criteria by delegated acts.

quote: The obligations set out in paragraph 1, points (a) and (b), shall not apply to providers of AI models that are released under a free and open-source licence
note: Condition: licence allows access, use, modification, distribution, and parameters incl. weights, architecture and usage information are public. 'This exception shall not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risks.'

quote: the Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts in accordance with Article 97 to detail measurement and calculation methodologies with a view to allowing for comparable and verifiable documentation
note: Sets measurement standards for Annex XI documentation (in particular points 2(d)-(e)). 53(6): may amend Annexes XI and XII 'in light of evolving technological developments'.

quote: The Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts in accordance with Article 97(2) to amend Annexes XI and XII in light of evolving technological developments.
note: 53(5): delegated acts to detail measurement and calculation methodologies for comparable, verifiable documentation (Annex XI points 2(d), (e)).

quote: The Commission may, by way of an implementing act, approve a code of practice and give it a general validity within the Union.
note: Examination procedure (Art. 98(2)).

quote: or if the AI Office deems it is not adequate following its assessment under paragraph 6 of this Article, the Commission may provide, by means of implementing acts, common rules
note: Codes 'shall be ready at the latest by 2 May 2025'; fallback also if a code cannot be finalised by 2 August 2025.

quote: the Commission may provide, by means of implementing acts, common rules for the implementation of the obligations provided for in Articles 53 and 55
holder: the Commission (AI Office takes preparatory steps)
note: Trigger: 'If, by 2 August 2025, a code of practice cannot be finalised, or if the AI Office deems it is not adequate'. 'Codes of practice shall be ready at the latest by 2 May 2025.'

quote: National competent authorities shall have the power to temporarily or permanently suspend the testing process, or the participation in the sandbox if no effective mitigation is possible
note: Authority to pause or stop. Trigger: significant risks to health and safety or fundamental rights identified during development and testing, with no effective mitigation possible. Sandboxes 'shall not affect the supervisory or corrective powers of the competent authorities'. Also coded Coordination/Design (inform AI Office) and Delivery/Design (mitigation).

quote: to deduce or infer an individuals’ political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, race, sex life or sexual orientation should be prohibited.
obligation: non-binding interpretation (recital, 'should be prohibited'); describes a prohibition
note: Prohibition of biometric categorisation systems that infer these sensitive attributes from biometric data. Exception: lawful labelling, filtering or categorisation of lawfully acquired biometric data sets, 'which can for example be used in the area of law enforcement'. Nearest named actors: providers and deployers.

quote: AI systems entailing such unacceptable scoring practices and leading to such detrimental or unfavourable outcomes should therefore be prohibited.
obligation: non-binding interpretation (recital, 'should be prohibited'); describes a prohibition
note: Social scoring prohibition; the recital addresses social scoring 'by public or private actors'. Lawful evaluation practices carried out for a specific purpose under Union and national law are not affected. Nearest named actors: public or private actors using such systems.

quote: The use of those systems for the purpose of law enforcement should therefore be prohibited, except in exhaustively listed and narrowly defined situations, where the use is strictly necessary to achieve a substantial public interest
obligation: non-binding interpretation (recital, 'should ... be prohibited'); describes a prohibition with exhaustive exceptions
note: 'Real-time' remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement. Exceptions: search for certain victims including missing persons; certain threats to life or physical safety or a terrorist attack; locating or identifying suspects of annex-listed offences punishable by at least four years. Nearest named actor: law enforcement authorities. See conditions in Recitals (34)-(37).

quote: the Commission shall adopt implementing acts specifying the detailed arrangements for the establishment, development, implementation, operation and supervision of the AI regulatory sandboxes.
note: Standard-setting. Common principles on: eligibility and selection criteria; procedures for application, participation, monitoring, exiting and termination, including the sandbox plan and exit report; terms and conditions for participants. Adopted by examination procedure (Art. 98(2)), i.e. with a committee of Member States.

quote: national competent authorities inform applicants of their decision within three months of the application
obligation: statutory duty (content the implementing acts 'shall ensure')
note: Admission decision. Sandboxes are open to any applying provider or prospective provider who meets eligibility and selection criteria 'which shall be transparent and fair'.

quote: participation in the AI regulatory sandbox is limited to a period that is appropriate to the complexity and scale of the project and that may be extended by the national competent authority
note: Duration decision held by the national competent authority.

quote: they shall specifically agree the terms and conditions of such testing and, in particular, the appropriate safeguards with the participants, with a view to protecting fundamental rights, health and safety
note: Trigger: national competent authorities consider authorising testing in real world conditions within a sandbox. Also coded Coordination/Design (cooperation with other authorities).

quote: AI systems shall be developed for safeguarding substantial public interest by a public authority or another natural or legal person
if_not_met: [inference] the further processing of personal data is not permitted under this Article ('may be processed solely ... when all of the following conditions are met')
note: Gate for further processing, in the sandbox, of personal data lawfully collected for other purposes, solely for developing, training and testing. Areas include '(v) efficiency and quality of public administration and public services', public safety and health, environment, energy, transport and critical infrastructure. Conditions are cumulative ((a)-(j)). Nearest named actors: the public authority or other person developing the system; [inference] applied by the supervising competent authority.

quote: any processing of personal data in the context of the sandbox neither leads to measures or decisions affecting the data subjects
if_not_met: [inference] the further processing is not permitted
note: Limits use: sandbox processing must not feed decisions about the data subjects, nor affect their data protection rights. Nearest named actor: the prospective provider.

quote: the processing of personal data in AI regulatory sandboxes shall be based on a specific Union or national law and subject to the same cumulative conditions as referred to in paragraph 1
holder: Law enforcement authorities (processing under their control and responsibility)
note: Applies to processing for prevention, investigation, detection or prosecution of criminal offences or execution of penalties. Art. 59(3) preserves other Union or national legal bases.

quote: The Commission shall, by means of implementing acts, specify the detailed elements of the real-world testing plan.
note: Standard for testing plans; examination procedure (Art. 98(2)).

quote: the market surveillance authority in the Member State where the testing in real world conditions is to be conducted has approved the testing in real world conditions and the real-world testing plan
holder: Market surveillance authority in the Member State where testing is to be conducted
obligation: mandatory approval gate (statutory), with tacit approval
if_not_met: testing may not be conducted ('only where all of the following conditions are met')
note: Tacit approval: 'where the market surveillance authority has not provided an answer within 30 days' the testing and plan 'shall be understood to have been approved'; where national law has no tacit approval, an authorisation is still required.

quote: the testing in real world conditions does not last longer than necessary to achieve its objectives and in any case not longer than six months
note: Duration limit; extendable once by six months 'subject to prior notification by the provider or prospective provider to the market surveillance authority, accompanied by an explanation'. Market surveillance authorities may derogate within sandboxes (Art. 76(2)). Nearest named actor: provider or prospective provider.

quote: where the seeking of informed consent would prevent the AI system from being tested, the testing itself and the outcome of the testing in the real world conditions shall not have any negative effect on the subjects
if_not_met: testing may not take place (Art. 60(4) conditions)
note: Public-sector carve-out: applies 'in the case of law enforcement'. Removes subjects' consent; substitute safeguards: no negative effect and 'their personal data shall be deleted after the test is performed'. Nearest actor: provider or prospective provider. See Art. 61 entries.

quote: the predictions, recommendations or decisions of the AI system can be effectively reversed and disregarded.
note: Override of outputs must be possible. Nearest named actors: the provider and the deployers who oversee the testing (Art. 60(4)(j)). Linked to Art. 61(1)(d) (arrangements for requesting reversal).

quote: Any subjects of the testing in real world conditions, or their legally designated representative, as appropriate, may, without any resulting detriment and without having to provide any justification, withdraw from the testing at any time
holder: Subjects of testing or their legally designated representative
note: Individuals decide to stop their own participation; may also 'request the immediate and permanent deletion of their personal data'. Could also be read as Accountability (rights of affected persons).
basis: AI pass B; different cell in pass A

quote: The provider or prospective provider shall adopt immediate mitigation measures or, failing that, shall suspend the testing in real world conditions until such mitigation takes place, or otherwise terminate it.
note: Duty to pause or stop. Trigger: serious incident during testing.

quote: freely-given informed consent shall be obtained from the subjects of testing prior to their participation in such testing
note: Subjects decide whether to take part. Nearest actor: provider or prospective provider. Trigger: before participation. Required information covers objectives, conditions, rights to refuse and withdraw, how to request reversal (coded Accountability), ID number and contact details. Could also be read as Accountability.
basis: AI pass B; different cell in pass A

quote: Microenterprises within the meaning of Recommendation 2003/361/EC may comply with certain elements of the quality management system required by Article 17 of this Regulation in a simplified manner
holder: Microenterprises (providers) without partner or linked enterprises
note: Scope exemption set by the Regulation. Art. 63(2): not exempt from other obligations, including Arts. 9-15, 72 and 73. Also coded Delivery/Resources (Commission guidelines).

quote: The designated representatives of the Member States shall adopt the Board’s rules of procedure by a two-thirds majority.
holder: Designated representatives of the Member States on the Board
note: Rules cover selection, mandate and tasks of the Chair, voting arrangements and organisation of activities and sub-groups. The Board is chaired by one Member State representative (Art. 65(8)).

quote: The Commission shall appoint the members of the advisory forum, in accordance with the criteria set out in paragraph 2, from amongst stakeholders with recognised expertise in the field of AI.
note: Appointing advisers. Terms: two years, extendable up to four (Art. 67(4)); forum elects two co-chairs (Art. 67(6)).

quote: The scientific panel shall consist of experts selected by the Commission on the basis of up-to-date scientific or technical expertise in the field of AI
note: Appointing experts. Panel established by implementing act (Art. 68(1)). Conditions include '(b) independence from any provider of AI systems or general-purpose AI models'. The Commission, in consultation with the Board, sets the number of experts and 'shall ensure fair gender and geographical representation'.

quote: Each Member State shall establish or designate as national competent authorities at least one notifying authority and at least one market surveillance authority for the purposes of this Regulation.
note: Appointing who decides. Authorities 'shall exercise their powers independently, impartially and without bias'; tasks may be split across several authorities.

quote: where an AI system is based on a general-purpose AI model and the model and system are provided by the same provider, the supervision should take place at Union level through the AI Office
note: Allocates supervisory competence. AI Office to have the powers of a market surveillance authority for this purpose; in all other cases national MSAs remain responsible. Also coded Coordination/Design.

quote: shall be subject to a prior authorisation granted by a judicial authority or an independent administrative authority whose decision is binding of the Member State in which the use is to take place
holder: a judicial authority or an independent administrative authority whose decision is binding
obligation: mandatory approval gate (prior authorisation for each use)
if_not_met: 'If such authorisation is rejected, the use shall be stopped with immediate effect and all the data, as well as the results and outputs of that use shall be immediately discarded and deleted.'
note: Issued upon a reasoned request (by the law enforcement authority). Urgency: use may start without authorisation if requested 'without undue delay, at the latest within 24 hours'. Authority grants only where satisfied 'on the basis of objective evidence or clear indications' that use is necessary and proportionate, limited to what is strictly necessary in time, geography and persons, taking account of Art. 5(2) elements.

quote: The Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts in accordance with Article 97 to amend Annex III by adding or modifying use-cases of high-risk AI systems where both of the following conditions are fulfilled
note: Conditions: Annex III area; risk equivalent to or greater than existing high-risk systems. Criteria (7(2)) incl. intended purpose, extent of use, data, autonomy and 'the possibility for a human to override a decision or recommendations', reported harms, dependence on outcome, imbalance of power vis-a-vis the deployer (status, authority), reversibility, benefits, existing redress. Art. 7(3): may remove systems no longer posing significant risk if protection not decreased.

quote: shall request an authorisation, ex ante, or without undue delay and no later than 48 hours, by a judicial authority or an administrative authority whose decision is binding and subject to judicial review
holder: the deployer of a high-risk AI system for post-remote biometric identification (requests); a judicial authority or an administrative authority whose decision is binding and subject to judicial review (decides)
obligation: mandatory approval gate (ex ante or within 48 hours)
if_not_met: If rejected, 'the use of the post-remote biometric identification system linked to that requested authorisation shall be stopped with immediate effect' and the linked personal data 'shall be deleted'. Also Art. 99(4)(e) (outside this part).
note: Context: investigation for targeted search of a person suspected or convicted of a criminal offence. Exception: initial identification of a potential suspect based on objective and verifiable facts. Each use limited to what is strictly necessary. No untargeted use without link to an offence, proceeding, threat or missing person. Member States may introduce more restrictive laws.

quote: The Commission may adopt, implementing acts establishing common specifications for the requirements set out in Section 2 of this Chapter
note: Conditions: standardisation request not accepted, not delivered on time, standards 'insufficiently address fundamental rights concerns', or non-compliant; and no reference published or expected. Conformity with common specifications gives presumption (41(3)); repealed when a harmonised standard is published (41(4)). Also coded Coordination/Design.

quote: The AI Office and the Board shall aim to ensure that the codes of practice cover at least the obligations provided for in Articles 53 and 55
holder: The AI Office and the Board
note: Issues: keeping documentation up to date, detail of training-content summary, identification of systemic risks, risk assessment and management measures. 56(4): codes set objectives, commitments and KPIs and account for interests of affected persons.

quote: The establishment of AI regulatory sandboxes shall aim to contribute to the following objectives:
note: Passive; nearest actors: Member States and competent authorities establishing sandboxes. Objectives: legal certainty; sharing best practices; innovation and an AI ecosystem; evidence-based regulatory learning; market access, esp. for SMEs. Points (b)-(e) fall on p. 89 (after line 4270) but belong to this passage.

quote: Testing in real-world conditions within the meaning of the AI Act26 is also not covered by that exclusion.
note: Scope: Art. 2(8) excludes research, testing and development before placing on the market (para 30) and Art. 2(6) excludes systems developed solely for scientific research (para 31), but not real-world testing nor systems later placed on the market. Example (para 32): a municipality testing facial recognition RBI in the streets at carnival with volunteers: 'the planned testing  must be  fully compliant with  the requirements for RBI systems in  the AI Act', unless in a sandbox or under Arts 60-61. Nearest named actor: the municipality in the example.

quote: The respect of the prohibitions in the AI Act are therefore not a sufficient condition for compliance with other Union legislation that remains applicable to providers and deployers of AI systems.
holder: Providers and deployers of AI systems
if_not_met: not stated (use may still be 'prohibited or unlawful based on other primary or secondary Union law')
note: Sets the applicable standards: other Union law (data protection, non-discrimination, consumer protection, employment, product safety) still applies. Para (50): the prohibitions and their exceptions 'may not be used to circumvent or as a justification to infringe obligations under other Union legislation'. Para (180): social scoring 'whether by public or by private parties' may also breach data protection law, including the rules on solely automated individual decision-making.

quote: provided that the system is not intended for, nor deployed in, sensitive contexts (e.g., health, education, elections) where serious harmful consequences are likely to occur
note: Passive; nearest actors: the provider (intended purpose) and deployers (deployment). Bears on the decision whether to deploy a generative AI system that may hallucinate in health, education or elections, including in public services [inference].

quote: AI -enabled subliminal techniques may be used in the psychological treatment of a mental disease or physical rehabilitation when carried out in accordance with the applicable law and medical standards, including obtaining the explicit consent
note: Exception for lawful medical treatment; the condition includes explicit consent 'of the individual or its legal representatives as a condition for use'. Nearest actors: treating health services [inference].

quote: If the analysed data spans a period of time and specific individuals are evaluated (such as migrants) for example to ascertain whether they are at risk of trying to abscond
holder: An authority for migration and asylum (example)
if_not_met: the prohibition 'may apply if all other conditions are fulfilled'
note: Hypothetical example, coded as design because it states what the prohibition covers, not what happened. Setting: 'a partly automated surveillance system at refugee camps' with cameras and motion sensors; this 'would qualify as ‘over a certain period of time’'. Para (155) also: the time condition should be 'assessed, taking all circumstances of the case into account to avoid circumvention of the scope of the prohibition' (holder not stated).

quote: National tax authorities use an AI predictive tool on all taxpayers’ tax returns in a country to select tax returns for closer inspection.
obligation: non-binding interpretation (illustrative example of a prohibited practice)
if_not_met: not stated in this passage; fines under para (55), for public authorities subject to Member State rules
note: Listed under 'Examples of detrimental or unfavourable treatment in  unrelated social contexts prohibited under Article 5(1)(c)(i)'. What makes it prohibited: the tool also uses 'unrelated data , such as taxpayers’ social habits or internet connections'. Hypothetical example coded as design (states what is prohibited).

quote: A social welfare agency uses an  AI system to estimate the probability of fraud by beneficiaries of household allowance s that relies on characteristics collected or inferred from social contexts with no apparent connection or relevance
obligation: non-binding interpretation (illustrative example of a prohibited practice)
if_not_met: not stated in this passage; fines under para (55), for public authorities subject to Member State rules
note: Unrelated characteristics named: 'having a spouse of a certain nationality or ethnic origin, having an internet connection, behaviour on social platforms , or performance at the workplace'. Footnote 122 refers to comparative literature on national benefit systems (report; not coded). The permitted counterpart is coded separately.

quote: A public labour agency uses an AI system to score unemployed individuals based on an interview and a n AI-based assessment for determining whether an individual should benefit from state support for employment .
obligation: non-binding interpretation (illustrative example of a prohibited practice)
if_not_met: not stated in this passage; fines under para (55), for public authorities subject to Member State rules
note: Prohibited because the score also uses variables 'collected or inferred from data and contexts with no apparent connection to the purpose  of evaluation, such as marital status, health data for chronic diseases, addiction'. Footnote 123 reports a similar Polish system abandoned as unconstitutional (report; not coded).

quote: A public agency uses an AI system to profile families for early detection of children at risk based on criteria such as parental mental health  and unemployment
obligation: non-binding interpretation (illustrative example of a prohibited practice)
if_not_met: not stated in this passage; fines under para (55), for public authorities subject to Member State rules
note: The example continues: the system also uses information on parents' social behaviour derived from multiple contexts; families are 'singled out for inspection' and children 'are taken from their families, including in cases of minor transgressions by the parents'. Listed as unjustified or disproportionate treatment prohibited under Art. 5(1)(c)(ii).

quote: A municipality use s an AI system to score trustworthiness  of residents  based on multiple data points related to their social behaviour in a variety of contexts.
obligation: non-binding interpretation (illustrative example of a prohibited practice)
if_not_met: not stated in this passage; fines under para (55), for public authorities subject to Member State rules
note: The score is used for 'blacklisting, i.e. withdrawal of public benefits, other serious punitive measures, and increased control or surveillance', based on minor misbehaviour (late library books, rubbish left out, late local taxes).

quote: A public authority uses an AI system  to control fraud in the student housing grant process that considers among the indicators the internet connections, family status or level of education  of beneficiaries
obligation: non-binding interpretation (illustrative example of a prohibited practice)
if_not_met: not stated in this passage; fines under para (55), for public authorities subject to Member State rules
note: These indicators 'do not seem relevant, nor justified'.

quote: A government introduces a comprehensive AI -based system that monitors and rates citizens based on their behaviour in various aspects of life
obligation: non-binding interpretation (illustrative example of a prohibited practice)
if_not_met: not stated in this passage; fines under para (55), for public authorities subject to Member State rules
note: People with a lower score face 'restricted access to public services' and other disadvantages; the system leads to excessive surveillance and penalties for minor infractions.

quote: Article 5(1)(c) AI Act prohibits unacceptable AI -enabled social scoring practices regardless of whether the AI system or the score are provided or used by public or private persons.
holder: Public or private persons providing or using the AI system or the score
if_not_met: not stated in this passage; fines under para (55)
note: The Guidelines add: 'scoring in the public sector may have very significant consequences for people due to an imbalance of power and a dependence on public services'.

quote: this score directly affects th ose persons (e.g. all employees in a company, students in a specific school whose behaviour has been evaluated), the practice may fall within the scope of Article 5(1) (c) AI Act
note: Scoring of legal entities is in principle excluded (e.g. effects on 'all citizens in a municipality in case of allocation of budget'), but aggregate scores built from individuals' behaviour that directly affect those individuals may be covered; case-by-case.

quote: Generally speaking, a delay is significant at least when the person is likely to have left the place where the biometric data was taken.
note: Line between prohibited real-time and permitted post-RBI. 'Without a significant delay' is not defined; 'it will have to be assessed on a case -by-case basis'. Para 312: a law enforcement authority that covertly photographs a person and submits it to a database 'for immediate search' 'may fall under the prohibition'.

quote: What constitutes an imminent threat to life or the physical safety of natural persons is ultimately defined and assessed at the level of the Member State based on its national laws, in accordance with EU law
obligation: statutory power bounded by EU law; non-binding interpretation
note: 'This will have to be laid down/referred to  in the laws Member States must adopt' to use the exception. For terrorist threats, the assessment of the threat 'is ma de at national level', but 'a genuine and present or genuine and foreseeable threat' is 'an autonomous notion of U nion law' to be assessed 'independently of national definitions' (para 345). A specific threat must be 'clearly defined , individualised and concrete' (para 342).

quote: to use real-time RBI for this purpose, the respective criminal offence must be punishable in the Member State concerned by a custodial sentence or a detention order for a maximum period of at least four years.
if_not_met: as for the Art. 5 prohibitions: fines under s. 2.9.2 (part 1) and interim injunctions in national courts (para 431)
note: Annex II gives an 'exhaustive list of serious crimes' (p. 109 [printed 104]); a suspect is a person for whom there are 'serious grounds' and 'sufficient evidence' already gathered (para 350); no European Arrest Warrant is required (para 353). Example (p. 132 [printed 127]): police live facial recognition for neighbourhood burglaries is 'not allowed to be deployed' even if targeted and limited in perimeter and time, because the offence is not listed in Annex II.

quote: subject to appropriate safeguards and conditions , as determined in national law and specified in the context of each individual urgent use case by the law enforc ement authority itself.
holder: the law enforcement authority (specifies safeguards for each urgent use); national law (determines safeguards and conditions)
obligation: statutory exception; its conditions use recital language ('should')
if_not_met: authorisation must be requested 'without undue delay' and within 24 hours (Art. 5(3)); if rejected, use ceases and data are deleted (para 402)
note: Urgency means it is 'effectively and objectively impossible to obtain an authorisation before commencing the use' (para 383, quoting Recital 35). Use 'should be restricted to the absolute minimum necessary'. The 24 hours run from when cameras are 'switched on' and the first comparison is made (para 400). Gives the deploying authority itself authority to set safeguards for the urgent use, pending authorisation.

quote: police authorities might be authoris ed by national law to perform retrospective facial recognition to compare images of criminal suspects with recorded facial images in a criminal database.
obligation: non-binding interpretation (scope); high-risk duties are statutory
note: Scope: outside Art. 5(1)(h) are biometric verification, retrospective (post) RBI, real-time use in private or online spaces, and use by private actors, including 'live facial recognition technology in schools for security purposes and school attendance'. These are high-risk (para 425); post-RBI for law enforcement is subject to 'additional conditions and safeguards' under Art. 26(10) from 2 August 2026 (para 427). Other uses 'must in any event comply with data protection rules' (para 428); the court and authority decisions cited there are reported cases (not coded). Example (pp. 132-133 [printed 127-128]): retrospective identification of a protest organiser 'is not prohibited by the AI Act' but is high-risk.

quote: any such other elements will have to be real, substantial and meaningful for them to be able to justify the conclusion that t he prohibition does not apply.
if_not_met: not stated (if the other elements are not real, substantial and meaningful, the prohibition applies)
note: Scope test against circumvention. Other situations 'will always need to be assess ed on a case-by-case basis'; 'the existence of certain pre -established objective and verifiable facts may  justify that conclusion'. Holder not stated: nearest actors are the providers and deployers who must judge whether their tool is prohibited, subject to market surveillance authorities and courts [inference].

quote: Such a system  will normally fall under the prohibition of Arti cle 5(1)(d) AI Act, since there is no reasonable suspicion of the involvement of a particular person in a criminal activity
if_not_met: as for the Art. 5 prohibitions: fines under s. 2.9.2 (part 1; up to EUR 35 000 000 or 7% of turnover; public-authority fines left to Member State rules; EU bodies up to EUR 1 500 000) and interim injunctions in national courts (para 431)
note: Hypothetical example, coded as design (the Commission's reading of scope), not practice. A tool reviewing all taxpayers' returns to predict criminal tax offences from traits 'such as double nationality, place of birth, number of children'; the Commission adds that it also falls within social scoring, Art. 5(1)(c). Same page: a law enforcement authority predicting terrorism 'solely based on individuals’ age, nationality, address, type of car, and marital status' 'may be assumed to be prohibited'; a police department's risk tool for children and adolescents: 'Such a system is also likely to fall under the prohibition'.

quote: In such a case, the individual crime risk assessments and predictions would also not be based solely on profiling or the assessment of personal characteristics and would therefore not be prohibited.
holder: law enforcement, judicial, prison/probation and customs authorities using AI to support human assessment (per the examples)
obligation: statutory exclusion; non-binding interpretation with examples
note: Scope exclusion with public-sector examples said to fall outside the prohibition: classification of suspicious crowd behaviour where 'there is a meaningful human assessment of th e AI classification'; police investigation of two suspects combining place-based and ANPR data; early-release risk assessment for prisoners; a judge using an AI risk tool at a pre-trial detention hearing; an officer assessing breach of non-custodial release conditions; customs risk assessment of goods 'subject to a human review'. Such systems are high-risk (para 204 entry).

quote: For offences that are not directly regulated by Union law , the national qualification of the offence is subject to scrutiny by CJEU since ‘criminal offence’ is a concept that has autonomous meaning within the EU law
note: Allocates authority over a scope boundary (criminal vs administrative offence). Footnote 143: 'it is for national courts to determine whether a non-criminal penalty may be regarded as ‘criminal’' using the Engel criteria. The Member States' classification 'is not conclusive' (para 218). Largely reports case law; coded because it says who settles the reach of the prohibition.

quote: existing facial databases built up prior to the entry into application of the prohibition, which are not further expanded through AI-enabled untargeted scraping, those databases and their use must comply with the applicable Union data protection rules.
obligation: non-binding interpretation (scope); the data protection duties are statutory
note: Scope: legacy databases not expanded by AI-enabled untargeted scraping fall outside the prohibition and are governed by data protection law. Also out of scope (paras 234-235): untargeted scraping of other biometric data such as voice; facial databases used for model training or testing where persons are not identified; systems generating images of fictitious persons (possibly Art. 50 transparency). Para 237: biometric identification itself 'is subject to specific rules in the AI Act'. Holder not stated.

quote: In light of the AI Act’s objective to ensure a high -level of fundamental rights protection, this  exception should be narrowly interpreted.
obligation: non-binding interpretation (narrow reading of a statutory exception)
if_not_met: not stated (uses outside the narrowed exception remain prohibited; fines as for Art. 5, s. 2.9.2)
note: Narrows reliance on the exception: 'therapeutic uses should be understood to mean uses of  CE-marked medical devices' (para 257); general wellbeing and stress monitoring is not covered, and a system to detect 'burnout or depression' 'would remain prohibited'; 'safety reasons' cover only 'the protection of  life and health', not property (para 258). Examples (p. 89 [printed 84]): assisting employees or students with autism falls within the exception; assessing wellbeing, motivation or satisfaction is prohibited.

quote: Providers must ensure their AI systems meet all relevant requirements before placing them on the market or putting them into service.
note: Verb: must ensure. Coded as Decision-making because the provider controls the pre-market gate (it can withhold placing on the market); the work of checking itself would be Delivery. Trigger: before placing on the market or putting into service; compares against 'all relevant requirements'; metric not stated. Providers outside the Union are covered if they place systems on the Union market or the output is used in the Union.
basis: AI pass B; different cell in pass A

quote: In the case of body -cams capable of RBI used by individual law enforcement agents, the untargeted filming during, for example , a demonstration with hundreds of participants will be considered to fulfil the condition of remoteness.
note: Brings officer body-cams within the prohibition's remoteness condition. Para 307: voice, gait and keystroke systems may also be RBI, though being an example 'does not imply that they are prohibited'.

quote: When a law enforcement authority covertly takes a picture of a person via a mobile device and submits it to a database for immediate search, depending on the circumstances, this may fall under the prohibition of Article 5(1)(h) AI Act.
note: Real-time condition. Para 310: 'without a significant delay' is assessed case by case; a delay is significant 'at least when the person is likely to have left the place'; a 'limited short delay' does not avoid the prohibition.

quote: prisons and border control are not publicly accessible spaces
note: Scope exclusions: online spaces; workplaces with entry control; prisons; border control. Para 316-317: a border crossing point is excluded but the street leading to it normally is not; airport common areas are publicly accessible, the border-control area is not. Para 314: offices of municipal civil servants may be non-public. Para 318: assessed case by case.

quote: The prohibition in Article 5(1)(h) AI Act applies to the use of RBI systems for  law enforcement purposes, irrespective of the entity, authority, or body carrying out the law enforcement activities.
holder: any entity, authority or body carrying out law enforcement activities
note: Law enforcement purposes include prevention and threats to public security (para 321). Para 322-323: covers public authorities and bodies entrusted by Member State law. Para 325: other bodies are covered only when entrusted with a specific law enforcement task.

quote: In both cases, the law enforcement authorities must instruct on all major aspects and supervise the other entity, as this requirement is inherent to the notion of acting ‘on behalf’ of a person.
obligation: mandatory ('must'); non-binding interpretation of a definition
note: Authority to direct and supervise delegated or requested entities. Also coded: Coordination/Design (delegation, para 324).

quote: Any other  use of  real-time RBI systems in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement purpose s which is not listed in Article 5(1)(h)(i)-(iii) AI Act is prohibited.
note: Exhaustive list of objectives. Examples given as prohibited: police real-time RBI to identify a shoplifter; a shopping mall entrusted by the police to find shoplifters (section 10.8, page 133); a stadium watchlist not linked to the event (page 131).

quote: the use of real-time RBI systems to search for that person would not be deemed to be for law enforcement purposes and  would therefore fall under the rules for such use under the GDPR.
note: Searches for a vulnerable missing person under an administrative procedure, with no suspicion of crime, fall outside the prohibition (GDPR applies instead). Para 334: Art. 5(1)(h)(i) only allows missing-person searches for law enforcement purposes.

quote: This will have to be laid down/referred to  in the laws Member States must adopt to make use of the exceptions to the prohibition on the use of real-time RBI for law enforcement purposes in publicly accessible spaces.
obligation: statutory duty for Member States that use the exception ('must adopt')
note: What counts as an imminent threat to life or physical safety is 'ultimately defined and assessed at the level of the Member State', in accordance with EU law. Para 341-343 give the Guidelines' reading of 'imminent', 'substantial' and 'specific'.

quote: the concept of ‘a genuine and present or genuine and foreseeable threat’, as used in Article 5(1)(h)(ii), is an autonomous notion of U nion law and should therefore be assessed, in principle, independently of national definitions.
note: Sets the standard against which national terrorist-threat assessments are read; national threat levels vary. Para 346: threshold drawn from CJEU data-retention and PNR case-law.

quote: ‘Authority’ over an AI system  should be understood as assuming responsibility over the decision to deploy the system and over the manner of its actual use.
holder: Deployers: natural or legal persons, public authorities, agencies or other bodies using AI systems under their authority
note: Locates authority over the decision to deploy, and over how the tool is used, with the deployer (for a public body, the body itself; see para 18). Personal non-professional use excluded (para 17, Art. 3(4)). Deployers are in scope if established in the Union or, if in a third country, the output is used in the Union.

quote: The police are not allowed to deploy real-time facial recognition technologies  in a broad, untargeted manner, i.e. in the hope of finding wanted criminal s and taking them off the streets.
note: Festival example. Offences must be in the Annex II list and punishable by a maximum of at least four years (para 351, 354); a European Arrest Warrant is not required (para 353). A targeted search for a named suspect believed to be present 'may be covered'.

quote: the deployment of a real-time RBI system in publicly accessible spaces  for law enforcement purposes  should only be authorized for targeted individuals.
obligation: statutory condition ('only to confirm the identity of the specifically targeted individual'); Guidelines' reading non-binding
note: Targeting condition. Para 358: use may only start to search for specific individuals the authorities have reason to believe are victims or involved in a listed scenario; for (ii) and (iii) the identity need not be known if a reference database of the group has been constituted.

quote: Third, the real-time use of RBI should be clearly limited in terms of geographic scope, duration, and the targeted person.
note: Limits on use. Para 365: geographic area based on 'objective and non -discriminatory factors', normally not a whole city or country; para 366: personal scope excludes untargeted identification; para 367: time limited to what is strictly necessary, extendable under applicable rules, never indefinite. Para 332 example: police searching for an abducted child 'must define a perimeter of deployment and duration of use'.

quote: The AI Act expressly excludes from its scope AI systems that are ‘placed on the market, put into service, or used with or without modification exclusively for military, defence or national security purposes
location: page 12 (printed p. 7), section 2.5.1, para (22); also paras (24), (26)
holder: Entities using AI exclusively for military, defence or national security purposes (any type of entity, including private operators entrusted by Member States)
note: Scope exemption. The exclusion depends on the purpose or use, not the entity. 'National security' does not cover road safety or the organisation or administration of justice (para 23). Para 24: a military or national-security system used for other purposes (civilian, humanitarian, law enforcement or public security) falls within scope (see Delivery/Design entry, para 24). Para 26: being in scope 'should not affect the ability of entities carrying out national security, defence and military activities to use that system' for those purposes; example: real-time RBI used by a national security agency to gather intelligence is excluded.

quote: ‘it is for the Member States to define their essential security interests and to adopt appropriate measures to ensure their internal and external security
obligation: Member State competence (case law), bounded by EU law
note: The document quotes the CJEU (Privacy International, C-623/17). The quotation continues: '[…] a national measure […] taken for the purpose of protecting national security cannot render EU law inapplicable and exempt the Member States from their obligation to comply with that law.' Sets who decides the reach of the national-security exclusion, and its limit.

quote: must be authorized by a judicial authority or an independent administrative authority prior to its use. This is the main principle.
holder: a judicial authority or an independent administrative authority whose decision is binding, of the Member State where the use takes place
if_not_met: use is prohibited; in urgency, if authorisation is rejected 'the use shall be stopped with immediate effect' and all data and outputs deleted (Art. 5(3) as quoted)
note: Prior authorisation of 'each use' (para 387), not of installation: police installing biometric-ready CCTV at a station need no authorisation, but need a FRIA before first use and authorisation before each use. Applies also when systems are operated by others on behalf of law enforcement, e.g. sport clubs or shopping malls (para 386).
