Art. 5(3): grant 'only where it is satisfied, on the basis of objective evidence or clear indications'. Check coded as Delivery/Design (para 380).

quote: the use of the AI system should be restricted to the absolute minimum necessary  and should be subject to appropriate safeguards and conditions , as determined in national law
holder: the law enforcement authority (urgent use); national law sets conditions
note: Urgency exception to prior authorisation; must be 'duly justified'. Urgency means it is 'effectively and objectively impossible' to obtain authorisation first. The safeguards are specified for each urgent case 'by the law enforc ement authority itself'. Authorisation must be requested within 24 hours (para 400).

quote: implying that the authorising authority needs to be independent from the authority using the RBI system.
note: Standard for who decides. Applies to the police and to investigative judges or prosecutors who supervise the police's use. Para 392: independence means acting 'completely freely', 'shielded from any instructions or pressure' (CJEU). Para 393: judicial authorities are in general independent. Para 390: the decision must be binding.

quote: if an authorisation request  in the case of urgency is rejected, the use of the real -time RBI system should be ceased with immediate effect.
note: Mandatory stop on refusal; 'Article 5(3) AI Act is explicit in this regard, without exception'. Deletion coded as Delivery/Design (para 402-404).

quote: even where the deployer of a real -time RBI system obtains an authorisation, no decision that produces an adverse legal effect on a  person may be taken based solely on the output of the ‘real-time’ RBI system.
holder: the deployer of a real-time RBI system
note: Bar on solely automated adverse decisions. Example: arrest and imprisonment solely on a facial-recognition match 'without any further checks'; checks could cover whether the person was elsewhere. This 'comes on top of' Art. 14 (next entries).

quote: National laws shall not exceed the limits set by Article 5(1)(h) AI Act and shall respect all further related conditions set forth in the AI Act.
note: Member States 'may not expand the objectives' beyond Art. 5(1)(h)(i)-(iii). Para 412: national law provides the legal basis.

quote: Member States may introduce, in accordance with Union law, more restrictive laws, i.e. laws with stricter requirements than those laid down in Article 5(1)(h) and (2) to (7) AI Act.
note: Power to tighten. Para 416 list: national law may narrow the objectives further.

quote: Each Member State that wishes to allow the use of the systems at issue must specify in its national laws such rules, which are aimed at providing relevant and complete information as to the use of real-time RBI systems to the authorising authority
obligation: statutory duty for Member States that choose to allow use
if_not_met: no legal basis, so use is prohibited (para 290, 326)
note: Rules on request, issuance and exercise of authorisations; Art. 5(5) also requires rules on supervision and reporting and on which objectives and offences are covered. Para 411: Member States 'remain free to decide whether to adopt such national laws'. The suggested contents of these laws (para 416 list, 'may regulate for example') are coded as separate entries.

quote: who are the competent authorities subject to Art icle 5(1)(h) AI Act  and the independent authorities in the M ember State competent for issuing (or refusing) an authorisation;
obligation: suggested content for national law ('may regulate for example'); non-binding
note: Appointing who uses and who decides. Other suggested items in the same list: detailed scope of objectives (possibly narrowed); written requests with detailed explanation; motivation and supporting evidence; description of technology and data-collection points; reference databases; retention; security; traceability; written procedure with hearing; grounds of refusal; decision deadlines; procedure for extending or modifying authorisations.

quote: the  designation of the authorising authority, which the Member State will have to establish before it can authorise the use of real-time RBI systems
if_not_met: the Member State cannot authorise use [inference: designation must come 'before it can authorise']
note: Appointing who decides. Para 417: Member States must establish at least one notifying and one market surveillance authority (Art. 70) and designate data protection authorities, or authorities meeting LED conditions, as market surveillance authorities for these purposes (Art. 74(8)).

quote: Whenever AI systems are used for such purposes, they wi ll fall within the scope of the AI Act.
holder: Police and other law enforcement authorities
obligation: statutory scope (as interpreted in non-binding guidelines)
note: Scope: AI used for prevention, detection, investigation and prosecution of criminal offences, execution of penalties, and safeguarding against threats to public security is within scope, as distinct from national security. The paragraph flags relevance to Art. 5(1)(d) (individual crime prediction) and 5(1)(h) (real-time RBI), coded in part 2.

quote: The activities of Europol and other Union security agencies, such as Frontex, fall within the scope of the AI Act.
holder: Europol, Frontex and other Union security agencies
note: Scope statement for EU agencies. Their market surveillance authority is the European Data Protection Supervisor (para 53).

quote: the AI Act does not apply to public authorities  in a third country or international organisations, where those authorities or organisations use AI systems in the framework of international cooperation or agreements for law enforcement and judicial cooperation
holder: Public authorities in third countries and international organisations (and private entities they entrust with specific tasks)
obligation: statutory scope exclusion, conditional on adequate safeguards
if_not_met: Exclusion does not apply where the framework lacks adequate safeguards for fundamental rights [inference from 'provided that' and 'for the exclusion to apply']
note: Scope exemption for law-enforcement and judicial cooperation with the Union or Member States, provided the third country or organisation 'provides adequate safeguards with respect to the protection of fundamental rights and freedoms of individuals'. Cross-ref Delivery/Design (assessment by market surveillance authorities), Accountability/Design (recipient authorities remain accountable) and Coordination/Design (alignment of agreements), all para 29.

quote: RBI systems that fall outside the  scope of the prohibition in Article 5(1)(h) AI Act include biometric verification/authentication systems and the retrospective use of (post-) RBI systems in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement purposes.
note: Also outside: real-time law enforcement RBI in private or online spaces; RBI by private actors, e.g. supermarkets, sports arenas, and 'live facial recognition technology in schools for security purposes and school attendance' (schools are listed among private actors; whether public schools are meant is not stated). Para 425: such uses are high-risk. Para 427: post-RBI also subject to Art. 26(10) from 2 August 2026. Para 428: other uses must comply with data protection rules (pointer; court cases given are practice, not coded).

quote: The application of real -time RBI however would be prohibited under the AI Act, in particular where it is the biometric system that decides upon the necessity to identify the persons for the purposes of law enforcement.
note: Example: police emotion screening of football fans that triggers real-time RBI automatically. The emotion screening itself 'is not prohibited' but is high-risk. Bears on who decides: the system must not decide on the need to identify. Other section 10.8 examples: stadium watchlist not linked to the event, prohibited; biometric-ready cameras installed is not prohibited but indiscriminate identification is; burglary suspect search, not allowed because the offence is not in Annex II.

quote: The prohibitions in that provision will apply in principle to all AI system regardless of whether they were placed on the market or put into service before or after that date.
note: Article 5 applies from 2 February 2025, with no grandfathering for systems already in use (fn 244). Covers legacy public-sector tools [inference].

quote: Those operators should therefore take necessary measures to ensure that they do not place on the market, put into service or use AI systems that could constitute prohibited practices under Article 5 AI Act.
holder: providers and deployers of AI systems
obligation: statutory duty ('fully applicable and mandatory'); 'should' for the measures
if_not_met: enforcement by affected parties in national courts, including interim injunctions (para 431); fines only from 2 August 2025 (para 430)
note: 'Ensure' coded as decision-making: operators control whether they place on the market or use. What the 'necessary measures' are is not stated.
basis: AI pass A; different cell in pass B

quote: During such a review, the Commission may decide to withdraw or amend these Guidelines.
note: Review trigger: 'as soon as this is necessary' in view of implementation experience, technological, societal and regulatory developments, market surveillance enforcement and CJEU interpretations.

quote: the AI Act does not apply ‘to any research, testing or development activity regarding AI systems or AI models prior to their being placed on the market or put into service’.
holder: Actors carrying out research, testing or development of AI systems or models before placing on the market (example names 'AI developers')
note: Scope exemption. Para 31: Art. 2(6) excludes AI 'specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development'. Para 32: the exclusion does not cover systems then placed on the market, and 'Testing in real-world conditions within the meaning of the AI Act is also not covered by that exclusion' (see Delivery/Design entry, para 32). Para 33 adds that all R&D 'should be carried out in accordance with recognised ethical and professional standards for scientific research' (not separately coded: pre-market research is outside the object).

quote: Any use by natural persons where they are acting on behalf or under the authority of a deployer acting in a professional capacity will also fall within the scope of the AI Act.
holder: Natural persons acting on behalf or under the authority of a deployer acting in a professional capacity
note: Scope: the Art. 2(10) exclusion covers only purely personal non-professional use; staff using AI under an organisation's authority (e.g. public officials [inference]) are within scope. Criminal activities 'cannot be considered purely personal activities'. Para 35: the exclusion covers only deployer obligations; the system remains in scope for providers and professional deployers.

quote: providers of AI systems cannot benefit from this exclusion if the AI system they place on the market or put into service constitutes a prohibited practice under Articles 5 AI Act.
holder: Providers of AI systems released under free and open-source licences
note: Scope: the open-source exclusion does not apply to high-risk systems, prohibited practices (Art. 5) or Art. 50 systems. Relevant to model providers in the value chain.

quote: If such systems involve unacceptable social scoring and fulfil the conditions of Article 5(1)(c) AI Act, their placing on the market, putting into service and use will be prohibited in the Union.
holder: Providers and deployers of AI systems that evaluate persons' entitlement to essential public assistance benefits and services
obligation: statutory duty (prohibition), as interpreted in non-binding guidelines
if_not_met: Fines under AI Act Art. 99 (para 55); for public authorities only if national rules provide
note: 'Such systems' = 'AI systems evaluating persons and determining if they are entitled to receive essential public assistance benefits and services, such as healthcare services and social security benefits that are classified as high-risk'. These are otherwise high-risk; the prohibition overrides where Art. 5(1)(c) conditions are met. Para 37 also: 'most AI systems that fall under an exception from a prohibition listed in Article 5 AI Act will qualify as high-risk'.

quote: Article 6(3) AI Act only results in an AI system being considered non-high-risk; it does not exclude  such AI system s from the scope of the AI Act and the prohibitions.
holder: Providers and deployers of Annex III systems considered not high-risk under Art. 6(3)
note: Scope: an Art. 6(3) derogation from high-risk status does not take a system out of the Art. 5 prohibitions.

quote: Deployers are thus expected not to use any AI system in a manner prohibited under Article 5 AI Act , including not to bypass any safety guardrails implemented by the providers of the system.
obligation: expected (statutory prohibition as interpreted in non-binding guidelines)
if_not_met: Fines under AI Act Art. 99 (para 55); for public authorities only if national rules provide
note: Constrains the deployer's decision on how a tool (including a general-purpose system) is used. Para 41 example: a general-purpose system that can infer emotions 'should not be used by deployers at the workplaces or in education institutions, unless an exception for medical or safety reasons applies'.

quote: providers also have a responsibility not to place on the market or put into service AI system s, including general-purpose AI systems,  that are reasonably likely to behave or be directly used in a manner prohibited
holder: Providers, including providers of general-purpose AI systems
obligation: statutory prohibition as interpreted in non-binding guidelines ('responsibility')
note: Constrains the provider's decision whether to place a system on the market. Fn 35: follows from the reference to placing on the market in all prohibitions except Art. 5(1)(h), which covers use only. Cross-ref Delivery/Design entry (safeguards, same paragraph).

quote: They are also expected to take appropriate measures if they become aware that  the system is misused for this specific prohibited purpose by specific deployers, for example, if such misuse is reported
holder: Providers of AI systems (example: general-purpose system with emotion recognition capability)
note: Coded as Decision-making because it implies provider authority to restrict or stop a specific deployer's use [inference]; the measures are not specified, so it could also be read as Delivery. Trigger: awareness of misuse, e.g. a report, or checks where 'the system is directly operated through a platform under the control of the provider'. No reporting channel is specified (to whom misuse is reported is not stated).

quote: the AI Act is not intended to provide the legal basis for the processing of personal data under Article  8 of Directive (EU) 2016/680.
holder: Competent law enforcement authorities (under Art. 3(7) LED) using biometric categorisation or real-time RBI
note: Bears on who authorises use: the AI Act does not itself authorise the processing; a legal basis must come from elsewhere (national law requirements for RBI exceptions are set out in section 10, part 2). Para 46 also: the AI Act 'applies as lex specialis to Article 10 LED' for biometric categorisation and real-time RBI for law enforcement, and 'the LED must also be complied with for any processing of personal data by competent law enforcement authorities'.

quote: Member States must designate their competent market surveillance authorities by 2 August 2025.
note: Appointing who enforces. Deadline: 2 August 2025.

quote: All market surveillance authorities should follow a Union safeguard procedure with a decision taken by the Commission48 determining whether the AI system  constitutes a prohibited practice.
holder: European Commission (decides); all market surveillance authorities (follow the procedure)
obligation: statutory power (Commission decision); MSAs 'should follow' the procedure
note: Authority to determine, in cross-border cases, whether a system is a prohibited practice rests with the Commission. Stated aim: uniform application 'so as to provide legal certainty to both providers and deployers'.

quote: Each Member State should lay down rules if and  to the extent that administrative fines may be imposed on public authorities and bodies established in that Member State  as providers and deplo yers of AI systems.
obligation: should (statutory discretion left to Member States)
note: Member States decide whether, and how far, their own public authorities can be fined for prohibited practices. Also coded as Accountability/Design (same passage, consequence for public authorities).

quote: Since violations of the prohibitions  in Article 5 AI Act interfere the most  with the freedoms of others and give rise to the highest fines , their scope should be interpreted narrowly.
note: Passive: addressed to whoever interprets and applies the prohibitions (nearest: market surveillance authorities, the Commission, providers and deployers). Sets how widely the standard reaches.

quote: the placing on the market, putting into service or use of an AI system that deploys subliminal techniques beyond a person’s consciousness or purposefully manipulative or deceptive techniques
location: page 23 (printed p. 18), section 3.2, Art. 5(1)(a) text; paras (60)-(62)
holder: Providers and deployers of AI systems
if_not_met: Fines up to EUR 35 000 000 or up to 7% of total worldwide annual turnover (para 55; Art. 99); for public authorities only if national rules provide; EU institutions up to EUR 1 500 000 (Art. 100)
note: Para 62: 'The prohibition, therefore, applies to both providers and deployers of AI systems, each within their respective responsibilities'. Four cumulative conditions (para 60): placing on market/putting into service/use; subliminal, purposefully manipulative or deceptive technique; objective or effect of materially distorting behaviour by appreciably impairing informed decision-making; causing or reasonably likely to cause significant harm; plus a plausible causal link (para 61). Intent is not required (paras 76, 83); covers systems that manipulate or deceive without any human intending it (paras 69, 73). Significant harm covers physical, psychological, financial and economic harm (para 86).

quote: the placing on the market, the putting into service or the use of an AI system that exploits any of the vulnerabilities of a natural person or a specific group of persons
location: page 36 (printed p. 31), section 3.3, Art. 5(1)(b) text; paras (98)-(100)
holder: Providers and deployers of AI systems
if_not_met: Fines up to EUR 35 000 000 or up to 7% of total worldwide annual turnover (para 55; Art. 99); for public authorities only if national rules provide; EU institutions up to EUR 1 500 000 (Art. 100)
note: Text continues: 'due to their age, disability or a specific social or economic situation, with the objective, or the effect, of materially distorting the behaviour ... in a manner that causes or is reasonably likely to cause that person or another person significant harm'. Four cumulative conditions and a plausible causal link (paras 98-99). Material distortion and significant harm interpreted as for Art. 5(1)(a) (paras 113-114). Vulnerable groups: children under 18 and older people (paras 104-106), persons with disabilities (paras 107-108), specific social or economic situation (para 109). Para 108: inaccessible design is not in itself exploitation.

quote: transient circumstances, such as temporary unemployment, over-indebtedness or migration status, may also be covered as a specific soci al or -economic situa tion.
holder: Providers and deployers of AI systems
note: Scope: 'specific' means a legal status or membership of a vulnerable social or economic group, e.g. persons in extreme poverty, ethnic or religious minorities (Recital 29); 'grievances or loneliness' are not covered. Para 112: migrants and refugees may be particularly susceptible. Bears on groups served by public employment, welfare and migration services [inference].

quote: Distinguishing manipulation from persuasion is crucial to delineate the scope of the prohibition in Article 5(1) (a) AI Act , which does not apply to lawful per suasion practices.
holder: Providers and deployers of AI systems
note: Scope exemption. Persuasion 'operates within the bounds of transparency and respect for individual autonomy' and 'explains the AI system’s objectives and functioning' (para 128); consent and awareness of the influence attempt (para 130); compliance with laws such as the GDPR makes lawful persuasion more likely (para 131). Para 133: advertising is not in itself manipulative.

quote: when carried out in accordance with the applicable law and medical standards, including obtaining the explicit consent of the individual or its legal representatives as a condition for use.
obligation: condition for use (explicit consent), non-binding interpretation (worked example)
if_not_met: Use outside these conditions is not covered by the carve-out [inference]
note: Carve-out from Arts. 5(1)(a)-(b) for AI-enabled subliminal techniques in psychological treatment or physical rehabilitation. Holder not named; nearest: those providing the treatment (health services, public or private [inference]). Coded as Decision-making because explicit consent is a gate on whether the tool may be used.

quote: the placing on the market, the putting into service or the use of AI systems for the evaluation or classification of natural persons or groups of persons over a certain period of time based on their social behaviour
location: page 53 (printed p. 48), section 4.2, Art. 5(1)(c) text; paras (146), (149)-(150), (170)
holder: Providers and deployers of AI systems, whether public or private persons
if_not_met: Fines up to EUR 35 000 000 or up to 7% of total worldwide annual turnover (para 55; Art. 99); for public authorities only if national rules provide; EU institutions up to EUR 1 500 000 (Art. 100)
note: Text continues: 'or known, inferred or predicted personal or personality characteristics', with the score leading to detrimental or unfavourable treatment (i) in unrelated social contexts and/or (ii) unjustified or disproportionate to the behaviour or its gravity. Three cumulative conditions (paras 149-150); applies to providers and deployers 'each within their respective responsibilities'. Para 146: 'broad scope of application in both public and private contexts'. Para 170: applies 'regardless of whether the AI system or the score are provided or used by public or private persons'; 'scoring in the public sector may have very significant consequences for people due to an imbalance of power and a dependence on public services'. Score may be a number, ranking or label (para 151); AI profiling may be covered (para 154).

quote: then this would qualify as ‘over a certain period of time’ and the prohibition in Article 5(1)(c) AI Act may apply if all other conditions are fulfilled.
holder: Authority for migration and asylum (example deployer)
note: Example: a migration and asylum authority runs a partly automated surveillance system at refugee camps and evaluates individuals over time, e.g. to ascertain whether they are at risk of absconding. The paragraph adds that 'it is important that this condition is assessed, taking all circumstances of the case into account to avoid circumvention of the scope of the prohibition'. Contrast para 177 (refugee-camp data for resettlement decisions out of scope).

quote: this AI-enabled social scoring practice will fall within the scope of the prohibition only if the AI-generated score plays a sufficiently important role in the final decision
holder: Public authority deploying an AI system whose output is combined with human assessment (example)
if_not_met: Prohibition applies where the condition is met (fines, para 55)
note: Human review does not automatically take a system out of scope: Art. 5(1)(c) 'does not require the evaluation or classification performed by the AI system to be the sole cause' and covers scoring 'combined with other human assessments', but 'the AI output must play a sufficiently important role in producing the social score'. Bears on human review and override of outputs. Metric for 'sufficiently important' not stated.

quote: A score may lead to detrimental or unfavourable treatment even if it is produced by an organisation(s) different from the one that uses the score .
holder: Organisations using a score produced by another organisation (example: public authority obtaining a creditworthiness score from a specialised company)
note: Scope covers scores bought in from third parties. Also relevant to Coordination (supply of scores between organisations) [inference].

quote: the detrimental or unfavourable treatment resulting from the score must take place in social context(s) unrelated to the contexts in which the data was originally generated or collected.
holder: Providers and deployers of AI scoring systems (examples: national tax authorities; social welfare agency; public labour agency)
note: Scenario 1. Data from unrelated contexts must be used 'without an apparent connection for the purpose of the evaluation or classification or in a manner that leads to generalised surveillance'; 'will require a case-by-case assessment'. Examples the document labels 'prohibited under Article 5(1)(c)(i)': national tax authorities using an AI tool on all tax returns that also uses 'taxpayers’ social habits or internet connections'; a social welfare agency estimating fraud by household allowance beneficiaries using a spouse's nationality or ethnic origin, internet connection, social platform behaviour or workplace performance; a public labour agency scoring the unemployed using marital status, chronic disease health data or addiction. Distinguished from lawful practices where law specifies relevant data (section 4.3). Cross-ref para 166 carve-out entry.

quote: data that is relevant for the allocation of the benefits and lawfully collected could be used to determine the risk of fraud , since public authorities pursue a legitimate aim in  verifying if social benefits are  correctly allocated.
note: Scope: what public bodies may do. Contrasts with the social welfare agency example in the same paragraph (Scenario 1 entry).

quote: A tax authorit y uses an AI system to detect child benefit fraud by profiling and assigning beneficiaries suspected of fraud to categories such as ‘deliberate intent/gross negligence’ using criteria such as low income, dual nationality, social behaviour
holder: Tax authority (example deployer); also public authority (student housing grant) and government (comprehensive rating system) in the same paragraph
obligation: non-binding interpretation (worked example of prohibited practice)
note: Both alternatives fulfilled at once. The example continues: files inspected, childcare benefit ceased, repayment demanded, families driven 'into severe financial hardship'; fn 124 points to the Dutch childcare benefits case and the SyRI judgment. Other examples in the paragraph: a public authority using internet connections, family status or education level as fraud indicators in a student housing grant process; a government system rating citizens' behaviour across life, restricting access to public services. Coded as design because the document presents these as prohibited cases, not as reports of practice.

quote: The prohibition under Article 5(1)(c) AI Act may also cover cases where awards or preferential treatment are given to certain individuals  or groups of persons , since this implies less favourable treatment of other individuals
holder: Providers and deployers of AI scoring systems used to grant awards or preferential treatment
note: Examples given: 'support employment programmes, (de-)prioritisation for housing or resettlement' — public-service allocation decisions [inference].

quote: The prohibition in Article 5(1)(c) AI Act only applies to the scoring of natural persons or groups of persons, thus excluding in principle scoring of legal entities
holder: Providers and deployers scoring legal entities
note: Scope exemption with a limit: if legal entities are scored on an aggregate of natural persons' behaviour or characteristics and 'this score directly affects those persons (e.g. all employees in a company, students in a specific school ...)', the prohibition may apply, case by case. Example of indirect impact outside scope: 'all citizens in a municipality in case of allocation of budget'.

quote: AI systems using data collected in refugee camps ( e.g., behavioural compliance) for decisions about resettlement or employment is not affected by the prohibition , given that this data is relevant for the purpose of assessment
holder: Deployers using refugee-camp data for resettlement or employment decisions (migration authorities [inference])
note: Condition: 'provided that the procedures under applicable Union migration law are fulfilled to ensure the treatment is justified and proportionate'. Contrast para 155 (absconding-risk surveillance example) and para 169 (resettlement prioritisation may be covered).

quote: AI-evaluation and scoring of individuals by police and other law enforcement authorities that collect data about individuals’ social behaviour from multiple contexts are out of scope of Article 5(1)(c) AI Act where those data are relevant
holder: Police and other law enforcement authorities
note: Conditions: data relevant 'for the specific purposes of the prevention, detection, prosecution and punishment of criminal offences, and where the detrimental treatment is justified and proportionate in accordance with substantive and procedural Union and national criminal and police law'. Points to Art. 5(1)(d), which imposes additional conditions on individual crime risk prediction (section 5, part 2).

quote: The prohibition, therefore, applies to both providers and deployers of AI systems, each within their respective responsibilities not to place on the market, put into service , or use such AI systems  for this specific purpose.
obligation: statutory duty (prohibition); the Guidelines' reading is non-binding interpretation
if_not_met: not stated in this passage (penalties apply from 2 August 2025, para 430)
note: Prohibition on individual crime-risk assessment based solely on profiling or personality traits. Verb in the Act: 'shall be prohibited'. Coded as decision-making because it removes the decision to place on the market or use. Exclusion: AI supporting a human assessment already based on objective and verifiable facts (para 185, 203). Line breaks in quotes are rendered as single spaces throughout.

quote: These Guidelines will be regularly reviewed in light of the experience gained from the practical implementation of Article 5 AI Act and technological and market developments.
note: Passive: reviewer not named; nearest named actor is the European Commission (author). Coded as Decision-making because revising the guidance resets the official interpretation. Trigger: experience from practical implementation, technological and market developments; frequency 'regularly', not specified. Section 12 'Review and update of the Commission guidelines' falls in part 2. The same paragraph reports that the drafting was informed by a stakeholder consultation and that Member States in the AI Board and the European Parliament were consulted (report of process, not coded).

quote: Article 5 AI Act prohibits the placing on the EU market, putting into service, or use of certain AI systems for manipulative, exploitative , social control or surveillance practices
location: page 7 (printed p. 2), section 2, para (8); overview table para (9)
holder: Providers and deployers of AI systems
obligation: statutory duty (prohibition); applies from 2 February 2025 (para 3); restated in non-binding guidelines
if_not_met: Fines up to EUR 35 000 000 or up to 7% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher (para 55; AI Act Art. 99); for public authorities and bodies only if and to the extent national rules provide (para 55); EU institutions, bodies and agencies up to EUR 1 500 000 (para 55; AI Act Art. 100)
note: General prohibition set by the EU legislature. Coded as Decision-making because it removes the provider's and deployer's discretion over whether such a tool may be placed on the market, put into service or used [inference]. Holder taken from para 15 (Guidelines focus on providers and deployers) and paras 62/150 (prohibitions apply to both 'each within their respective responsibilities'). The overview table (para 9) lists Art. 5(1)(a)-(h); (a), (b) and (c) are coded separately from their body text in this part; the body sections for (d)-(h) fall in part 2. Para 11: the Art. 5(1)(h) real-time RBI prohibition 'only applies to their use'. Para 14: 'use' is to include any misuse, reasonably foreseeable or not. Cross-ref Accountability entries on penalties (para 55).

quote: it will be classified as a high-risk AI system (as referred to in Annex III, point 6(d), AI Act) if intended to be used by law enforcement authorities or on their behalf
holder: law enforcement authorities or those acting on their behalf (users of the excluded systems)
note: Scope routing: crime-risk tools that fall in the exclusion are not prohibited but enter the high-risk regime (also stated at para 185, which adds Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies supporting law enforcement, and 'must comply with all relevant requirements and obligations under the AI Act'). Restates the AI Act. See the human-oversight entries from the same paragraph (Delivery/Design, Delivery/Resources, Decision-making/Design, Decision-making/Resources).

quote: Those persons should also intervene in order to avoid negative consequences or risks, or stop the use of the AI system if it does not perform as intended.
obligation: recommended ('should'); non-binding interpretation of a statutory duty
note: Authority to override and to stop use, held by the human overseer. Trigger: risk of negative consequences, or the system not performing as intended. Also coded: Delivery/Design and Resources entries for para 204.

quote: the prohibition may be assumed to apply, in particula r, when private actors are entrusted by law to exercise public authority and public powers
holder: private actors entrusted by law to exercise public authority for crime prevention, or acting on behalf of law enforcement authorities
obligation: statutory duty (prohibition); scope reading is non-binding interpretation ('may be assumed')
note: Value-chain / contractor duty. Example: a private company supplying AI crime-analytics software asked by a law enforcement authority to predict human-trafficking offenders 'could be prohibited'. Para 209 extends to private entities under a legal obligation to assess crime risk (e.g. anti-money laundering); para 210-211 exclude private entities profiling for their own ordinary business.

quote: In principle, such policing does not involve an assessment of a specific individual . They therefore fall outside the scope of the prohibition.
note: Scope exclusion for location-based, geospatial or place-based crime prediction. Examples given: area crime-likelihood scores to deploy patrols; customs predicting narcotics locations from trafficking routes; police gunshot detection. Holder unnamed; scope is set by the Act and read by the Commission. See next entry for the limit (para 213).

quote: To the extent that an AI system  carries out location -based predictive policing and then considers the risk score of the location as an aspect in the profiling of a person , that system should be considered person -based
note: Limit on the location-based exclusion: once a location score feeds the profiling of a person (e.g. place of residence in a high-crime area), the system is person-based and 'in principle covered', though it may fall outside on other grounds (page 75 example).

quote: Such systems are out of scope of the prohibition because any prediction of a likelihood of a natural person to be involved in an import or export of illicit goods is not solely based on profiling
note: Worked examples of public-sector tools outside the prohibition because they support human assessment based on objective facts: crowd-behaviour classification with 'a meaningful human assessment'; police armed-robbery investigation; prisoner early-release risk tool; judge's pre-trial detention tool; probation officer's breach-risk tool; customs risk tool 'subject to a human review'. Hypothetical classifications, not reports of practice.

quote: The prohibition in Article 5(1)(d) AI Act applies only to individual predictions and risk assessments of natural persons, thus typically excluding crime predictive systems that profile legal entities such as companies or non-governmental organisations.
note: Scope exclusion. Examples: a tax or customs authority assessing companies' fraud risk; customs tools for instructions to legal entities. Para 216: the prohibition may apply where a natural person acts through a legal entity as a sole trader or independent professional.

quote: The prohibition in Article 5(1)(d) AI Act applies only for the prediction of criminal offences, thus excluding administrative offences from its scope
note: Example in the same para: a public authority using AI in an administrative investigation of minor offences or irregularities in tax, procurement or expenditure processes is outside the prohibition. Para 218: whether an offence is criminal is an autonomous EU-law concept subject to CJEU scrutiny; national classification is not conclusive (Engel criteria, fn 143).

quote: The prohibition, therefore, applies to both providers and deployers of AI systems, each within their respective responsibilities, not to place on  the market, put into service or use such AI systems.
obligation: statutory duty (prohibition); the Guidelines' reading is non-binding interpretation
if_not_met: not stated in this passage (penalties apply from 2 August 2025, para 430)
note: Prohibition on AI systems that create or expand facial recognition databases through untargeted scraping from the internet or CCTV. Applies only to tools placed on the market or put into service 'for this specific purpose' of untargeted scraping. Para 236: pre-existing databases not further expanded this way must comply with Union data protection rules (pointer to other law, not coded separately).

quote: If a scraping tool is instructed to collect  images or video containing human faces only of specific individuals or a pre-defined group of persons, then the scraping becomes targeted
note: Scope exclusion for targeted scraping, e.g. 'to find one specific criminal  or to identify a group of victims'; para 230 example of crawlers collecting images of trafficking victims posted by traffickers. Para 233: reverse image search on a received picture is targeted scraping. Limited by the anti-circumvention entry (para 230-231).

quote: Untargeted scraping should be interpreted in a manner that does not allow circumvention of the prohibition.
note: Anti-circumvention rule: building a database step by step, selecting specific groups each time, 'should fall within the prohibition' where the end result is functionally the same as untargeted scraping; para 231: where targeted and untargeted searches are combined, the untargeted scraping is prohibited.

quote: The prohibition, therefore, applies to both providers and deployers of AI systems, each within their respective responsibilities, not to place on the market, put into service or use such AI  systems.
obligation: statutory duty (prohibition); the Guidelines' reading is non-binding interpretation
if_not_met: not stated in this passage (penalties apply from 2 August 2025, para 430)
note: Prohibition on AI systems inferring emotions in the workplace and education institutions, except for medical or safety reasons. Limited to inferences from biometric data (para 245, 250); text-based sentiment analysis is out of scope (para 251). Public employers and public institutions are covered [inference from para 254-255, which draw no public/private line for workplaces and expressly include public education institutions].

quote: The notion of ‘workplace’ in Article 5(1)(f) AI Act should also be understood to apply to candidates during the selection and hiring process
note: Scope: 'workplace' read broadly, independent of employee/contractor/trainee/volunteer status, including recruitment. Examples given as prohibited: emotion tracking of call-centre staff, of hybrid-team calls, during recruitment and during the probationary period.

quote: If only deployed for personal training purposes, emotion recognition systems are allowed if the results are not shared with HR responsible persons and cannot impact the assessment, promotion etc. of the person trained
if_not_met: the use falls back within the prohibition [inference: 'provided that  the prohibition is not circumvented']
note: Condition limiting who may see outputs and what they may affect. Parallel condition for education (para 255): role-play training of actors or teachers is allowed 'if the results cannot impact the evaluation or certification of the person being trained'.

quote: The reference to education institutions is broad and should be understood to include both public and private institutions.
note: Covers all levels, vocational and continuous training, online and blended settings, and candidates during admission. Examples given as prohibited: an institution requiring students to use an emotion-recognition language app; exam proctoring that detects anxiety; inferring interest or attention; use in admissibility tests; use on teachers and students. Gaze tracking alone is not emotion recognition.

quote: therapeutic uses should be understood to mean uses of  CE-marked medical devices.
obligation: non-binding interpretation (narrow reading of an exception)
if_not_met: use outside the exception remains prohibited ('would remain prohibited', para 257)
note: Exception 'should be narrowly interpreted' (para 256). General wellbeing and workplace stress monitoring are not covered; burnout or depression detection 'would remain prohibited' (para 257). 'Safety' means protection of life and health only, not property against theft or fraud (para 258).

quote: any use for medical and safety reasons sh ould always remain limited to what is strictly necessary and proportionate, including limits in time, personal application and scale, and should be accompanied by sufficient safeguards.
note: Limits on the scope of a permitted use (time, persons, scale). Related checks coded as Delivery/Design (necessity assessment; expert opinion) and Delivery/Resources (expert opinion).

quote: Employers and educators should only deploy emotion recognition systems for medical and safety reasons in case of an explicit need.
note: Decision whether to deploy. Purpose limitation in the same para: 'Data collected and processed in this context may not be used for any other purpose'; the page 89 example adds that an employer 'may not use the data for other purposes, such as assessing the employee’s work performance'. Footnote 167 (worker consultation) coded as Coordination/Design.

quote: Emotion recognition systems that classify as high-risk systems pursuant to Article 6(2) and Annex III(1)(c) AI Act  will need to comply with the high -risk requirements in Chapter III Section 2 AI Act and the transparency obligation of Article 50(3) AI Act.
note: Scope routing: permitted emotion recognition enters the high-risk and transparency regimes (also para 239, 266). Restates the AI Act. Para 266: such systems may still be prohibited under Art. 5(1)(a)-(b) or other Union law.

quote: the Union or Member States may keep or introduce ‘laws, regulations or administrative provisions which are more favourable to workers in terms of protecting their rights in respect of the use of AI systems by employers’.
note: Power to set stricter worker-protection rules. Same para: collective bargaining agreements more favourable to workers 'may also be allowed or encouraged'. Example: Member States may bar emotion recognition at work even for medical purposes.

quote: a public authority develops a scoring system  in-house and deploys it to predict the risk of fraud of household allowance beneficiaries, thereby putting it into service.
holder: Public authority (developing and deploying an AI system in-house)
note: Scope: in-house development and deployment by a public authority counts as 'putting into service', so such tools fall within Art. 5. Para 16: the provider 'could also be a public authority that develops the system in -house and puts it into service for its own use'; para 19: an operator that develops and uses its own system is both provider and deployer. Illustrative example; coded as design because it states how the rule applies to public authorities, not what any authority has done.

quote: Also out of scope are systems that are used in the medical field for example care robots, or medical practitioners using emotion recognition systems during an examination at their workplace, and voice monitors that analyse emergency calls.
note: Scope exclusions relevant to public services (emergency calls, medical care). Para 267-268: crowd-control systems for public order and event safety normally fall outside, since they do not infer emotions of a specific person or are not used in the workplace or education. Limits coded in the two para 270 entries.

quote: The prohibition, therefore, applies to both providers and deployers of AI systems, each within their respective responsibilities, not to place on the market, put into service or use such AI systems.
obligation: statutory duty (prohibition); the Guidelines' reading is non-binding interpretation
if_not_met: not stated in this passage (penalties apply from 2 August 2025, para 430)
note: Prohibition on biometric categorisation of individuals to infer race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation. Systems not prohibited are high-risk (para 287, Annex III point 1(b)).

quote: Article 5(1)(g) AI Act also provides that the prohibition in that provision does not apply to the l abelling or filtering of lawfully acquired datasets  in the area of law enforcement
note: Scope exception. Example: a law enforcement authority labelling and filtering a dataset suspected of containing child sexual abuse material, by gender, age, eye and hair colour, scars, or abusers' hand features, 'is permitted'. Para 285: labelling by protected characteristics may be needed for data quality to prevent discrimination (Arts. 10 and 17 cited).

quote: In accordance with Article 5(5) AI Act, Member States are free to decide whether and in which of the three situations the use of real-time RBI systems in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement purposes is permitted  in their territory.
note: Member States decide whether any exception is available nationally. Para 326: Art. 5(1)(h)(i)-(iii) is not itself a legal basis; only domestic law meeting Art. 5(2)-(7) can allow use. See the Member-State national-law entries (para 411-418).

quote: In the absence of national legislation allowing and regulating such use, law enforcement authorities and entities acting on their behalf may not deploy such systems  for law enforcement purposes.
holder: law enforcement authorities; entities acting on their behalf
if_not_met: such use is prohibited as from 2 February 2025 (para 326)
note: National legislation complying with the AI Act is 'a pre-requisite of such use'. Repeated at para 326.

quote: Article 5(1)(h) AI Act  only prohibits the use of real -time RBI systems in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement purposes, so that only deployers of such systems are concerned by that provision.
holder: deployers (law enforcement authorities and entities acting on their behalf)
obligation: statutory duty (prohibition, subject to exhaustive exceptions)
if_not_met: not stated in this passage (penalties apply from 2 August 2025, para 430)
note: Prohibition on real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement. Placing on the market and other RBI uses are not prohibited but are high-risk (Art. 6(2), Annex III point 1(a)); authorised uses also fall under the high-risk rules. Exceptions only under Art. 5(1)(h)(i)-(iii) with Art. 5(2)-(7) safeguards (para 289).

quote: Such non-real-time use is not prohibited, but subject to additional safeguards for the deployment of high-risk AI systems (Article 26(10) AI Act).
note: Scope routing for retrospective RBI by law enforcement. Para 427: Art. 26(10) applies from 2 August 2026. Safeguards are not described in this document.

quote: AI systems that are intended to be used for biometric verification fall outside the scope of the prohibition in Article 5(1)(h) AI Act
note: Example: comparing a traveller's face at an e-gate with the passport image. Para 305-306: identity confirmation for access to a service, device or premises is not 'remote'; active involvement requires stepping consciously in front of a camera; being informed of cameras is not enough.

quote: All manipulative, deceptive and exploitative AI applications that are not reasonably likely to cause significant harms are in principle outside the scope of the prohibitions without prejudice to other Union law that still applies
holder: Providers and deployers of AI systems
note: Scope exemption. Examples include an engaging companionship system without other manipulative practices, a therapeutic chatbot using subliminal techniques to help users quit smoking, music recommendations by emotion, and manipulative techniques 'used in security training and other learning simulations that mimic phishing attempts' (relevant to public bodies' staff training [inference]).

quote: the person or group of persons must be  treated less favourably compared to other s without necessarily requiring a particular harm or damage  (for example, in the case of scoring practices where people are singled out for additional inspections
holder: Providers and deployers of AI scoring systems
note: Definition of 'unfavourable treatment': being singled out for additional inspections in fraud cases can suffice (relevant to public fraud-detection tools [inference]). 'Detrimental' treatment requires harm. Discrimination is not a necessary condition; Art. 5(1)(c) 'could therefore cover unfair treatment beyond EU non-discrimination law'.

quote: where an AI scoring system may be prohibited  is if the treatment resulting from the score  is unjustified or disproportionate to the gravity of the social behaviour.
holder: Providers and deployers of AI scoring systems (examples: public agency profiling families; municipality scoring residents)
note: Scenario 2. Examples the document labels 'prohibited under Article 5(1)(c) ii)': a public agency profiling families for early detection of children at risk using parents' social behaviour from multiple contexts, leading to inspection and removal of children for minor transgressions; a municipality scoring residents' trustworthiness, with low scores used for 'withdrawal of public benefits, other serious punitive measures, and increased control or surveillance'. 'The treatment may also be ‘unjustified’, such as lacking a legitimate aim.' Cross-ref Delivery/Design entry (case-by-case proportionality assessment, same paragraph).

quote: the scoring of natural persons is not at all times prohibited, but only in the limited cases where all of the conditions of Article 5(1)(c) AI Act  are cumulatively fulfilled
holder: Providers and deployers of AI systems evaluating natural persons
note: Legitimate practices named include 'fraud prevention and detection, law enforcement', service quality and claims handling; 'not per se prohibited, if lawful and undertaken in line with the AI Act and other applicable Union law and national law'. Para 176 conditions: lawful, specific purpose, data from the related context, treatment justified and proportionate. Para 177: compliance with sectoral law specifying relevant data 'may thus ensure' the practice is out of scope; example includes health data collected to diagnose patients. Cross-ref entries for refugee-camp and police examples (para 177).

quote: not allow automation strategies to be driven by untested assumptions or utopian beliefs about technology potential
obligation: recommended ('It is therefore important'), non-binding; state-of-play section
note: Full sentence opens: 'It is therefore important to be realistic about what benefits (and risks) a particular technology will deliver in a given context'. A condition on decisions about automation. Nearest actors: governments and public administrations. No test or evidence threshold specified.

quote: any use of machine technology by governm ent must therefore be considered from an administrative law perspective, including ethical and human rights perspectives
location: page 13 (printed p. 11), Section 1.4 'The unique role of the public sector'
note: Verb 'must ... be considered'. Introductory framing: any government use of machine technology is to be judged against administrative law, ethics and human rights. Coded Decision-making because it conditions whether and how government may use the tool [inference]. See also the Accountability/Design entry at Rec 1.1 (administrative-law control). Trigger: any use; criteria: administrative law, ethical and human rights perspectives; metric: not stated.
basis: AI pass B; different cell in pass A

quote: A focus must be put on the proportionality between benefits and risks while taking ethics into full account.
note: Criterion for decisions on using AI: proportionality between benefits and risks, with ethics taken into account. Holder not stated; nearest actor: the public sector using AI. [inference] Decision-making because it governs whether and how AI is used.

quote: regulation through checklists of technologies and systems is not enough, and would need to be complemented with assessment tools and models taking into account both, technologies and the different framework conditions for their specif ic use
note: About how AI regulation is designed: checklists should be complemented with assessment tools and models that take context into account. Holder not stated; nearest: regulators and policymakers. Could also be read as Delivery/Resources (assessment tools).
basis: AI pass A; different cell in pass B

quote: In sensitive areas where fundamental human rights may be at stake, such a delegation from human to AI -enabled solutions would have to come with necessary precautions, rules and regulations,
note: Trigger: delegating decisions from humans to AI in sensitive areas where fundamental rights are at stake. Requires precautions, rules and regulations 'in order to avoid a potentially deeper systematisation and perpetuation of existing biases'. Footnote 23 points to the Commission White Paper on AI (2020). Holder not stated; nearest: public administrations that delegate decisions.

quote: It is therefore important to be realistic about what benefits (and risks) a particular technology will deliver in a given context, and not allow automation strategies to be driven by untested assumptions or utopian beliefs
note: Applies to decisions on automation strategies: benefits and risks should be assessed realistically in context, not assumed. Holder not stated; nearest: public bodies setting automation strategies.

quote: Private partners may assist by making solutions available, but it is not in thei r mandate to decide how AI will fit the overall aims and goals of the public organisation.
holder: public organisation; Private partners (excluded from deciding)
note: Says where authority lies: private partners supply solutions but do not decide how AI fits the public organisation's aims. Preceding sentence: 'public organisations need to include AI within their strategies and work practices.' Context: description of national strategies led by the private sector.

quote: The use of AI in the public sector must be safe, lawful, trustworthy and effective.
location: page 27 (printed p. 25), Section 3.2, Area of Intervention 1
note: Framing standard for Intervention Area 1. It is followed by: actions 'are to ensure that ... mitigation measures are identified so that risks related to AI applied in the public sector are minimised'. No check, holder or trigger is specified. Similar wording in Rec 1.1 (p. 30): AI applied by the public sector 'should always take in the highest possible consideration basic principles aimed at respecting human rights'.

quote: effective regulation must be in place that can unleash the potential of AI, while mitigating its risks and removing barriers.
obligation: recommended ('must be in place', in a non-binding handbook)
note: Holder not stated; nearest: legislators and regulators at EU and national levels. Rationale given: designing, developing and using AI imply ethical and socio-economic risks, 'especially when applied by the public sector'.

quote: to develop fair, non-discriminatory and transparent AI-enabled public services, focus should be put primarily on the use of AI, rather than on the specific technology and its components.
note: Sets the scope of regulation and governance: the use of AI, not the technology. Repeated in the executive summary and Annex 1; the body text is quoted. Holder not stated; nearest: regulators and policymakers.

quote: Existing regulations at the EU level should act as springboard for alignment at the national  level
note: Continues: 'these would need to be contextualised and enriched by the experience of their concrete implementation in specific contexts in order to allow for further improvements without over-regulating.' Holder not stated; nearest: national regulators and Member States. Also has a Coordination element (alignment across levels).

quote: Efforts should therefore be concentrated on streamlining and making sense out of the vast portfolio of existing relevant regulations, rather than developing additional ones.
note: Prefers streamlining existing instruments to writing new ones. Instruments named on p. 31: HLEG Ethics Guidelines, GDPR, UNESCO recommendation, the proposed AI Act. Holder not stated. The p. 30 mention of the GDPR Art. 22(1) limit on automated decision-making reports existing law and is not coded separately.

quote: when planning, piloting or using AI-enabled technologies, public administrations should make sure that ethical, legal and administrative principles identified at the EU level are followed
note: 'Ensure'-type duty; the document does not say whether administrations approve/stop or do the checks themselves. Coded Decision-making because the duty attaches to planning, piloting or using, which the administration controls [inference]. Trigger: planning, piloting, use. Compared against: EU ethical, legal and administrative principles and 'related digital principles'. Metric: not stated. The five factors that follow are coded separately. Cf. section 2.1.4: 'It is of the utmost importance that AI -enabled solutions are applied ... in full compliance and alignment with European values'.
basis: AI pass B; different cell in pass A

quote: the identification of criteria for the application and use of AI in compliance with EU principles and values, in addition to those used for the assessment of enabling underlying technologies
obligation: recommended ('fundamental factors to be taken into account')
note: Setting criteria is standard-setting. Holder not stated; nearest: public administrations (preceding sentence). Annex 1 wording: 'The identification of criteria for EU-compliant applications and use of AI'.

quote: Government strategies should envisage the adoption of such approaches especially at the local level
note: Governments set co-creation as a direction in their strategies. Cross-reference: the Coordination/Design co-creation entry. The text adds: 'Citizen involvement might not always be desirable or feasible, depending on the stage of development'.

quote: Establish at the EU level common criteria for the  testing of AI, following relevant standardisation activities and guidelines.52
note: Standard-setting for testing AI. Footnote 52 cites ISO/IEC TR 29119-11, Guidelines on the testing of AI-based systems, from an international standards body, as an example. Annex 1 adds 'following recent standardisation activities and guidelines on how to assess and test AI'. Holder not stated; nearest: EU institutions.

quote: Include scalability as a formal precondition  to benefit from EU funding pro grammes foreseeing AI-related activities.
if_not_met: not stated explicitly; as a 'formal precondition to benefit from EU funding programmes', a project not meeting it would not receive that funding [inference]
note: A funding eligibility condition set by whoever runs EU funding programmes; not named, nearest: EU institutions. [scope doubt] Concerns adoption and scaling rather than assurance.

quote: Reward the use of instruments that would enhance innovation replicability and scalability  through spreading and scaling approaches  at the early stages of solution development
note: A funding criterion. Examples: innovation procurement schemes and reusable solutions. Holder not stated. [scope doubt] Concerns adoption and scaling.

quote: Develop and align procurement guidelines at the EU level , providing directions and criteria for developing national guidelines in compliance with EU principles and regulations.
note: EU-level guidelines set criteria for national procurement guidelines (standard-setting). Context: AI procurement raises 'compliance with GDPR, ethical principles, and human -centricity aspects'. Also a supplier-contract (Coordination) matter. Holder not stated.
basis: AI pass B; different cell in pass A

quote: Promote a catalyst role of AI for environmental sustainability  to allow other examples of beneficial use of AI in different application areas.
note: Sets a direction: using AI for environmental sustainability. [scope doubt] Promotes adoption.

quote: Public administrations should play a leading role in ensuring that, while promoting AI -based solutions to enable public sector environmental policies, the use of AI withi n their organisations does not lead to environmental damage.
note: 'Ensure'-type duty: coded Decision-making because the administration controls AI use in its organisation [inference]. No mechanism or check named (could be Delivery).
basis: AI pass B; different cell in pass A

quote: Sustainable AI  is promoted as a mandatory prerequisite in AI strategies  of public administrations and governments, both at the international and national levels, including in public procurement frameworks
holder: public administrations and governments (international and national levels)
obligation: recommended ('it is recommended that'); content: make sustainable AI a 'mandatory prerequisite' in strategies
note: Strategy-setting. Extends to public procurement frameworks (a Coordination element), 'in compliance with EU values and environmental sustainability principles'.

quote: Citizen participation and pro -active involvement in public deliberation, is especially important when there is a need to establish if and when to deploy AI
note: Continues: 'not only to address environmental issues, but also in any decision to be taken by public administrations involving the use of AI-based technologies.' Bears on the decision whether and when to deploy AI. Also a Coordination element (citizen participation).

quote: after proper assessment, based on deep knowledge of the issue at stake and fundamental data and information gathered through public consultation and participation, it would be more appropriate and/or environmentally sound to choose alternative paths, rather than AI-based solutions.
note: Recognises that, after an assessment informed by public consultation, choosing not to use AI may be the better option. This amounts to authority to decline AI. Trigger: before deployment [inference]. Holder not stated; nearest: public administrations.

quote: Any AI project should be selected on the basis of clear pre -requisites and implemented taking into account and incorporating these sets of values at early phases.
location: page 46 (printed p. 44), Section 4 'Perspective timing for interventions'
holder: not stated (preceding sentence: 'all relevant stakeholders (see Annex 1)')
note: AI projects are to be selected against 'clear pre-requisites', which are not specified, and values 'such as inclusiveness, trustworthiness and transparency'. Trigger: project selection and early phases.

quote: Umbrella AI frameworks should link impac t assessment indicators to internationally recognised value-based principles,  especially regarding ethics and a trustworthy use of AI
holder: not stated (developers of umbrella AI frameworks)
note: Standard-setting for impact assessment frameworks. It defines what assessments compare against: EU, OECD and UNESCO principles. The frameworks should also 'take into account emerging impact assessment frameworks', for example the AI Impact Assessment of the ECP Platform for the Information Society in the Netherlands (non-state; a mention; footnote 90).

quote: When deciding whether to impose an administrative fine and when deciding on the amount of the administrative fine in each individual case, the competent authorities should assess all relevant circumstances of the specific situation
note: Factors: 'nature, gravity and duration of the infringement and of its consequences', negligent or intentional character, aggravating or mitigating circumstances, 'the degree of cooperation with market surveillance authorities'.

quote: During such a review, the Commission may decide to withdraw or amend these Guidelines.
obligation: power of the Commission over its own non-binding guidance
note: Verb: may decide. The Commission sets the interpretive standard; the guidelines call themselves 'a first interpretation with practical examples'. Review triggers: practical experience in implementation, technological, societal and regulatory developments, market surveillance enforcement actions and CJEU interpretations (para (155)). Consultation on the review coded as Coordination/Design.

quote: Testing in real world conditions  (inside or outside of AI regulatory sandboxes)  is not covered by that exclusion.
note: Scope of the research and development exclusions (paras 21-22). Systems put into service or outputs used for purposes other than sole scientific research must comply (para 21). [inference] Bears on public-sector pilots run in real conditions.
basis: AI pass A; different cell in pass B

quote: providers and deployers of open- source AI systems within the scope of Article 50 AI Act still need to ensure compliance with their respective transparency obligations.
holder: Providers and deployers of open-source AI systems
note: Scope: open-source licensing does not exempt Art. 50 systems. Providers of free and open-source components that are not themselves AI systems are outside Art. 50 (para 24).

quote: Cases of products and services blending AI-generated responses with human -curated content fall within the scope of Article 50(1) AI Act and require disclosure for the specific outputs in the interaction that are AI -generated
note: Scope and human review: disclosure is not needed where AI outputs 'have been properly reviewed and sent by humans as the main interlocutors' (same para), and the 'mere possibility for humans to intervene or review' must not be used to circumvent disclosure (page 12-13). Indirect use is excluded, e.g. 'if customer service representatives use AI assistance tools to help them communicate with natural persons' (page 12). [inference] Bears directly on public officials using AI assistants to answer citizens. Nearest named actor: providers.

quote: The exception should be interpreted restrictively given that it deprives natural persons from the protection and the right to be informed
note: Scope of the obviousness exception. Obvious (no disclosure needed), page 18: 'An internal employee-facing assistant for properly trained staff who is AI literate and aware that they are using AI systems for internal organisational purposes (e.g. HR, legal, procurement, compliance or IT support)'; professional code assistants; tools for trained health professionals. Not obvious, page 19: 'AI chatbots embedded in online platforms or assistance support tools (helpdesks)'. [inference] Internal public-body assistants may be exempt; citizen-facing helpdesks not.

quote: The law authorising the use of the AI system must clearly specify the purposes and circumstances of permitted use and provide for appropriate safeguards to protect the rights and freedoms of third parties.
holder: not stated (the law-maker: Union law or Member States' national law)
obligation: non-binding interpretation of a statutory exception
note: Law-enforcement exception. Para 48: it 'may also cover interactive (or generative) AI systems used by other Union or national public authorities' authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute crime. Specific AI systems need not be named in law. The same reasoning is applied to Art. 50(2)-(4) (paras 93, 109, 125, 139).

quote: There may also be limited cases of “industrial AI applications” or “business to business applications” (excluding public and consumer -facing AI systems )
note: Exemption from marking and detection only if all three conditions hold: strictly technical output (including 'internal documentation processes'); perceived only by a limited pre-defined number of professionals within provider and deployer; not intended to be shared outside, with safeguards (e.g. cloud isolation, role-based controls). Public-facing systems are excluded. Related narrow cases: less robust metadata for closed in-product environments (para 86); ephemeral real-time content with in-experience disclosure (para 88).

quote: Editing goes beyond standard editing  if the content is changed in a  material way (substantive modifications, structural changes etc.)  that affect its meaning, style  or intent.
obligation: non-binding interpretation of a statutory exception
note: Scope of the standard-editing and non-substantial-alteration exceptions (paras 90-92); 'requires a case-specific assessment' (para 91). Exempt examples include grammar correction, 'AI-generated translations of text' and 'Transcriptions of conversations'. Marking required for 'AI-generated summaries of text ; paraphrasing or rewriting text that changes style, structure and meaning' (page 30). [inference] Relevant to public-sector summarisation and drafting tools.

quote: Article 50(3) AI Act makes such use possible when permitted under the legal rules governing the  powers of law enforcement authorities to use emotion recognition and biometric categorisation systems
obligation: non-binding interpretation of a statutory exception
note: Exemption: unlike the other Art. 50 exceptions, no explicit authorising law is needed; it suffices that the legal rules on law-enforcement powers permit non-transparent use, 'subject to appropriate safeguards'.

quote: When the deep fake combines multiple characters (e.g. informative and creative), the informati ve character should always prevail and require compliance with the standard labelling requirements.
note: Scope of the lighter regime for evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous works (paras 119-123), to be 'interpre ted strictly'; content that is 'exclusively informative or commercial' such as news reporting is excluded. [inference] Public-body communications would usually be informative.

quote: These Guidelines are non -binding. Any authoritative interpretation of the AI Act may ultimately only be given by the Court of Justice of the European Union (‘CJEU’).
holder: Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU)
note: Final authority over interpretation rests with the CJEU; the Commission's reading is non-binding. Bears on the level of obligation of every entry in this document.

quote: texts should be considered to address public interest matters  if they  cover topics on politics  and democratic processes , public administration and services, the administration of justice and law enforcement
note: Scope: public administration and services are named as matters of public interest. Published = accessible to 'an indeterminate, fairly large number of unrelated, potential readers' (para 131(i)); short texts not communicating knowledge, opinions or facts are out (para 131(ii)).
basis: AI pass A; different cell in pass B

quote: Editorial control refers to the control exercised in practice by a responsible editorial entity (e.g. an editor-in-chief) over the content having the authority to approve, alter or reject the substance of the text
obligation: condition for relying on an exception (non-binding interpretation)
note: Authority to approve, alter or reject AI-generated text before publication. Also linked to the human review entry (Delivery) and editorial responsibility (Accountability, para 138). 35 words.

quote: an AI -generated police warning regarding a terrorist threat published on social media
holder: Deployers whose use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences
obligation: non-binding interpretation of a statutory exception
note: Example of the law-enforcement exception for AI-generated public-interest text without human review; same exception for deep fakes (para 125). Points 46-48 apply (see the Art. 50(1) law-enforcement entry).

quote: If a code of practice is not deemed adequate pursuant to Article  50(7) AI  Act, the Commission may adopt an implementing act specifying common rules for the implementation of the obligations of Article 50(2), (4) and (5) AI Act
note: Standard-setting power; the implementing act would apply 'to all relevant providers and deployers'. 39 words.

quote: Those authorities can take enforcement actions in relation to the obligations listed in  Article 50 AI Act on their own initiative or following a complaint
holder: Market surveillance authorities; the AI Office; the European Data Protection Supervisor
note: Authority to act against non-compliant systems; specific measures not listed here (powers 'laid down in those regulation s'). Also coded as Accountability/Design.

quote: According to Article 113 AI Act, Article 50 AI Act will apply as from 2 August 2026.
note: Timing. All in-scope systems must comply on that date regardless of placement date. The AI Omnibus gives providers of generative systems placed before 2 August 2026 until 2 December 2026 for Art. 50(2) marking only; interactive disclosure applies from 2 August 2026 (page 51). Footnote 50: the high-risk grandfathering rule does not cover Art. 50.

quote: The Commission will review these Guidelines as soon as  necessary in view of practical experience gained in the implementation of the transparency obligations
obligation: statement of intent ('will'); power to withdraw or amend ('may')
note: Trigger: as necessary, including enforcement experience and CJEU interpretations. 'the Commission may decide to withdraw or amend these Guidelines.' Also coded as Coordination/Design (consultation).

quote: a company or another organisation (e.g. a public authority) that has developed an interactive AI system (e.g. chatbot)  in-house and puts it into service in the Union for its own use
note: Scope: brings a public body's own in-house AI tools within the provider duties of Art. 50(1) and (2). Para 10 defines providers as 'natural or legal persons, public authorities, agencies or other bodies'; para 12 defines deployers the same way. A company that modifies another provider's system and puts it into service under its own name 'becomes a provider of the new system' (page 7).
basis: AI pass A; different cell in pass B

quote: The ‘authority’ over an AI system should be understood as assuming responsibility over the decision to deploy the system and over the manner of the actual use of the system (including its outputs).
holder: Deployers (natural or legal persons, public authorities, agencies or other bodies using AI systems under their authority)
note: Defines who holds deployment decisions. Technical control is not required 'so long as the deployer takes the decision for what purposes and how to use the AI system (including in decentralised workflows and group corporate structures)'. A firm that merely commissions an agency without controlling its AI use 'is not a deployer' (page 8).

quote: Any use by natural persons acting on behalf or under the authority of a deployer acting in a professional capacity will fall within the scope of the professional deployer’s transparency obligations
note: Scope: the personal non-professional exclusion does not cover individuals acting for a professional deployer; their use counts toward that deployer's Art. 50(3) and (4) duties. [inference] Covers public officials using AI at work. Nearest named actor: the professional deployer.
basis: AI pass A; different cell in pass B

quote: c ompliance with the transparency obligations under Article 50 AI Act for a particular AI system  cannot be interpreted as indicating that the use of that AI system or its output is lawful under the AI Act.
note: Scope: Art. 50 compliance does not authorise use; systems may also be prohibited (Art. 5) or high-risk (Art. 6). Footnote 14: deployers of high-risk systems that make or assist decisions must also inform persons under Art. 26(11); notices may be combined. Quote keeps the extraction error 'c ompliance'.

quote: The Guidelines will be formally adopted by the Commission at a later date, when all language versions are available. It is only from that moment that these Guidelines will be applicable.
obligation: statutory power (Commission adopts guidelines); the guidelines themselves are non-binding
note: Status: C(2026) 5054 approves the content of the draft guidelines (20.7.2026); formal adoption is announced for later and is not recorded in this document. Annex para 3 repeats the Art. 96(1)(d) basis.

quote: A clear set of rules should be defined to assess the scalability or production of such initiatives.
note: Rules for moving pilots and proofs of concept (e.g. 'chabots', sic) into production. Who defines them: not stated; nearest named actor: Parliament's administration.

quote: AI solutions and services to be used to support the work of Members must aim solely at enhancing their capabilities in fulfilling their mandate.
note: Scope limit on AI used for Members. Nearest named actor: Parliament's administration.

quote: AI solutions and services developed or acquired by the administration shall aim at supporting innovation as well as at improving the efficiency of services and processes
note: Scope/purpose limit on the administration's AI, covering both in-house and procured tools.

quote: They set out the key principles, to which the administration should adhere when building its AI readiness and managing the AI operating model.
note: 'They' = the Strategic Orientations for the use of AI in Parliament (paras 7-14). Sets direction for the administration.
