quote: As a rule, coordinated containment of AI will be required to ensure it remains under human control.
location: page 3, II. Compliance and control, para 12
obligation: requirement in internal framework ('will be required', 'as a rule')
note: Human control over AI (authority to contain/override). 'As a rule' implies exceptions, which are not stated. Who exercises control: not stated.

quote: The AI governance framework must therefore include the relevant aspects of data governance that are being developed at Parliament.
location: page 3, II. Compliance and control, para 14
note: Sets the scope of the framework to include data governance, which the text says is still 'being developed'.
basis: AI pass A; different cell in pass B

quote: A dedicated governance framework shall ensure that priority is given to develop an AI capability that responds to Parliament's requirements and strategic orientations.
note: Priority-setting assigned to 'a governance framework', not an actor. Nearest named actor: the Governance Board (para 16).

quote: a dedicated governance framework is proposed, providing for a Governance Board, an AI Centre of Competence, an AI roadmap and an Inter-DG network of AI business partners.
note: Creates the governance structure. Next sentence: the framework 'shall ensure consistency in the treatment of AI initiatives, with clear accountability and transparency'. Status: proposal awaiting Bureau approval (para 26).

quote: The Governance Board shall ensure that the validation process for the AI solutions proposed is in place.
obligation: requirement in internal framework ('shall'); proposal awaiting Bureau approval
note: Validation gate for AI solutions. The Board must ensure the process exists; the document does not say the Board itself approves, pauses or stops individual solutions, nor who runs the validation. See also paras 24-25 (content of validation).

quote: It shall approve the AI roadmap as well as ensure a transversal involvement of the administration's services and end users.
obligation: requirement in internal framework ('shall'); proposal awaiting Bureau approval
note: 'It' = the Governance Board. Approval of the roadmap (priorities, direction). The involvement element is also coded as Coordination/Design.

quote: The Secretary-General shall appoint the Chair of the Board.
note: Appointing who decides.

quote: An AI roadmap should be established by the ICT services of the administration in cooperation with the Inter-DG network to support the development of Parliament's AI capability.
location: page 4, III. Implementation tools, AI Roadmap, para 19
holder: ICT services of the administration, in cooperation with the Inter-DG network
note: Drafting of priorities; approval rests with the Governance Board (para 16). 'In cooperation with the Inter-DG network' is a coordination element. Content (paras 19-20): key capabilities, AI projects, regular assessment of long-term safety and risks, technical readiness, assessment process, end-user engagement.
basis: AI pass A; different cell in pass B

quote: Non-compliance with the assessment process should lead to the suspension of the AI project.
location: page 4, III. Risk and impact assessment processes, para 25
note: Suspension of a project (pausing a tool). The document does not say who decides on suspension; nearest named actor: the Governance Board (para 16). Also coded as Accountability/Design.

quote: The assessment frameworks should be regularly reviewed to include new elements in line with the evolution of the technology and the auditing methods.
location: page 4, III. Risk and impact assessment processes, para 25
note: Updating the assessment standard. Trigger: regular (interval not stated). Who reviews: not stated.
basis: AI pass A; different cell in pass B

quote: The members of the Bureau are invited to: - approve the governance framework for AI in the Parliament, as outlined in this note.
location: page 5, IV. Decision, para 26 (same request on page 1, Summary)
note: Approval gate for the framework. Status: proposal; Bureau approval is not recorded (a redacted block follows para 26). The note says the WG ICT 'endorsed the governance framework' on 22 February 2024 (page 1; para 5).

quote: the focus of the guidelines is to address the fourth category: legal and ethical challenges and risks.
note: Sets the scope of the guidelines. The other three categories (cultural readiness, technology readiness, competency) are left as 'a matter for work on individual projects' (same paragraph). Nearest named actor: Parliament's administration / individual projects.

quote: This should not preclude, however, the possibility to investigate AI technologies in order to build expertise and awareness of the risks, including AI-enabled cyber-threats, such as deep fakes.
note: Exemption-like carve-out from the lifecycle compliance requirement for exploratory investigation. EDGE CASE: partly concerns AI used by others against the body (AI-enabled cyber-threats, deep fakes). Nearest named actor: Parliament's administration.
basis: AI pass A; different cell in pass B

quote: AI systems should not limit or condition the democratic process, freedom of expression, or the possibility to refuse AI services.
location: page 5, III. Ethical and Lawful Artificial Intelligence, Rationale
note: Standard. 'the possibility to refuse AI services' is close to a user opt-out, which could also be read as Accountability, but no route, addressee or consequence is stated. Nearest named actor: Parliament's administration.

quote: AI systems must not threaten the dignity, integrity, liberty, privacy, safety and security of human beings in society and at work.
location: page 5, III. Ethical and Lawful Artificial Intelligence, Rationale
note: Standard limiting what AI may be used for; phrased about AI systems, not an actor. No check, trigger or metric stated. Nearest named actor: Parliament's administration.
basis: AI pass A; different cell in pass B

quote: AI systems considered for use in Parliament must comply with Regulation (EU) 2018/1725
location: page 6, III. Secure and privacy compliant Artificial Intelligence, Rationale
note: [inference] Works as a condition on which AI systems may be used. The same sentence says the Regulation requires transparency about collection, use and storage of data and user controls over how their data is used. Nearest named actor: Parliament's administration.
basis: AI pass A; different cell in pass B

quote: Establish a charter for responsible data handling by IT providers using or developing AI solutions.
location: page 6, Secure and privacy compliant Artificial Intelligence, Requirements
note: Standard-setting for IT providers (whoever sets the standard is decision-making). Also coded as Coordination/Design. Nearest named actor: Parliament's administration.

quote: The Members of the Working Group are invited to: -Endorse the Guidelines for the responsible use of Artificial Intelligence in the European Parliament.
location: page 7, IV. Conclusion (same request on page 1, Summary, where the body is called 'Working Party')
holder: Members of the Bureau Working Party (Working Group) on ICT Innovation Strategy
note: Approval gate for the guidelines themselves. Status: proposal put for endorsement; endorsement is not recorded in this document. Author: Director-General (acting), DG Innovation and Technological Support.

quote: is also the notifying authority for the application of the single application and unified assessment procedure referred to in paragraph 8, unless the Member State designates another notifying authority for this Regulation.
location: Art. 1(14), inserting AI Act Art. 28(9); p. 21
obligation: statutory default rule; Member State power to designate otherwise
note: Appointing who decides on designation of conformity assessment bodies. Default: the notifying authority designated under Annex I Section A legislation.

quote: The Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts in accordance with Article 97 in order to amend Annex XIV, in light of technical progress, advances in knowledge or new scientific evidence
location: Art. 1(16), replacing AI Act Art. 30(2); p. 21
note: Sets scope categories for designation of notified bodies (adding, withdrawing or moving codes, categories or types). Annex XIV(1): 'Only conformity assessment bodies that have been designated in accordance with this Regulation may carry out conformity assessments and only for the activities related to the types of AI systems concerned.' Subject to Art. 97 controls (Accountability entry).

quote: The Commission shall request, in accordance with Regulation (EU) No 1025/2012 of the European Parliament and of the Council (*) and without undue delay, the European standardisation organisations to develop standardisation deliverables, including, as appropriate, harmonised standards
location: Art. 1(17), adding to AI Act Art. 40(2); p. 21
note: Standardisation mandate (standard-setting). Purpose: joint compliance and presumption of conformity with Chapter III Sections 2-3 and Annex I legislation. No duty on the standardisation organisations stated here. Recital 21: deliverables 'should help reduce legal uncertainty, avoid unnecessary duplication of conformity assessment activities, testing, documentation and reporting obligations'.

quote: such systems shall be deemed to comply with the cybersecurity requirements set out in Article 15 of this Regulation.
location: Art. 1(18), inserting AI Act Art. 42(3); p. 22
note: Sets which standard satisfies the Art. 15 cybersecurity requirement: high-risk AI systems within the Cyber Resilience Act (Reg. 2024/2847) meeting its Art. 12(1) conditions. Set by the Regulation itself; nearest named actors: providers/manufacturers. Could also be read as the comparator of a Delivery check.
basis: AI pass A; different cell in pass B

quote: The Commission, taking utmost account of the opinion of the Board, shall assess whether adherence to those codes of practice is adequate to ensure compliance with the obligations laid down in paragraphs 2 and 4 of this Article
location: Art. 1(20), replacing AI Act Art. 50(7); p. 22
holder: European Commission (taking utmost account of the Board's opinion)
note: Commission decides adequacy of codes of practice on marking and labelling AI-generated content (Art. 50(2) providers' marking; 50(4) deployers' disclosure). Recital 41: such codes 'have limited legal effect, and in particular do not grant a presumption of conformity'. The approval-by-implementing-act empowerment is removed. Cross-ref Delivery/Resources (Art. 50(7) codes).
basis: AI pass B; different cell in pass A

quote: If it deems the code of practice to be inadequate, the Commission may adopt an implementing act specifying common rules for the implementation of those obligations
location: Art. 1(20), replacing AI Act Art. 50(7); p. 22
obligation: statutory duty to assess; statutory power to adopt implementing act
if_not_met: if a code is inadequate the Commission 'may adopt an implementing act specifying common rules'
note: Codes of practice on 'detection, marking and labelling of artificially generated or manipulated content' (obligations in Art. 50(2) and (4), not restated here). Commission assesses adequacy 'taking utmost account of the opinion of the Board', per Art. 56(6) procedure, examination procedure Art. 98(2). Recital 41: codes 'do not grant a presumption of conformity'; implementing-act approval of codes removed. Cross-ref Resources/Delivery (Commission encourages codes) and Resources/Decision-making (Board opinion).

quote: The Commission, taking utmost account of the opinion of the Board, shall assess whether the codes of practice cover the obligations provided for in Articles 53 and 55
location: Art. 1(21), replacing AI Act Art. 56(6); p. 23
note: Approval-type decision on codes for general-purpose AI model providers (model providers sit inside public-sector tools). Recital 41: 'Providers should be able to rely, pursuant to Article 53(4) and Article 54(2) ... on codes of practice assessed as adequate pursuant to Article 56(6)'; the implementing-act approval route is removed.

quote: pursuant to a specific sandbox plan agreed between the providers or prospective providers and the competent authorities, ensuring that appropriate safeguards are in place.
location: Art. 1(22)(d), replacing AI Act Art. 57(5); p. 23
holder: Competent authorities; providers or prospective providers
note: Participation conditional on an agreed plan [inference: authority can withhold agreement]. 'Where applicable, the sandbox plan shall incorporate the real-world testing plan referred to in Articles 60 and 60a.' Sandboxes are 'for a limited time before their being placed on the market or put into service'.
basis: AI pass A; different cell in pass B

quote: the Commission shall adopt implementing acts specifying the detailed arrangements for the establishment, development, implementation, operation, governance, and supervision of the AI regulatory sandboxes.
location: Art. 1(23), amending AI Act Art. 58(1); p. 24
note: Standard-setting for sandboxes 'to avoid fragmentation'. New point (d): 'detailed rules applicable to the governance of AI regulatory sandboxes ... including as regards the involvement of and supervision by the competent data protection authorities, where relevant, and the coordination and cooperation at national and Union level.'

quote: Member States that choose to allow testing as referred to in paragraph 1 shall, individually or jointly, adopt frameworks for real-world testing.
location: Art. 1(25), inserting AI Act Art. 60a(2); p. 25
obligation: statutory power to allow; statutory duty to adopt frameworks if allowed
note: Decides whether real-world testing is allowed for AI-enabled products under Annex I Section B legislation, 'with a view to assessing and verifying the conformity of those systems with the requirements laid down in Articles 8 to 15' (Art. 60a(1)). Cross-ref Coordination/Design (notify Commission) and Decision-making/Design (testing plan).

quote: include the provision of a mandatory real-world testing plan to be agreed between the provider or prospective provider and the national competent authority or relevant authority
location: Art. 1(25), inserting AI Act Art. 60a(5)(a); p. 25
holder: Member States (frameworks); national competent authority or relevant authority; provider or prospective provider
obligation: mandatory approval gate (agreed testing plan), via Member State frameworks
note: Frameworks must also (b) ensure compliance with Art. 60(2), (3), (4)(d)-(j) and (5)-(9), reading market surveillance authority as the national competent or relevant authority; (d) 'ensure a high level of protection of health safety and fundamental rights'. Cross-ref Accountability/Design Art. 60a(5)(c).
basis: AI pass A; different cell in pass B

quote: the Commission shall adopt delegated acts in accordance with Article 97 in order to supplement this Regulation by specifying the high-risk AI systems concerned
location: Art. 1(3), inserting AI Act Art. 2(13); p. 16
note: Verb: shall adopt. Scope and exemptions: requirements in Art. 9-15 and 17-25 for Art. 6(1) high-risk systems 'may be limited' where Annex I Section A legislation gives equivalent or higher protection and the overall level of protection is not reduced. Commission specifies systems, requirements, conditions and scope of limitation. Delegated act subject to EP/Council objection (see Accountability/Design entry on Art. 97).

quote: The AI Office shall be exclusively competent for the supervision and enforcement of the obligations under this Regulation in relation to the following AI systems:
location: Art. 1(31)(b), replacing AI Act Art. 75(1); pp. 26-27
note: Appointing who supervises and decides. (a) AI systems based on general-purpose AI models where model and system are by the same provider or same undertaking, except Annex I products, Annex III point 2, 'AI systems provided by law enforcement authorities, border management authorities and financial institutions, insofar as those AI systems fall under Article 74(6)', and Annex III point 8 administration of justice; (b) AI systems that are or are integrated into very large online platforms or search engines. Applies to providers; to deployers 'only when they are also the provider or form part of the same undertaking'. Recital 31: other deployers remain under national supervision; systems of Union institutions stay with the EDPS (Art. 74(9)). [inference] Public bodies deploying such systems are supervised nationally.

quote: Before taking a decision that would have the effect of prohibiting or restricting the AI system being made available or put into service on a national market, or a decision to withdraw or recall the AI system
location: Art. 1(31)(c), inserting AI Act Art. 75(1d); p. 27
obligation: statutory power with mandatory prior notification
note: Authority to stop, restrict, withdraw or recall a tool within Art. 75(1). Also coded Coordination/Design (prior notification and consultation).

quote: If a notified body to which the Commission has delegated tasks under this paragraph does not perform those tasks adequately, the Commission may withdraw the delegation with immediate effect.
location: Art. 1(31)(c), inserting AI Act Art. 75(1e); p. 27
obligation: statutory duty to entrust; statutory power to withdraw
if_not_met: for notified bodies not performing adequately: 'the Commission may withdraw the delegation with immediate effect'
note: 'The Commission shall entrust the performance of those tests or assessments to notified bodies designated in accordance with this Regulation, in which case the notified body shall act on behalf of the Commission.' Appointing and removing who carries out checks.
basis: AI pass A; different cell in pass B

quote: the AI Office shall, where relevant, order the operator concerned to take the necessary measures to ensure compliance with the relevant provisions of this Regulation within a reasonable period specified therein
location: Art. 1(32), inserting AI Act Art. 75c(3); p. 31
note: Authority to direct corrective action by a provider or same-undertaking deployer. Corrective actions under Art. 16 Reg. 2019/1020 are enforceable by penalty payments (75c(5)(e)); their content is not restated here.

quote: referred to in Article 113, only if, as from that date, those systems are subject to significant changes in their designs.
location: Art. 1(39)(a), replacing AI Act Art. 111(2); p. 35
note: Scope exemption: high-risk systems already on the market before Chapter III applies are covered only after significant design change. Recital 39: applies per type and model; 'Any significant change to the design of that AI system ... should trigger the obligation of the provider to fully comply'. Nearest named actor: provider. Exception for public-authority systems: see Delivery/Design entry (2 August 2030).

quote: (i) 2 December 2027 as regards AI systems classified as high-risk pursuant to Article 6(2) and Annex III; and
location: Art. 1(40)(b), replacing AI Act Art. 113(c); p. 35
note: Chapter III Sections 1-3 apply from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) and 2 August 2028 (Annex I); new Art. 5 prohibitions from 2 December 2026; Art. 102-110 from 27 July 2026. Set by EP and Council as legislator. Recital 40: delay due to late standards and late establishment of national competent authorities.

quote: the placing on the market, the putting into service or the use of an AI system that generates or manipulates realistic images, videos, audio or similar material of an identifiable natural person’s intimate parts
location: Art. 1(7)(a), inserting AI Act Art. 5(1)(ba); p. 18
holder: Providers (placing on the market, putting into service); deployers (use)
if_not_met: not stated in operative text; recital 15 refers to penalties 'which may be laid down pursuant to Article 99(1)' and notes prohibitions 'do not preclude prosecution' under other law
note: Decides whether a tool may be placed on the market or used (prohibited practice), without the person's explicit consent. Point (bb) prohibits systems generating child sexual abuse material 'except where a “without right” defence applies under national law' (separate entry). Art. 5(1a): providers caught only where intended purpose, or foreseeable and reproducible outcome without reasonable and adequate safeguards; deployers only where they use the system 'for the purpose of generating or manipulating such material'. Art. 5(1b): manipulation not increasing exposure is excluded. Recital 16: without prejudice to national remedies for individuals. Also coded Delivery/Design (provider safeguards).

quote: except where a “without right” defence applies under national law
location: Art. 1(7)(a), inserting AI Act Art. 5(1)(bb); p. 18; recital 13, p. 6
obligation: statutory exemption (defence defined by national law)
note: Exemption from the child sexual abuse material prohibition. Recital 13: covers 'the legitimate generation, or manipulation of child sexual abuse material by the authorities in order to conduct criminal proceedings or to prevent, detect or investigate crime' and red-teaming to assess compliance. Nearest named actors: 'the authorities' (law enforcement, public authority: Member State) and national law. Public-sector use carve-out.

quote: AI systems that are solely used for non-safety related aspects of user assistance, performance optimisation, service efficiency, automation or convenience or quality control shall not qualify as safety components.
location: Art. 1(8), inserting AI Act Art. 6(1a); p. 18
note: Scope rule set by the Regulation itself; narrows Art. 6(1) high-risk classification. Art. 6(1b): systems whose 'failure or malfunctioning ... would endanger health and safety shall qualify as safety components'. Recital 7: the safety function is an intended purpose 'determined by the provider of the system' (nearest named actor: provider). Art. 6(1c) excludes products needing third-party assessment solely for non-health-and-safety risks. [inference] Service-efficiency tools embedded in Annex I products fall outside Art. 6(1) unless failure endangers health and safety.

quote: when adopting implementing acts pursuant to paragraph 1 concerning AI systems which are safety components within the meaning of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the requirements set out in Chapter III, Section 2, of that Regulation shall be taken into account.
location: Art. 2(2), adding Reg. 2018/1139 Art. 31(3); p. 38 (same wording in Art. 2(1)-(7), pp. 38-39)
obligation: statutory duty ('shall be taken into account')
note: Civil aviation standard-setting. Passive; nearest named actor: the Commission (recital 44: 'the Commission, when adopting any relevant delegated or implementing acts').

quote: The Commission shall adopt delegated acts in accordance with Article 47 of this Regulation to amend Annex III to this Regulation by adding health and safety requirements in respect of Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems
location: Art. 3(1), adding to Reg. 2023/1230 Art. 8; pp. 39-40
obligation: statutory duty (delegated acts to apply by 2 August 2028)
note: Machinery moved from Annex I Section A to Section B of the AI Act (Art. 1(41)), so AI Act applies to AI machinery only via Art. 2(2). Requirements 'shall ensure that the relevant requirements set out in Chapter III, Section 2, and Articles 17, 19, 72 and 73 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 are reflected'. Until machinery-specific standards exist, AI Act harmonised standards/common specifications give presumption of conformity (Reg. 2023/1230 Art. 20(10)).

quote: related to products covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section B of Annex I, only Article 6(1), Article 60a and Articles 102 to 112 shall apply.
note: Scope/exemption set by the Regulation itself (nearest named actor: European Parliament and Council as legislator). Arts 57-59 (sandboxes) apply only once AI Act high-risk requirements are integrated into the Section B law. Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 is moved to Section B by Art. 1(41) (p. 36), so AI-enabled machinery falls under this narrower scope.

quote: for the purposes of this definition, a component fulfils a safety function where its intended purpose is to prevent or mitigate risks to health and safety of persons or property
note: Classification turns on 'intended purpose'. Recital 7 (p. 3) names who sets it: 'The safety function should be an intended purpose of the system, which is determined by the provider of the system.' So the provider effectively decides whether a component is a safety component [inference from recital 7]. Cross-ref Art. 6(1a)-(1c) entry.

quote: is only prohibited where the deployer uses the system for the purpose of generating or manipulating such material or performance.
if_not_met: not stated in this text beyond Art. 99(1) Member State penalties
note: Narrows the deployer side of the new prohibitions. Recital 12: the prohibition on use does not cover lawful purposes 'even in cases where the AI system lacks reasonable and adequate safeguards', 'nor does it cover accidental generation or manipulation of such content'.

quote: A notifying authority that has been designated pursuant to the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I is also the notifying authority for the application of the single application and unified assessment procedure
holder: Member State; notifying authority under Annex I Section A legislation
obligation: statutory default allocation; Member State power to designate otherwise
note: Appointing who decides on designation: default is the sectoral notifying authority, 'unless the Member State designates another notifying authority for this Regulation'.

quote: The Commission shall entrust the performance of those tests or assessments to notified bodies designated in accordance with this Regulation, in which case the notified body shall act on behalf of the Commission.
note: Appointing who carries out the pre-market check. Cross-ref Accountability/Design (withdrawal of delegation) and Delivery/Design (Art. 75(1e)).

quote: Chapter III, Sections 1, 2, and 3, with the exception of Article 6(5), shall apply from:
note: Set by the Regulation (European Parliament and Council as legislator). High-risk rules delayed to '2 December 2027' (Art. 6(2)/Annex III) and '2 August 2028' (Art. 6(1)/Annex I). New Art. 5 prohibitions apply from 2 December 2026; Arts 102-110 from 27 July 2026. Recital 40 cites 'delayed availability of standards' and 'delayed establishment of national competent authorities'.

quote: Information about the general-purpose AI model provided in the Summary should cover data used in all stages of the model training, from pre -training to post -training, including model alignment
holder: European Commission (AI Office), as author of the Template
obligation: non-binding interpretation ('should'), given legal weight by Art. 53(1)(d) reference to the template
note: Sets the scope of the disclosure standard. Excludes 'other input data used during the model’s operation (e.g. through retrieval augmented generation)' from mandatory sections 'unless the model actively learns from this input data'. Para 18-19: Commission's 'careful balancing exercise' with trade secrets; detail varies by source (licensed data limited; private datasets listed only if publicly known; 'large' public datasets listed). Para 22: no 'exact mix and composition of data sources'. Para 4: the Template 'holds important legal value'.
basis: AI pass A; different cell in pass B

quote: The Commission will monitor the implementation of the Template  annexed to this Explanatory Notice and where necessary review the Notice and the Template
note: Authority to revise the standard, 'in view of practical experience gained and of the pace of technological, societal and market developments'; may review before 2 August 2026. Also coded Delivery/Design (monitoring).

quote: the objective should be to move from a model based primarily on oversight towards one based on the integration of security directly into development and operational processes at company level.
location: Impact on vulnerability and patch management, 'The Secure SDLC revolution'; p. 10
note: Direction-setting on the governance model for vulnerability detection and remediation. Edge case: AI-accelerated discovery. Same bullet: 'integrators and end users should be enabled to detect vulnerabilities as early as possible'.
basis: AI pass A; different cell in pass B

quote: it may be useful to establish EU-wide state-of-the-art benchmarks for the security evaluation of advanced AI models, including standardised testing against cyber ranges, exploitability metrics, and simulations of chained attacks
note: Standard-setting for security evaluation of frontier models ('to set a consistent bar for assessing their capabilities'); the testing itself would be Delivery. Unnamed 'European level' actor. Same bullet: 'the existing legal frameworks, including NIS2, CRA and the EU AI Act14 should be leveraged, to ensure that systemic risks stemming from the most advanced AI models are assessed and mitigated.' Next bullet: 'Leverage and build on existing initiatives at European and Member State level' (none named). Concerns models that may be used by or against public bodies.

quote: In accordance with the AI Act and the Code of Practice for General Purpose AI, adequate risk mitigations for AI models with advanced cyber capabilities need to be identified.
note: Passive; deciding what counts as adequate mitigation. Nearest named actors (fn 14, a report of the AI Act): providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk and the European AI Office. Model providers in the value chain.
basis: AI pass A; different cell in pass B

quote: Develop common frameworks for the deployment of AI-enabled security tools that prioritise human oversight, auditability, and human-gated triage for decision making.
note: Standard-setting for deploying AI tools (incl. by public bodies). Content: human oversight and human-gated triage (see Delivery/Design entry) and auditability (who audits not stated). Executive summary stakeholder bullet: 'human-gated AI workflows need be integrated across incident response and threat modelling'.

quote: Require critical infrastructure operators to attest zero-trust baselines, resilient incident response capabilities during annual audits, and clear escalation paths for AI-accelerated incidents.
obligation: recommended (that national authorities issue a requirement)
note: Mandate-setting by national authorities. Edge case: concerns AI used by attackers against the organisation ('AI-accelerated incidents'), not AI tools used by it. Also coded Accountability/Design (attestation in annual audits).

quote: Direct government agencies and critical infrastructure operators to reduce ineffective security tooling and complement their cybersecurity stack with AI-enabled platforms capable of ingesting, correlating, and acting on threat data.
holder: National authorities (direct); government agencies and critical infrastructure operators (adopt)
note: Directive to adopt AI tools in government agencies (decision whether a tool is used). Which authority directs, and on what legal basis, not stated.

quote: critical service providers may be forced to use autonomous patching, as organisational approval is simply too slow.
holder: Critical service providers; human Change Advisory Boards
note: Who authorises automated interventions. Body text p. 8, 'Authority Gap': 'the inability of human Change Advisory Boards (CABs) to authorise interventions in just the few minutes available to counter autonomous exploits.' Risk noted: 'automated updates could accidentally break systems'. Not a recommendation; coded as design because it sets out where approval sits [judgement].

quote: A cross-cutting challenge will be to ensure that foreseen solutions will keep the human in the middle.
location: Security fundamentals, '4. Talent and human capital'; p. 12
note: Human authority over AI-assisted security solutions. Continues: 'humans will still need to understand the environments they assume responsibility for'. Could also be read as Delivery (human review) or Accountability (responsibility); I chose Decision-making because it keeps a human in charge. Cross-ref Delivery/Resources (skills).
basis: AI pass B; different cell in pass A

quote: key questions include how to prioritise incidents when they all meet regulatory thresholds, which CSIRTs structures can operate without prioritisation, and how sectoral CSIRTs can be supported when national capacity is saturated.
location: page 12, Security fundamentals matter more than ever, 2. Incident response
note: Questions on setting priorities; nearest actors are national authorities and CSIRTs [inference]. The last question is about support between CSIRTs (also Coordination). Edge case: AI-accelerated incident surges.

quote: The “Authority Gap” refers to the inability of human Change Advisory Boards (CABs) to authorise interventions in just the few minutes available to counter autonomous exploits.
location: page 8, Impact on Vulnerability & Patch Management, 'The Velocity Asymmetry and the Authority Gap'
obligation: ENISA analysis of a challenge; no requirement or recommendation verb
note: About who authorises changes: human approval boards are described as too slow, and ENISA says 'The necessity of autonomous patching ... will be challenging'. Page 11 adds that 'critical service providers may be forced to use autonomous patching, as organisational approval is simply too slow', with the risk that 'automated updates could accidentally break systems'. Smaller organisations are expected to find this harder. Coded because it concerns human authority over automated remediation; it is analysis, not a requirement.

quote: An AI system should be responsibly and efficiently decommissioned when it is no longer needed or is replaced by a more advanced solution.
location: p.11, s.3.2 Lifecycle of an AI system (phase 9)
note: Retirement. Trigger: no longer needed or replaced. Who decides is not stated. Annex 3 lists no risks for this phase.

quote: Define a quality assurance policy for the training personal dataset which:
note: Standard-setting: the policy describes data types and acquisition methods, preparation steps, 'a definition of the quality criteria and measures' and 'the quality threshold'. Who adopts it is not stated. The check against it is coded as Delivery.

quote: Verify whether the problem at stake could be solved by effectively and efficiently using algorithms other than machine learning or deep learning ones
note: Bears on whether an ML-based AI system is used at all. Who decides is not stated. Could also be read as a Delivery check.

quote: allowing humans to monitor, modify, or approve decisions in real time
note: Human-in-the-loop oversight during operation: authority to modify or approve outputs. Who the humans are is not stated. Described as a form of human review, not a requirement. Linked to Delivery entry on measure 6.

quote: EUIs must ensure they have a valid legal basis before using personal data to train AI systems.
location: p.30, s.5.3 Principle of data minimisation
note: Precondition gate before training. Fn 75 quotes the EDPS GenAI Orientations on web scraping (reported, not coded here).

quote: Enforce RBAC to limit who can access, modify or interact with the AI system based on their role in the organisation.
note: [inference] Coded as Decision-making because it sets who has authority to modify the AI system; the document presents it as a technical security control, so it could be Delivery. Who defines the roles is not stated.

quote: the risk analysis and the risk evaluation aspects are too dependent on the specific processing context and their assessment is better left to each organisation in line with  their own risk criteria
note: Standard-setting: the organisation sets its own risk criteria ('such as risk appetite and tolerance', p.8) against which risks are judged acceptable or requiring treatment. The guidance 'refrains from ranking their likelihood and severity' (p.4).

quote: evaluate the likelihood and impact of the risks, and decide on the mitigating measures to address them, as well as
note: Sentence continues on p.9: 'on the residual risks'. Verb: should ('EUIs should perform a thorough analysis ...'). EUIs decide on treatment and residual risk; ISO 31000 options on p.8: avoid, mitigate, transfer or accept. Who within the EUI decides is not stated. Analysis itself coded as Delivery; p.9 entry covers risks that cannot be mitigated.

quote: the EUI is unable to mitigate by reasonable means the risks posed by the planned AI system and thus a different solution to the organisation’s needs has to be found
note: Do-not-proceed outcome: where the analysis concludes risks cannot be mitigated by reasonable means, the planned AI system is not used as planned. Who in the EUI decides is not stated. Same passage coded as Accountability and Coordination (prior consultation).

quote: it is also important to acknowledge , already in the procurement cycle , making a risk evaluation before any budget is actually committed for a solution that would bring undesirable risks to the organisation
location: p11, Section 3.3 Procuring an AI system
note: [inference] Works as a pre-commitment gate: risk evaluation before budget commitment for a procured AI system. No decision-maker named; nearest named actors are 'EUIs' staff involved in the procurement of AI systems'. Verb: 'important to'. Also coded as Delivery/Design (the risk evaluation).

quote: Selection and award criteria (Article 170): Evaluate offers based on predefined criteria (e.g. price, quality, sustainability).
note: Selection of the AI product among tenders. The document presents the Financial Regulation process as 'the process followed by EUIs' (p11). Annex 3 lists 'Selection' as the phase for risks 4.1.1 (uninterpretable system) and 5.2.5 (unclear provider information). Criteria named are examples; no data-protection criterion is set here.

quote: For the purpose of this Guidance , the principle of fairness is understood as requiring controllers to identify, measure and mitigate these biases
note: EDPS sets the interpretive standard it applies (fairness = identify, measure, mitigate bias). The obligation it implies for controllers is coded as Delivery/Design (p16-17). Standard set by EDPS; checks done by controllers.

quote: The outcome of this evaluation helps the organisation decide whether to avoid, mitigate, transf er, or accept the risks, depending on their severity and organisational goals.
note: Decision on risk treatment (avoid/mitigate/transfer/accept) after comparing analysis results 'against the organisation's risk criteria (such as risk appetite and tolerance)'. Risk treatment is iterative: 'If the remaining risk is deemed acceptable, no further action is necessary'; if not, 'additional measures are taken'. Presented as the ISO method the guidance adopts, not phrased as an obligation.

quote: an entity that determines “why” and “how” processing takes place includes an organization that decides to develop an AI system, use a service provider for development, and/ or deploy a generative system
holder: controller (an organization that decides to develop, commission or deploy)
note: Names who holds decision authority (controller). An entity creating a training dataset on its own account may also be a controller; joint controllers jointly determine purposes and means; a processor (e.g. an AI developer working for an EUI) has no control over purposes and essential means.
basis: AI pass B; different cell in pass A

quote: EUIs should conduct a thorough assessment on a case-by-case basis and document the results in their records of processing activities.
location: PDF p.10 (printed p.9), s.3 Roles and responsibilities
note: Allocation of controller/processor/joint-controller roles across the generative AI supply chain, which fixes who carries the obligations. Section 2 also recommends: 'Formally determine and document all roles and responsibilities in relation to the processing operation'. AI Act terms provider/developer/deployer 'do not correspond' to these roles. Documentation in records also bears on Accountability.
basis: AI pass B; different cell in pass A

quote: By default, the EDPS considers that AI models are likely to require a thorough evaluation of the likelihood of identification to reach a conclusion on their possible anonymous nature.
note: EDPS sets the standard for treating a model as anonymous: likelihood of extraction from the model and of obtaining personal data from queries 'should be insignificant' for any data subject. The evaluation itself is coded as Delivery/Design. Extraction has two spaces after 'EDPS' at the line end; joined with one space here.
basis: AI pass B; different cell in pass A

quote: the EDPS recommends EUIs to use different sources of personal data, where possible.
note: Choice of data source: avoid web scraping where possible. Safeguards if web scraping is used are coded as Delivery.

quote: When relying on internal rules, these internal rules should precisely define the scope of the interference with the right to the protection of personal data
note: Nearest named actor: the EUI adopting internal rules. Standard-setting: rules should identify purpose, categories of data subjects and data, controller and processors, storage periods, and 'concrete minimum safeguards'. 'the greater the interference, the more robust and detailed the rules and safeguards should be'.

quote: distinct lawful grounds should be identified for processing carried out during the development phase, and the deployment phase
note: Precondition for processing. 'EUIs should make a thorough assessment on a case-by-case basis'; most common ground Art. 5(1)(a) (public interest), which needs a legal basis in EU law (Art. 5(2)) and EUIs 'should demonstrate' the task or official authority; Art. 5(1)(b) legal obligation 'challenging'; consent only in limited circumstances; legitimate interest (GDPR) not available under the EUDPR. A GPA Resolution box (PDF p.21) reports that developers, providers and deployers must identify the legal basis at the outset; reported, not coded.

quote: However, in this case, the controller must stop the processing operations concerned.
note: Trigger: consent withdrawn. If there is no other lawful basis, 'the relevant data must be deleted by the controller', which the EDPS says poses 'a significant challenge to the functionality of the generative AI system'.

quote: These transfers can only occur if the EUI in question has instructed the entity processing personal data on their behalf or allowed them
obligation: statutory duty restated (can only occur if)
note: The EUI authorises transfers (or EU or Member State law requires them), including cloud-based generative AI and data provided to train, test or validate a model. Transfers must comply with Chapter V and the original purpose. Also coded as Accountability (EUIs accountable for transfers).

quote: they must determine whether the subsequent processing is compatible with the initial purpose for which the personal data was collected.
note: Trigger: reuse of data collected for training for another processing activity. Comparator: Art. 6 criteria. Gates reuse; could also be read as a Delivery check.

quote: it is essential to assess each phase of the generative AI lifecycle separately from a data protection perspective and define a specific purpose of processing.
location: PDF p.23 (printed p.22), s.8 Purpose limitation
note: Nearest named actor: controllers / EUIs. Setting scope per stage (training, testing, fine-tuning, deployment). The conclusion box (PDF p.24) says EUIs should establish purposes 'before processing personal data'. The purpose should be defined 'even in the early stages of development'.

quote: EUIs must also verify that the purpose in question cannot be achieved by processing other data, such as synthetic or anonymised data before deciding that personal data is necessary to process in the first place.
location: PDF p.25 (printed p.24), s.9 Data minimisation
obligation: non-binding interpretation of a statutory duty (must)
note: Gate before deciding to process personal data. Trigger: before processing.
basis: AI pass A; different cell in pass B

quote: EUIs should carefully assess data accuracy throughout the whole lifecycle of the generative AI systems and reconsider the use of such systems if the accuracy cannot be maintained.
location: PDF p.27 (printed p.26), s.10 Accuracy (conclusion box [inference from layout])
note: Stop/reconsider decision. Trigger: accuracy cannot be maintained. Content not in the body text, so coded from the box. Also the if_not_met for the accuracy duty (Delivery).

quote: EUIs must be very attentive to the weight that the information provided by the system has in the final steps of the decision-making procedure
note: Continues: 'and whether it has a decisive influence on the final decision taken by the controller'. Keeps the final decision with the controller; also determines whether Art. 24 applies. Notes risks for 'vulnerable populations and children'.

quote: Where generative AI  systems are planned to support decision- making procedures, EUIs must consider carefully whether to put them into operation if their use raises questions about their lawfulness
location: PDF p.30 (printed p.29), s.12 (conclusion box [inference from layout])
note: Go/no-go decision. Continues: 'or their potential of being unfair, unethical or discriminatory decisions'. Box content not in body text. The worked example (PDF p.31) shows an EUI deciding not to use a screening system until bias risk is eliminated; example not coded.

quote: In managing AI decision-making tools, EUIs must consider carefully how to ensure that the right to obtain human intervention is properly implemented.
location: PDF p.30 (printed p.29), s.12 Automated decisions
obligation: non-binding interpretation of a statutory duty (must consider)
note: Human intervention (override). 'of paramount importance in case EUIs deploy autonomous AI agents that can perform tasks and make decisions without human intervention or guidance'. Linked to Accountability entry on Art. 24 safeguards.

quote: If the controller demonstrates that it is unable to identify the individual, Articles 17-22 of the Regulation do not appl y.
obligation: statutory exemption restated; good practice (inform the data subject)
note: Exemption from rights handling where the controller cannot identify the individual (e.g. transformed training data). But if the individual provides identifying information 'the controller has to handle the request' (Art. 12(2)); good practice: inform the data subject what additional information may be provided.
basis: AI pass B; different cell in pass A

quote: a controller does not need to erase or alter all machine learning models based on the data concerned for erasure or rectification, unless the model itself contains such data or can be used to infer it
note: Scope of the erasure/rectification duty as it reaches trained models. Quote spans a page break with footnote 51 in between.
basis: AI pass B; different cell in pass A

quote: EUIs can develop and deploy their own generative AI solutions or can alternatively deploy for their own use solutions available on the market.
note: Build-or-buy choice. 'In both cases, EUIs may use providers to obtain all or some of the elements'.

quote: Clearly define the specific purpose for processing of the g enerative AI  and identify the appropriate legal basis for its deployment.
location: PDF p.8 (printed p.7), s.2 (recommendation 'Define Purpose and Legal Basis')
note: Setting scope. Detailed in s.7 (lawful ground per phase) and s.8 (purpose per lifecycle stage), coded separately.

quote: As an EUI, there is no obstacle in principle to develop, deploy and use generative AI systems in the provision of public services, providing that the EUI's rules allow it, and that all applicable legal requirements are met
location: PDF p.8 (printed p.7), s.2 Can EUIs use generative AI?
note: Conditions for use: the EUI's own rules allow it and all legal requirements are met, 'especially considering the special responsibility of the public sector'. Authority rests with the EUI under its own rules; who within the EUI decides is not stated.

quote: EUIs must consider carefully when and how to use generative AI responsibly and beneficially for public good.
location: PDF p.9 (printed p.8), s.2 (conclusion box [inference from layout])
note: Whether and how to use. Box adds: 'All stages of a generative AI solution life cycle should operate in accordance with the applicable legal frameworks'.

quote: Such lawful ground is not applicable in the context of the Regulation.
holder: EUIs (service providers may rely on it under the GDPR)
note: Scope: legitimate interest, which 'Service providers of g enerative AI models may use' under the GDPR for collecting training data, is not available to EUIs under the EUDPR. Relevant to value chain: provider and EUI may rely on different bases.

quote: EUIs have an obligation to identify a distinct lawful ground for the processing carried out at every stage of the generative AI  lifecycle, during both the development and deployment phase.
note: Authorisation basis per lifecycle stage. 'EUIs should make a thorough assessment on a case-by-case basis'; most common ground likely Art. 5(1)(a) public task; Art. 5(1)(b) legal obligation 'challenging'; consent limited.

quote: The legal basis for the processing must be laid down in EU law.
holder: EUIs (basis to be laid down by EU law)
note: Who authorises: EU law (the legislator), for processing on public-task or official-authority grounds. The EU law 'should be clear and precise and its application should be foreseeable'; 'the greater the interference, the more robust and detailed the rules and safeguards should be'. Demonstration duty coded as Accountability/Design.

quote: for a SA to agree with the controller that a given AI model may be considered anonymous, it should check at least whether it has  received sufficient evidence
obligation: non-binding interpretation addressed to SAs, which 'should take utmost account' of the Opinion (para 15); verb 'should'
note: Verb 'should'. Authority over scope: whether a model trained on personal data falls outside the GDPR as anonymous is decided by the SA case by case (para 34: 'the determination of whether an AI model is anonymous should be assessed, based on specific criteria, on a case-by-case basis'; executive summary names 'competent SAs'). Evidence must show, with reasonable means, (i) personal data related to the training data cannot be extracted and (ii) outputs do not relate to training-data subjects. Trigger: a controller's claim of anonymity. Compared against: likelihood of extraction or of obtaining personal data via queries, to be 'insignificant' (para 43); no quantified metric. Para 43: 'By default, SAs should consider that  AI models are likely to require a thorough evaluation of the likelihood  of identification'. Para 134: 'a mere assertion of anonymity of the model is not enough to exempt it from the application of the GDPR'. EDPB standard coded separately (Decision-making/Design, para 43); controller's answerability coded Accountability/Design (paras 45, 57).

quote: the likelihood of obtaining, intentionally or not, such  personal data from queries , should be insignificant 37 for any data subject
obligation: non-binding interpretation (standard set in an opinion that SAs 'should take utmost account' of)
note: Standard-setting: the EDPB sets the anonymity threshold SAs are to apply: both (i) the likelihood of direct (including probabilistic) extraction of training personal data and (ii) the likelihood of obtaining such data from queries should be insignificant, taking into account 'all the means reasonably likely to be used' and unintended (re)use or disclosure of the model. '37' is a footnote marker in the extraction. The Opinion is advisory, so this could alternatively be read as Resources (guidance to SAs); coded Decision-making because it sets the standard. Applied by SAs (Decision-making/Design, para 38).

quote: the roles and responsibilities of the parties that process personal data in the context of the development or deployment of an AI model should be assessed before the processing takes place
note: Passive. Nearest named actors: 'the parties that process personal data', i.e. controllers, joint controllers and processors. Allocation of who is responsible is to be settled before processing 'in order  to define the obligations of the controllers or joint controllers, and of processors (if any), from the outset'. Trigger: before processing. See also paras 112 and 125 (ascertaining roles and joint controllership 'is an essential step'). Bears on value chains where a public body deploys a model developed by another party [inference].
basis: AI pass A; different cell in pass B

quote: it is for controllers to identify the approp riate legal basis for their processing activities
obligation: statutory duty (recalled; no hierarchy between legal bases)
note: Recall of the GDPR: the controller decides which legal basis it relies on for development and deployment processing. The body text (para 60) only recalls that 'the GDPR does not establish any hierarchy between the different legal bases'; the controller's role is stated only in the executive summary, so that is quoted.

quote: If the pursuit of the purpose is also possible through an AI model that does not  entail processing  of personal data, then  processing personal data should be considered as not necessary.
if_not_met: not stated (the passage concludes that processing 'should be considered as not necessary')
note: Standard for the necessity step of the legitimate-interest test; 'particularly relevant for the development of AI models'. Verb 'should be considered'. Passive; nearest named actors: controllers, who carry out the assessment (para 66), and SAs, who 'should pay particular attention to the amount of personal data processed' (para 73). Technical safeguards short of anonymisation may help meet the test (para 75).
basis: AI pass B; different cell in pass A

quote: ordering the erasure of the whole dataset used to develop the AI model and/or the AI model itself.
note: Authority to stop or limit an AI model: on a finding of infringement 'SAs may impose corrective measures', e.g. a fine, a temporary limitation on the processing, erasing the unlawfully processed part of the dataset or, where not possible and proportionate, erasure of the whole dataset and/or the model itself. SAs 'enjoy discretionary powers' (para 113); proportionality factors: risks to data subjects, gravity, technical and financial feasibility, volume of data (para 116); SAs may take into account remediation such as retraining (para 114). Corrective measures on the initial processing would in principle affect subsequent processing such as deployment (para 120). SA measures are without prejudice to AI Act authorities (para 117). Also coded Accountability/Design (sanctions, para 114).

quote: If it can be demonstrated that the subsequent operation of the AI model does not entail the processing of personal data, the EDPB considers that the GDPR would not apply
note: Scope decision (scenario 3: unlawful development, then anonymisation): the unlawfulness of the initial processing 'should not, therefore, impact the subsequent operation of the model'; personal data processed in deployment after anonymisation remains subject to the GDPR, and its lawfulness is not affected by the initial unlawfulness (para 135). But 'a mere assertion of anonymity of the model is not enough to exempt it from the application of the GDPR'; SAs assess anonymity on the Question 1 criteria and remain competent to intervene on the development-phase processing (para 133). Advisory: see note on the para 43 entry.

quote: Deployers and other users of the generative AI systems will be given access to the logging policies and granted control over what is logged and how data is stored, accessed and how long it is retained
holder: Deployers and other users of the generative AI systems (control); Signatories who are providers (must grant it)
obligation: mandatory under the Code ('will') where a Signatory implements the optional logging; adherence voluntary
if_not_met: not stated (compliance monitored by competent market surveillance authorities; no consequence stated)
note: Authority over what is logged: deployers (which may include public bodies using a generative AI system [inference]) control what is logged, storage, access and retention, 'with clear procedures for limited retention periods, access controls, security' and 'secure and immediate deletion of logs containing output data after its intended purpose has been fulfilled'. Applies only where the provider uses the optional logging. Access to logging policies coded Decision-making/Resources.
basis: AI pass A; different cell in pass B

quote: Signatories may restrict access to detection mechanisms associated to watermarking techniques for free-form text to the extent that they have a lower level of reliability and robustness
holder: Signatories who are providers of generative AI systems
obligation: optional ('may'); access for expert users is mandatory ('will')
note: Authority over who may use a detection tool, because such detection may give 'misleading or low -confidence results'. But Signatories 'will ensure that  access for these expert end-users is granted' (including competent MSAs, other regulators and law enforcement), and restrictions 'will be limited in time'. The same applies to optional forensic detection (Measure 2.2).

quote: Signatories are entitled to retire a detection solution as long as it is replaced by an alternative detection solution.
holder: Signatories who are providers of generative AI systems
obligation: entitlement under the Code, conditional on replacement ('will' conditions)
note: Authority to stop a tool: retirement allowed only with a replacement that 'yields the same or better detection capabilities and is backward compatible'. If stopped without replacement (e.g. business closure), the solution goes to MSAs (Delivery/Resources entry).

quote: methods and benchmarks  endorsed by the AI Office after consultation of the AI Board and the taskforce described in Measure 3.5
holder: AI Office (after consultation of the AI Board and the taskforce)
obligation: anticipated standard-setting; prospective, no endorsement recorded
note: Standard-setting: endorsed evaluation methods and benchmarks would replace internal benchmarks for testing (Measure 4.2) and underpin proof of alternative marking techniques (Measure 1.1). The Code does not say when or how endorsement happens.

quote: This Section of the Code applies only to Signatories in so far as they are deployers of AI systems that generate or manipulate image, audio or video content constituting a deep fake
note: Sets who is bound: deployers of AI systems producing deep fakes or 'text published with the purpose of informing the public on matters of public interest', defined as AI-generated text published 'without human review or editorial control and where no natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility'. Scope set by the Code itself (the Working Group 2 chair and vice-chairs are named). The Art. 50(4) legal text reproduced in the Code (p.29) exempts uses 'authorised by l aw to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offence' and human-reviewed text with editorial responsibility. Bears on public bodies publishing AI-generated public information [inference].

quote: Signatories and the associations of which they are part may jointly establish common good practices for their sector or industry
holder: Signatories and the associations of which they are part
note: Standard-setting within sectors: good practices may detail how to implement the measures and must be 'fully aligned with the measures set out below', while allowing sector tailoring and extra transparency. Recital (b) says the same. Publication of the good practices coded Accountability/Design.

quote: This obligation shall not apply where the use is authorised by l aw to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offence.
holder: Deployers of an AI system that generates or manipulates deep fakes (exempted where the use is authorised by law)
note: Scope exemption from the deep-fake disclosure duty; the same exemption applies to published text, which is also exempt where it has undergone human review or editorial control and someone holds editorial responsibility. This is the Act's text reproduced in the Code, not a Code measure; coded because it sets scope for public authorities. Artistic, creative, satirical or fictional works have a lighter regime (Commitment 3).

quote: update the EU icon to ensure state -of-art disclosure at all times including in line with user experience (UX) standards
obligation: aim of the task force ('will, inter alia, aim to'); participation voluntary
note: Standard-setting: the task force aims to update the EU icon, develop non-visual and audio-only versions and a common EU-wide audio solution (Measure 1.1), and identify common methods for disclosing the type of AI involvement. Its composition, convenor and decision procedure are not stated; Annex 1 says the AI Office developed the current icons.

quote: a natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility for the publication
holder: Natural or legal person with editorial responsibility (identified by the Signatory)
obligation: commitment under the Code (mandatory for Signatories relying on human review); adherence voluntary
note: Authority over publication of AI-generated text sits with a named natural or legal person, identified by 'name, role and contact details' (Commitment 4(a)). Also coded Accountability/Design (publication of contact details).

quote: This Section of the Code applies to Signatories who are providers of generative AI systems falling within Article 2 and Article 50(2) AI Act
note: Sets who is bound (scope and exemptions). Holder not stated: the scope is set by the Code itself; the cover names the Working Group 1 chair and vice-chairs. Value chain: 'providers of generative AI models that are placed on the Union market independently from AI systems and third -party providers of marking and detection solutions may also, on a voluntary basis, adhere'. Recital (g): 'simplified ways of compliance for SMEs and SMCs, including startups, should be possible'. Exemptions inside measures: a single marking layer suffices for products in a closed environment and for free-form text (Measure 1.1); no watermark needed for 'very short text' under 200 tokens (Sub-measure 1.1.2, Glossary).

quote: provided that they can prove to the competent market surveillance authorities, based on recognised performance evaluation methods and benchmarks, that their technique(s) achieve at least the same, if not superior, level of robustness, reliability, effectiveness, and interoperability
holder: Competent market surveillance authorities (judge the proof); Signatories who are providers of generative AI systems (must prove)
obligation: conditional route under the Code (Signatories 'will also be able to demonstrate compliance'); prospective
note: Approval-type gate for departing from the default two-layer marking: providers may use alternative or single techniques if they prove equivalence to MSAs. Status: 'In the future'. Pending recognised benchmarks, Signatories 'may demonstrate compliance through documented internal testing against the requirements in Commitment 3, subject to review by the competent market surveillance authorities'. Compares against: Art 50(2) and Commitment 3 requirements; metric: recognised performance evaluation methods and benchmarks.

quote: Recognise the public sector as a strategic domain in (national) AI strategies by deciding on dedicated actions, governance arrangements and priority use cases.
holder: Member States (recommendations addressed to Member States and public administrations)
note: Body: 'The first step in this direction is the assessment and, where necessary, revision of national AI strategies'. The body also quotes the Strategy ('the Commission calls for Member States to align their national AI strategies to the sectoral approach'), a report of another instrument, not coded separately.

quote: Recognising the public sector as a strategic domain requires clear governance arrangements, dedicated resources and well-defined responsibilities across levels of administration.
note: Governance arrangements and well-defined responsibilities across levels (who decides). Also coded as Decision-making/Resources (dedicated resources).

quote: Clear and measurable objectives will enable public administrations to track progress and take timely corrective action
note: Corrective action after monitoring against objectives. Who sets the objectives and who decides the correction: not stated. Related: Delivery/Design monitoring entry.

quote: public administrations should establish pathways that integrate technological development with softer elements, such as skills development, process reengineering and awareness raising, to ensure that AI adoption generates public value and aligns with the EU’s vision and priorities.
note: Heading: 'Develop structured pathways that prioritise public-value-driven AI solutions and enable their scaling across administrations'. 'This approach begins with identifying the areas where AI can be most effectively applied and deciding which applications of the technology will yield the greatest value.'

quote: Public administrations have a pivotal role to play in reinforcing EU digital sovereignty by promoting the adoption of AI solutions that reduce strategic dependency on non-EU providers.
note: Heading: 'Use public sector demand strategically to strengthen the European GovTech ecosystem and EU digital sovereignty.' Procurement priority. Also: 'public administrations might consider measures such as targeted funding, incentives and regulatory support for European AI GovTech companies.'

quote: The public sector must lead the way in adopting AI across the European Union, thus influencing the EU private market and driving AI innovation across industries and the economy.
note: Verb: must. Sets direction (adopt AI, lead the market); no tool, decision-maker or check named. Signed by directors at JRC, DG DIGIT and the AI Office (DG CNECT). [inference] Largely rhetorical; a checker may judge it too general to code.

quote: Public administrations are encouraged to pursue widespread adoption of AI. However, they should be wary of rapidly introducing AI solely to increase the number of AI applications.
note: Verbs: 'are encouraged', 'should be wary'. Direction on whether and how fast to adopt; warns against adoption driven by 'funding opportunities, political expectations or broader trends'.

quote: Throughout the adoption process – and after deployment – public administrations should monitor whether AI solutions are delivering the intended public value, tracking progress through key performance indicators, and deciding if adjustments are needed.
note: 'deciding if adjustments are needed' gives administrations the decision to adjust a deployed tool after monitoring; who within the administration decides is not stated. Also coded as Delivery/Design (monitoring).

quote: AI adoption should be firmly rooted in the existing EU policy and regulatory framework and in the values that shape both the European approach to AI and the specific mandate of the public sector.
note: Nearest named actor: public administrations. Sets the standard adoption decisions should meet: three anchoring dimensions (public sector core mandate; EU regulatory framework on AI; EU vision and priorities, Figure 2). Trigger: 'They should be considered from the outset of any AI project and integrated into each stage of development and adoption.'

quote: public administrations must ensure that its adoption supports the public sector’s primary mission, which is to create public value by addressing collective needs and safeguarding fundamental rights and the well-being of society.
obligation: recommended ('must ensure'; no legal basis cited)
note: Verb: must ensure. [inference] Decision-making because administrations decide whether to adopt; no approver or stop point named.

quote: While the risks vary depending on the specific application, they need appropriate governance and oversight.
note: Context: 'AI solutions can inherently have a margin of error, and by their nature they may lead to unexpected outcomes.' Neither who governs or oversees, nor how, is stated. Could equally be coded as Accountability (oversight).

quote: The scale, complexity and intrusiveness of AI solutions should correspond to the public need they address. AI should therefore be adopted only where it provides demonstrable added value
note: Proportionality test for the decision to adopt. Continues '...compared with less complex or less resource-intensive alternatives' (hyphen split in source). Nearest named actor: public administrations. Trigger: decision whether and how to adopt. Metric: not stated.

quote: administrations should take these principles into account when designing, procuring and adopting AI solutions.
note: Subject word 'Public' is on the previous page, before a footnote and page break. Principles are those 'first consolidated in the work of the High-Level Expert Group on AI'. Also: 'EU legislation and guiding principles provide the normative framework within which AI adoption in the public sector must take place.'
basis: AI pass A; different cell in pass B

quote: This broader vision should influence how public administrations in the EU operate, not only as facilitators of market growth but also as users and procurers of technology.
note: Procurement priority. Continues: 'In this context, prioritising EU-made solutions  is increasingly seen as relevant.' See also Recommendation 5.

quote: AI should be introduced only when both the administration and its surrounding environment are adequately prepared.
note: Gate on whether to introduce AI. Nearest named actor: public administrations. Trigger: before introduction. Compares against technological, organisational and contextual enabling factors. Who judges readiness: not stated.

quote: Putting such arrangements in place may entail establishing dedicated AI strategies for development and adoption, clearly establishing roles and responsibilities, creating oversight mechanisms and promoting collaboration
note: Context: 'Clear internal governance arrangements are necessary to guide the ethical and effective use of AI'. Elements: AI strategies, roles and responsibilities (who decides). Nearest actor: public administrations. Also coded as Accountability/Design (oversight mechanisms).

quote: These external factors should be acknowledged and considered when deciding on the AI adoption approach
note: External factors: 'political expectations or funding opportunities'. Applies to the decision on the adoption approach.

quote: public administrations should pinpoint areas where AI can be applied, focusing on their specific needs and identifying domains where AI can deliver the most value
note: Setting priorities for where AI is applied. Supported by the report's application fields and use cases (coded as Decision-making/Resources).

quote: AI should therefore be adopted only where it provides demonstrable added value compared with less complex or less resource-intensive alternatives.
note: Proportionality test for whether to adopt. Passive; nearest actor public administrations. Compared against: less complex or less resource-intensive alternatives. Who judges 'demonstrable' and how: not stated.

quote: Clear internal governance arrangements are necessary to guide the ethical and effective use of AI in decision-making processes
note: Putting them in place 'may entail establishing dedicated AI strategies for development and adoption, clearly establishing roles and responsibilities, creating oversight mechanisms and promoting collaboration'. Appointing who decides is implied but no role is named. Also coded Accountability/Design.

quote: The first step in this direction is the assessment and, where necessary, revision of national AI strategies to align with the sector-specific, bottom-up and use-case-driven approach proposed in the Strategy.
note: Heading: 'Recognise the public sector as a strategic domain in (national) AI strategies by deciding on dedicated actions, governance arrangements and priority use cases.' Setting national direction. The quoted Commission call to Member States is a report of the Strategy.

quote: a downstream modifier is considered to be the provider of a general-purpose AI model is that the training compute used for the modification is greater than a third of  the training compute of the original model
note: Indicative criterion. Fallback if original compute unknown: one third of 10^25 FLOP (systemic-risk model) or of 10^23 FLOP (para 61). Fine-tuning counts as modifying (footnote 12); who controls weights matters (footnote 13). A public body fine-tuning a model could be such a modifier [inference].

quote: If one of these rights (i.e. rights to access, use, modify, and redistribute) is missing, the licence cannot be considered free and open-source under the AI Act.
if_not_met: provider not exempt from Art. 53(1)(a)-(b) and Art. 54 (para 75)
note: Exemption scope. Exceptions never apply to systemic-risk models (paras 70-71). Disqualifying licence restrictions (para 80); monetisation, including personal-data collection, defeats the exception (paras 82-86); parameters and usage information must be public (paras 87-89).

quote: request measures from providers, including implementing mitigation  measures and recalling the model from the market (Article 93  AI Act)
note: Authority to stop (recall). From 2 August 2026 (paras 103, 112). Also power to request information (Art. 91).

quote: t he Commission has the  exclusive competence to enforce compliance of providers of general-purpose AI models
holder: European Commission (implemented through the AI Office)
note: Enforcement authority over GPAI model providers, with and without systemic risk; implementation entrusted to the AI Office (Art. 3(47)). Powers listed in para 103 (coded separately).

quote: providers of general-purpose AI models placed on the market before 2 August 2025 are not required to conduct retraining or unlearning of models, where it is not possible to do this  for actions performed in the past
holder: European Commission (interpretation); applies to providers of models placed on the market before 2 August 2025
note: Also where training-data information 'is not available, or where its retrieval would cause the provider disproportionate burden'. Art. 111(3), quoted in para (106) across a page break, gives these providers until 2 August 2027. The condition (disclosure) is coded as Accountability/Design.

quote: The AI Office will monitor the situation and , if necessary, work to set out a common approach for external model evaluators, for instance, by involving the network of evaluators and other subject-matter experts.
note: Possible standard for external model evaluators (testing). 'the Commission plans to take into account during enforcement that the ecosystem of external model evaluators is still developing'. Status: not yet done. Also coded as Coordination/Design.

quote: During its review, the Commission may decide to withdraw or amend these guidelines.
note: Trigger: review 'as soon as it becomes necessary in the light of practical experience', technological, societal and market developments, enforcement experience and CJEU rulings. Also see Coordination/Design (input to review).

quote: an indicative criterion for  a model to be considered a general-purpose AI model is that its training compute is greater than 1023 FLOP and it can generate language
note: Continues: '(whether in the form of text3 or audio4), text-to-image, or text-to-video.' '1023' = 10^23 (superscript lost; 3 and 4 are footnote markers). Para (20): meeting the criterion without significant generality means not a GPAI model, and vice versa. Para (16): approach 'may change'. Decides which models, and so which providers, are in scope.

quote: the Commission considers the lifecycle of a general -purpose AI model to begin at the start of the large pre -training run
note: Any later development by or for the provider is the same model; modification by other actors is handled in Section 3.2. Effect: documentation, copyright policy and systemic-risk duties run across the whole lifecycle (para (23)).

quote: Under Article 51(3) AI Act, the Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts, in line with Article 97 AI Act, to amend the thresholds set out in Article 51(1) and (2) AI Act.
note: Also 'empowered to introduce additional benchmarks and indicators'. Sets the threshold that triggers systemic-risk duties (10^25 FLOP presumption, Art. 51(2)).

quote: Upon receiving a notification with arguments for why the model does not present systemic risks, the Commission will assess the arguments and decide whether to accept or reject them
obligation: statutory power (procedure described in non-binding guidelines)
note: Test: 'sufficiently substantiated arguments manifestly calling into question this presumption' (para (36)); considers how far compute exceeds the threshold and benchmark scores (para (38)); mitigations 'are not suitable grounds' (para (39)). Decisions possible from 2 August 2025 (para (104)). Also coded as Accountability/Design.

quote: the Commission may designate a general-purpose AI model as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk on its own in itiative (ex officio) or following a qualified alert from the scientific panel
note: Grounds (para (43)): Annex XIII criteria, or failure to notify. Obligations apply from when the provider is informed (Annex XIII route) or from when the threshold was met (failure to notify) (para (44)). Also coded as Coordination/Design (scientific panel alert).

quote: a general-purpose AI model is used for internal processes that are essential for providing a product or service to third parties or that affect the rights of natural persons in the Union.
holder: European Commission (interpretation); applies to actors that develop a general-purpose AI model
note: Last of nine examples of placing on the market; examples 'require case-by-case assessment' (para (52)). Para (47) quotes the provider definition: 'a natural or legal person, public authority, agency or other body that develops … a general-purpose AI model'. [inference] A public body developing a GPAI model and using it internally in ways affecting people's rights could thereby be a provider; public bodies are not discussed.

quote: The downstream actor integrating the model into an AI system and placing the system on the Union market or putting  it into service in the Union may be the provider of the system.
holder: European Commission (interpretation); applies to upstream and downstream actors
note: The upstream actor that first makes the model available in the Union is the model provider; the downstream integrator 'has  to comply with the applicable requirements and obligations for AI systems laid down in the AI Act'.
