basis: AI pass A; different cell in pass B

quote: Developing and applying certification and labelling approaches based on common sustainability principles aligned with the EU environmental policies
note: A check against 'common sustainability principles aligned with the EU environmental policies, such as the Green Deal and the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals'. Labelling is a public-facing signal and could also be read as Accountability. Example given: AI4CITIES pre-commercial procurement (practice).

quote: start measuring their impact on AI -enabled public solutions in a systematic fashion.
location: page 46 (printed p. 44), Section 4 'Perspective timing for interventions'
note: Systematic measurement of the impact of AI-enabled public solutions. Trigger: ongoing and systematic. Compares against framework conditions and influencing factors. Metric not stated. Context: 'a lack of impact measurement frameworks that could be used as benchmarks'.

quote: It would also monitor the current implementation and use of AI in the public sector throughout Europe, including descriptions and information sources.
note: Sector-wide monitoring of how AI is implemented and used. Trigger: ongoing [inference]. Compares against: not stated. Metric: not stated. The observatory would also track 'emerging technologies displaying potential application and impact when associated to AI' and cross-cutting issues: interoperability, standards, data management, legal and ethical frameworks.

quote: they concern different information that must be provided to the natural persons, but they can be combined in single notifications
location: Annex, === page 11 (printed p. 10), Section 2.5, fn (14) to para (25)
holder: Deployers of high-risk AI systems that make or assist in making decisions related to natural persons (Art. 26(11)) who are also subject to Art. 50
note: Relevant to public bodies using high-risk AI in decisions about people, who must tell people they are subject to its use under Art. 26(11) [inference]. The two notices are 'complementary'; para (25): Art. 50 compliance 'does not replace, limit or affect obligations arising under other provisions of the AI Act'.

quote: require disclosure for the specific outputs in the interaction that are AI -generated, unless th ose AI outputs have been properly reviewed and sent by humans as the main interlocutors with the natural persons
location: Annex, === page 13 (printed p. 12), Section 3.1.1, para (30) iii
holder: Providers of AI systems directly interacting with natural persons (products and services blending AI-generated responses with human-curated content)
if_not_met: Fines (para (152)): 'may be fined up to EUR 15 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 3% of its total worldwide annual turnover'; EU institutions, bodies and agencies 'may be subject to administrativ e fines of up to EUR 750 000'.
note: Sets when human review takes an output out of the disclosure duty: only where outputs are 'properly reviewed and sent by humans as the main interlocutors' (standard of review not further defined). Also: 'the mere possibility for humans to intervene or review the AI system’s outputs should not be used to circumvent the application' of the duty. Indirect use is outside Art. 50(1), e.g. 'if customer service representatives use AI assistance tools to help them communicate with natural persons'; so are 'backend decision -support systems where the user only sees the AI output without possibility for direct interaction with the system' (examples, === page 14). Relevant to public-service contact centres and caseworker tools [inference]. Trigger: per output.

quote: the characteristics of natural persons belonging to vulnerable groups due to their age (e.g. children or the elderly) or disability are taken into account to the extent that the AI system is intended or reasonably likely to interact
holder: Providers of AI systems directly interacting with natural persons
if_not_met: Fines (para (152)): 'may be fined up to EUR 15 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 3% of its total worldwide annual turnover'; EU institutions, bodies and agencies 'may be subject to administrativ e fines of up to EUR 750 000'.
note: One of two conditions on the provider's free choice of disclosure technique; the other is Art. 50(5). Also: information 'must also be provided in an accessible format for natural persons with disabilities'; 'Where the system may interact with children, t hose notifications must be  child-friendly, age -appropriate'. Fn (19): a system meant for any member of the public includes vulnerable groups, so public services open to all are covered [inference]. Para (35): information adapted where interaction with vulnerable groups is reasonably foreseeable.

quote: “business to business applications” (excluding public and consumer -facing AI systems ) where the proportionality principle and the limited benefits for the transparency objectives  means that no marking and detection of AI-generated or manipulated outputs is required
holder: not stated (providers of generative AI systems benefit; who decides that the conditions are met is not stated)
if_not_met: If any condition fails, marking and detection apply [inference]
note: Three cumulative conditions: strictly technical output (incl. 'internal documentation processes'); perceived only by 'a limited pre-defined number of natural persons acting in a professional capacity within the organisation of the provider and the deployer'; not intended to be shared outside the company, with safeguards (e.g. cloud isolation, role-based controls). Public-facing systems are excluded. Whether a public body's internal-only tools can use the exemption is not addressed [inference].

quote: AI-generated summaries of text ; paraphrasing or rewriting text that changes style, structure and meaning beyond mere grammatical and minor stylistic correction
location: Annex, === page 30 (printed p. 29), Section 4.3, examples after para (92)
holder: Providers of AI systems generating or manipulating text
if_not_met: Fines (para (152)): 'may be fined up to EUR 15 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 3% of its total worldwide annual turnover'; EU institutions, bodies and agencies 'may be subject to administrativ e fines of up to EUR 750 000'.
note: Listed under 'Examples of semantic changes that require marking under Article 50(2) AI Act'. The standard-editing exception covers, among others, 'AI-generated translations of text' and 'Transcriptions of conversations'. Whether an alteration is substantial 'requires a case-specific assessment' (para (91)); who assesses is not stated (nearest: provider). Relevant to public-sector summarisation, translation and transcription tools [inference].

quote: Deployers are required to inform natural persons concerned that they are exposed to  an emotion recognition system or to a biometric categorisation system, which is being operated.
holder: Deployers of emotion recognition systems and biometric categorisation systems
if_not_met: Fines (para (152)): 'may be fined up to EUR 15 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 3% of its total worldwide annual turnover'; EU institutions, bodies and agencies 'may be subject to administrativ e fines of up to EUR 750 000'.
note: Must inform 'all natural persons exposed to the operation of the AI system, including children' (para (106)), at the latest at first exposure (para (108)), clearly, distinguishably and accessibly; means depend on place of deployment (e.g. 'train station') (para (107)). Informing does not make the use lawful (para (110)); emotion recognition is also high-risk and prohibited at work and in education (paras (25), (102)). Deployers 'can consider adding notifications' to data protection notices (para (110)).

quote: Human review refers to the deliberate  examination of the substance of the content by one or more natural persons possessing relevant knowledge and professional judgement pertaining to the subject matter under scrutiny
holder: Deployers relying on the human-review exception (the reviewers: natural persons with relevant knowledge)
obligation: non-binding interpretation (condition for relying on a statutory exception)
if_not_met: Exception does not apply, so the AI-generated text must be labelled [inference]
note: Check: human review of AI-generated text. Trigger: before publication, and again after any substantive AI change (para (136)). Compared against the substance and accuracy of the content; fact-checking is the minimum (coded separately). Not enough: 'Superficial, solely formal  or procedural check s (e.g. spell-checking or grammatical correction), the mere existence of an editorial policy , automated review processes  or cursory editorial approval' (para (135)). Metric: not stated. Public-sector example: 'AI-generated public safety warnings approved by a public official before being distributed to citizens, under the responsibility of the relevant public agency for civil protection' (examples after para (138)). Reviewer staffing coded as Delivery/Resources.

quote: Information will not be considered to be provided in a clear and distinguishable manner where it can be easily overlooked or missed by natural persons under normal exposure or interaction conditions
holder: Providers and deployers subject to Art. 50(1)-(4)
if_not_met: Fines (para (152)): 'may be fined up to EUR 15 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 3% of its total worldwide annual turnover'; EU institutions, bodies and agencies 'may be subject to administrativ e fines of up to EUR 750 000'.
note: Clear = 'noticeable, easy to understand by and accessible'; distinguishable = 'easy to identify as separate from other information'. Insufficient: 'only included as  part of a manual or hidden under layers of menu options on an online interface, part of terms of use'. Where children are in the audience, fn (40) lists requirements (child-friendly, in the official language(s) of the Member State, etc.).

quote: the information obligation applies to each output of an AI system with respect to any natural person exposed to the content
holder: Providers and deployers subject to Art. 50(2) and (4)
if_not_met: Fines (para (152)): 'may be fined up to EUR 15 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 3% of its total worldwide annual turnover'; EU institutions, bodies and agencies 'may be subject to administrativ e fines of up to EUR 750 000'.
note: Trigger: 'at the latest at the time of the first interaction or exposure', including each new person's first exposure; for interactive systems information 'should, at least, be provided once at the start of an interactive session'. If people may not see content from its start, disclosure at the beginning should be complemented later.

quote: must be aware of the applicable accessibility requirements ( e.g. under Directive 2016/2102 (41) and Directive 2019/882 (42)) and assess whether their product, service or content needs to comply with those rules
holder: Providers and deployers of AI systems within the scope of Art. 50(1)-(4)
note: Directive 2016/2102 concerns 'the accessibility of the websites and mobile applications of public sector bodies' (fn (41)), so public bodies are directly concerned [inference]. Check: assess whether the product, service or content must comply; if so 'ensure accessibility of the information'. 'Article 50 AI Act does not impose distinct or additional accessibility requirements.'

quote: This requires all in scope AI systems placed on the market or put into service in the Union to be compliant with that provision on that date
holder: Providers and deployers of in-scope AI systems
if_not_met: Fines (para (152)): 'may be fined up to EUR 15 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 3% of its total worldwide annual turnover'; EU institutions, bodies and agencies 'may be subject to administrativ e fines of up to EUR 750 000'.
note: Trigger: 2 August 2026, regardless of when the system was placed on the market. The AI Omnibus gives providers of generative systems placed before that date 'a transitional period to bring their systems in conformity by 2 December 2026', for Art. 50(2) marking only; disclosure for interactive systems applies from 2 August 2026. The high-risk grandfathering rule (Art. 111(2)) does not apply to Art. 50 (fn (50)).

quote: Conversely, if texts that have been generated or manipulated before 2 August 2026 are published on or after that date, they need to be labelled
holder: Deployers publishing AI-generated or manipulated text on matters of public interest
if_not_met: Fines (para (152)): 'may be fined up to EUR 15 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 3% of its total worldwide annual turnover'; EU institutions, bodies and agencies 'may be subject to administrativ e fines of up to EUR 750 000'.
note: Trigger: publication on or after 2 August 2026. No retroactive marking or labelling of content generated (or text published) before that date; holders of pre-existing unlabelled deep fakes are 'encouraged' to label them without disproportionate efforts such as 'auditing of pre-existing content databases'.

quote: ensure all relevant transparency obligations in Articles 50(1), (2) and (5) AI Act are met at the latest when those systems are placed on the market or put into service
holder: Providers of interactive or generative AI systems
if_not_met: Fines (para (152)): 'may be fined up to EUR 15 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 3% of its total worldwide annual turnover'; EU institutions, bodies and agencies 'may be subject to administrativ e fines of up to EUR 750 000'.
note: Timing of the provider duties. Trigger: at the latest at placing on the market / putting into service, then ongoing: 'All natural persons interacting with the AI system or exposed to its outputs in scope must be effectively and consistently informed throughout the lifecycle' (para (11)), 'irrespective of who the deployers or other users of the system are'. Transparency to be 'embedded into the system’s design and operation'.

quote: Any substantive AI intervention occurring after the human review or editorial control process has taken place will therefore cause the exception to become void.
holder: Deployers relying on the human-review or editorial-control exception
if_not_met: The exception becomes void and the text must be treated as AI-generated or manipulated (para (136))
note: Trigger: on change after sign-off. 'Where AI systems are used to modify, supplement, or reformulate content following editorial sign-off, the resulting content must be treated as AI -generated or manipulated'.

quote: Testing in real world conditions  (inside or outside of AI regulatory sandboxes) is not covered by that exclusion.
holder: Providers (and deployers) testing AI systems in real-world conditions
note: Coded as Delivery because it sets when the transparency duties start: pilots in real-world conditions remain subject to Art. 50; the R&D exclusions cover only research before placing on the market or the sole purpose of scientific research (paras (21)-(22)). Relevant to public-sector pilots and sandboxes [inference].
basis: AI pass B; different cell in pass A

quote: Providers of such systems  are nevertheless encouraged to design those models , components, and services in a manner described in paragraph 27 below, insofar as this is proportionate and feasible.
holder: Providers of free and open-source AI components (software, data, models, tools, services or processes) that are not AI systems
note: Value-chain actor. Para 27 describes model-level transparency measures (identification of interactive AI, marking of AI-generated content).

quote: providers of other GPAI models and of other generative AI models are also encouraged to implement appropriate transparency measures at the model level
holder: Providers of other GPAI models and of other generative AI models
obligation: encouraged; for GPAI models with systemic risk, may form part of a statutory mitigation duty
note: Model providers' duties (value chain). Measures: identification of interactive AI systems and marking of AI-generated content. Where the system is built on the same provider's GPAI model, measures 'could also be implemented at the model level'. Also coded as Coordination/Design (helps downstream providers).
basis: AI pass A; different cell in pass B

quote: providers of AI systems directly interacting with natural persons, who must design and develop their systems in such a way that the natural persons concerned are informed that they are interacting with an AI system.
holder: Providers of AI systems directly interacting with natural persons
if_not_met: fines up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3% of worldwide annual turnover; EU institutions, bodies and agencies up to EUR 750 000 (para 152)
note: Core Art. 50(1) duty; repeated at para 32. Scope test: AI system, intended to interact, directly, with natural persons (para 30). In scope (examples, page 13): chatbots 'in various contexts (e.g. public service, customer support, complaints management...)', 'AI hotline for incidents, fraud or other reporting', AI agents. Out of scope (page 14): recommender systems, spam filters, automated translation or transcription tools, search and retrieval without generating content, 'backend decision -support systems where the user only sees the AI output'. Also coded as Accountability/Design (para 35).

quote: AI agents must be designed and developed in such a way that they disclose both their artificial nature and the person on whose behalf they are acting
holder: Providers of AI agents capable of interacting with natural persons
note: Rationale: 'the need for transparency of the origin and the delegation of authority and accountability for the consequences of their actions'. Where the provider cannot tell in advance whether the agent will meet natural persons, the agent 'should be designed at the architecture level, and instructed, to disclose itself' whenever reasonably likely. Agents 'should also disclose themselves, to the persons instructing them at key steps (e.g. at the point of authorisation, reporting, validation etc.' and at every new interaction. Trigger: each interaction and key steps. Fn (21) points to EU Digital Identity Wallets for verifiable agent identity (Delivery/Resources).
basis: AI pass B; different cell in pass A

quote: the agent should be designed at the architecture level, and instructed, to disclose itself as such  in every situation where it is reasonably likely that the agent may interact with a natural person
note: Applies where the provider cannot determine in advance whether the agent will meet natural persons. Agents should also disclose themselves to those instructing them 'at key steps (e.g. at the point of authorisation, reporting, validation etc.' and at every new interaction. Trigger: before placing on the market and in each interaction. Also coded as Accountability/Design.

quote: Providers are responsible for ensuring that, after the AI system’s placement on the market or putting into service, natural persons interacting with the AI system are effectively and consistently informed throughout the lifecy cle of the AI system
note: Trigger: at the latest at first interaction (Art. 50(5)), then ongoing through the lifecycle. Quote keeps the extraction error 'lifecy cle'.

quote: The information must also be provided in an accessible format for natural persons with disabilities, as specified in Article 50(5) and Recital 132 AI Act
note: Accessibility and vulnerable groups (age, disability). Footnote 19: if a system is meant to interact with any member of the public, vulnerable groups are included and 'should be considered by providers'. Notifications for children 'must be' child-friendly and age-appropriate (same para). [inference] Public-facing public-service tools fall here.

quote: The design of the AI system with multimodal and accessible disclosure approaches is recommended as a best practice .
note: Techniques listed: textual banners and first-turn greetings (e.g. 'You are interacting with an AI system'), spoken statements, visual cues, multimodal combinations. Choice may depend on 'the available resources of the providers, in particular Small and Medium Sized Enterprises (SMEs)'.

quote: Certain techniques are not necessary and, when used alone, insufficient for effectively fulfilling the transparency obligation in Article 50(1) and (5) AI Act
note: Insufficient alone: disclosures only in terms and conditions, URLs or documentation; machine-readable marks not perceivable at interaction; ambiguous signals such as 'assistant'; generic statements like 'Services on this website use AI'; 'this system uses LLMs'. Works as the standard the disclosure is checked against.

quote: in certa in riskier contexts, periodic reminders and context-aware disclosures are likely to be necessary to ensure continued user awareness.
note: Trigger: ongoing in riskier contexts, which include vulnerable persons and 'financial advice, insurance, legal assistance, health advice , and complaints handling'. Otherwise a single prominent notice before first interaction 'is likely to suffice'. Quote keeps 'certa in'.

quote: Providers must also design and develop the AI system to  ensure disclosure in all situations where the AI system is being asked questions relating to its nature or to the origin of the interaction
note: Trigger: on being asked, or where the person is likely to be misled or confused about AI origin (same sentence).

quote: To be able to rely on the first exception, providers will need to assess and demonstrate: i) the obvious artificial  nature of the interaction to ii) a natural person who must be  reasonably well -informed, observant and circumspect
obligation: condition for relying on an exception (non-binding interpretation)
note: Assessment. Trigger: before relying on the 'obvious' exception. Compared against: the 'average consumer' standard of EU consumer law (para 43), set by target and foreseeable audience, vulnerable groups, digital and AI literacy, social, cultural and linguistic factors (para 44). Metric: none; qualitative. 'demonstrate' also coded as Accountability/Design. 37 words.

quote: If a respective system can both be used for law enforcement purposes, as well as for other regular purposes, the applicability of the exemption should be assessed in light of the particular deployment.
if_not_met: transparency obligations apply to the other uses
note: Assessment per deployment. Trigger: each deployment. Nearest named actors: providers; Union or national public authorities using the system.

quote: Such systems may be used , but they  remain subject to  the transparency obligation under Article  50(1) AI Act, so natural persons must be informed they are interacting with such systems.
holder: Providers of AI systems available to the public that offer a functionality to report criminal offences (e.g. police, other law enforcement authorities, public authorities, financial institutions)
note: Exception to the law-enforcement exception. Examples: 'AI-enabled police chatbots deployed on official police websites or mobile applications', 'AI-powered telephone hotlines operated by the police', 'AI-assisted fraud reporting hotlines or digital portals operated by financial institutions or public authorities', and virtual assistants for witness statements. Also: 'Transparency obligations continue to apply where the same AI system is deployed for other purposes' than authorised law enforcement (para (48)). The examples describe human officers validating reports, but no human-review duty is set here.
basis: AI pass B; different cell in pass A

quote: First, providers must ensure that the outputs of the AI system are marked in a machine-readable format. Second, providers must ensure that the outputs are detectable as artificially generated or manipulated  content.
holder: Providers of generative AI systems (including GPAI systems and agentic systems) generating or manipulating synthetic audio, image, video or text
if_not_met: fines up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3% of worldwide annual turnover; EU institutions, bodies and agencies up to EUR 750 000 (para 152); fulfilling only one element 'will not suffice to comply' (para 70)
note: Core Art. 50(2) duty. Scope: paras 56-63 (text, image, audio, video, multimodal, 3-D, VR, digital twins; AI agents' perceptible outputs, para 63). Out of scope: short outputs, source code, machine-to-machine outputs, closed-loop intermediate outputs (para 68), reproductions or rankings of existing content, internal analytics that 'extract and structure data, but do not summarise it' (para 65). Providers are 'not required to record or keep a full provenance chain' (para 73). Transition for systems placed before 2 August 2026: until 2 December 2026 (para 153).

quote: Providers must ensure that the combination of the technical solutions for marking and detection holistically meet all aforementioned requirements to the legally required degree
if_not_met: fines (para 152); non-adhering providers may face more requests for information and access (para 148)
note: Check. Criteria (para 79): effectiveness; reliability ('accurately identify ... in nominal conditions'); robustness ('under varying conditions, covering both common alterations and adversarial attacks'); interoperability. Compared against: 'generally acknowledged state of the art' and technical standards (paras 80-83), within technical feasibility and costs (paras 81, 85). Metric: none numeric. Trigger: ongoing (para 83). Para 81: feasibility 'is not dependent on the specific resources and capabilities of individual providers'.

quote: Providers must continuously adapt their marking and detection solutions in a timely and proportionate manner as the technology and state of the art evolves.
note: Trigger: on change in the state of the art; ongoing. Compared against: state of the art (defined para 83 with reference to Commission Implementing Decision C(2025) 3871, footnote 28).

quote: for the purpose of marking and detection the information related to the creator of the content should not be processed and any other personal data processed should be deleted as soon as the purpose of detection is fulfilled
holder: Providers of AI systems employing marking and detection solutions
obligation: statutory duty under other law (Commission's non-binding interpretation)
note: Data-protection limits on marking and detection: data protection by design and default, data minimisation, security and confidentiality. 38 words.

quote: The information must be provided at the latest at the time of the first interaction with or exposure to the AI system in accordance with Article 50(5) AI Act.
holder: Deployers of emotion recognition systems and biometric categorisation systems
note: Trigger: first interaction or exposure; earlier provision allowed. Means not prescribed (para 107): writing, standardised icons, orally; depends on place (e.g. 'train station'), addressees, exposure type. Deployers 'can consider adding notifications' to data-protection notices (para 110). Also coded as Accountability/Design.

quote: Whether the level of resemblance is appreciable is a case -by-case assessment  to be done by the deployer  based on an objective comparison between the simulated subject and the deep fake content
note: Assessment. Trigger: each piece of content. Compared against: the simulated subject; whether content would falsely appear authentic is assessed 'as a whole' and objectively, intent not required (para 114), with regard to the foreseeable audience including children, the elderly and persons with lower AI literacy (para 115). Deployers 'are not expected to consider potential further dissemination' beyond the foreseeable audience (para 115). Metric: none.

quote: Article 50(4), first subparagraph, AI Act obliges deployers of AI systems that generate or manipulate image, audio or video content constituting a deep fake to ‘disclose that the deep fake content has been artificially generated or manipulated ’.
holder: Deployers (professional use) of AI systems generating or manipulating deep fake image, audio or video content
if_not_met: fines (para 152); non-adhering deployers may face requests for information on labelling (para 148)
note: Labels must be 'understandable and perceivable by natural persons' without technical tools; 'deployers cannot rely on the machine-readable marking' by the provider. Deployers may adhere to an adequate code of practice (para (118)). Where content is both informative and creative, 'the informati ve character should always prevail' (para (122)). Examples of deep fakes include a 'realistic synthetic avatar of a company CEO' and a video 'of an individual resembling a politician'; relevant to public bodies using synthetic presenters [inference]. Attenuated regime for evidently artistic, creative, satirical or fictional works (paras (119)-(123)).
basis: AI pass B; different cell in pass A

quote: Labelling or disclosure methods applied in accordance with Article 50(4), first subparagraph, AI Act should be understandable and perceivable by natural persons (e.g. with visible or audible labels), without them needing to rely  on any specific technical tools
holder: Deployers of AI systems generating or manipulating deep fakes
note: Deployers 'cannot rely on the machine- readable marking embedded in the content by the provider' (same para). Also coded as Accountability/Design.

quote: deployers need to ensure that the rights and freedoms of third  parties (including e.g. their right to the protection of personal data or intellectual property rights) are adequately safeguarded and respected, when creating or publishing deep fake s
note: Safeguards apply even to artistic or satirical deep fakes. Footnote 34: 'This equally applies to published texts informing the public on matters of public interest.' Paras 127-129 point to data protection, IP and personality-rights law (reports of other law, not coded separately). 37 words.

quote: texts should be considered to address public interest matters  if they  cover topics on politics  and democratic processes , public administration and services, the administration of justice and law enforcement
holder: Deployers of AI systems generating or manipulating published text
note: Brings much public-sector communication within the text-labelling duty [inference]. The list continues: fundamental rights, public security, public health, environment, consumer safety and any development 'that may be relevant subject of public debate'. 'Published' means accessible to an indeterminate, fairly large number of readers; 'organisation-internal texts or communications' are not published (para (131) i).
basis: AI pass B; different cell in pass A

quote: obliges deployers of AI systems that generate or manipulate text which is published with the purpose of informing the public on matters of public interest to disclose that such text has been artificially generated or manipulated
holder: Deployers of AI systems generating or manipulating text published to inform the public on matters of public interest
note: Public bodies publishing AI-generated public information are in scope [inference]; example in scope: 'AI-generated message on a meteorological institute’s social media profile warning citizens about stormy weather'. Labels must be 'clear and perceivable by natural persons' without technical tools; deployers may use an adequate code of practice. Exceptions: human review or editorial control plus editorial responsibility (para (133)ff) and use authorised by law for law enforcement (para (139)). Internal or private texts are not 'published' (para (131) i).
basis: AI pass B; different cell in pass A

quote: Fact-checking the accuracy of the content is a minimum requirement that should be part of that review .
holder: Deployers relying on the exception (review by natural persons with relevant knowledge)
obligation: condition for relying on an exception (non-binding interpretation, 'should')
if_not_met: exception unavailable; disclosure required. 'Any substantive AI intervention occurring after the human review or editorial control process has taken place will therefore cause the exception to become void.' (para 136)
note: Human review of AI outputs. Defined as 'deliberate examination of the substance of the content by one or more natural persons possessing relevant knowledge and professional judgement'. Trigger: before publication. Compared against: accuracy (fact-checking); metric not stated. Insufficient: superficial or procedural checks, 'the mere existence of an editorial policy', automated review, cursory approval (para 135). Example (page 45): 'AI-generated public safety warnings approved by a public official before being distributed to citizens, under the responsibility of the relevant public agency for civil protection.'

quote: the information to be provided in accordance with Article 50(1) to (4) AI Act should be provided to the natural persons concerned in a clear and distinguishable manner, at the latest at the time of the first interaction or exposure.
holder: Providers and deployers subject to Article 50(1)-(4)
note: Horizontal standard for all disclosures. Not clear and distinguishable if 'only included as part of a manual or hidden under layers of menu options' or in terms of use (para 142). Trigger: first interaction or exposure for each new person and, for content, 'each output' (para 143). Footnote 40 sets six conditions for notices to children. 39 words.

quote: they must ensure accessibility of the information conveyed in line with Article 50 AI Act in accordance with the applicable accessibility requirements.
holder: Providers and deployers of AI systems within scope of Article 50(1)-(4)
obligation: statutory duty where the accessibility law applies (Commission's non-binding interpretation)
note: Holders 'must be aware of the applicable accessibility requirements' and assess whether they apply. Directive 2016/2102 covers 'websites and mobile applications of public sector bodies' (footnote 41), so [inference] public bodies' disclosures fall under it. 'Article 50 AI Act does not impose distinct or additional accessibility requirements.'

quote: they should carry out a gap analysis that compares the measures they have implemented with the measures set out by a code of practice that is assessed as adequate.
holder: Providers and deployers that are not signatories to an adequate code of practice
if_not_met: more requests for information and access (para 148)
note: Check. Compared against: the measures of an adequate code of practice. Trigger: not stated. Metric: not stated. Also coded with the Accountability entry for para 148.

quote: deployers of AI systems  and other actors who are in the possession of or disseminate pre-existing unlabelled deep fakes are, nonetheless,  encouraged to do so
holder: Deployers of AI systems and other actors possessing or disseminating pre-existing unlabelled deep fakes
obligation: encouraged (pre-existing content); statutory duty for older texts published on or after 2 August 2026
note: No retroactive marking or labelling required, but 'if texts that have been generated or manipulated before 2 August 2026 are published on or after that date, they need to be labelled'. No 'auditing of pre-existing content databases' expected.

quote: Providers must ensure their interactive or generative AI systems have transparency embedded into the system’s design and operation
holder: Providers (natural or legal persons, public authorities, agencies or other bodies)
if_not_met: fines up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3% of worldwide annual turnover; EU institutions, bodies and agencies up to EUR 750 000 (para 152)
note: Trigger: 'at the latest when those systems are placed on the market or put into service', then throughout the lifecycle 'irrespective of who the deployers or other users of the system are' (same para). Applies whether established in or outside the Union (para 10).

quote: Relevant use cases must be identified, tested and validated through an inclusive process, involving the end-users.
note: Testing and validation of use cases for Members. Trigger: before use [inference]. Compared against: not stated. Metric: not stated. End-user involvement could also be read as Coordination. Nearest named actor: Parliament's administration.

quote: The administration will address inherent risks through continuous oversight during the entire lifecycle of the product or service.
location: page 3, II. Compliance and control, para 12
note: Monitoring. Trigger: ongoing, whole lifecycle. Compared against: not stated. Metric: not stated.

note: Edge case: a defence against AI used by attackers; no AI tool of the authority is involved. Body text p. 12: 'Proactive scanning of critical infrastructure by National CSIRTs becomes even more relevant.'

quote: Risk assessments should blend logging and monitoring requirements with runtime AI guards, access controls, and threat intelligence sharing, to enable real-time detection and response.
holder: Service providers, including newly expanded providers under the scope of NIS2
note: Risk assessment, logging and monitoring; trigger: ongoing ('real-time'). Preceding sentence: service providers 'must harden operations against AI-scale threats such as adaptive phishing, model poisoning, and supply-chain pivots' (model poisoning concerns their own AI models). ENISA has no power to impose 'must' (legal notice).

quote: Developers of AI models should train their models to be structurally constrained (stronger than a guardrail), and ensure that such models are suggesting code that is secure by design/default.
note: Model provider duty in the value chain. Check/metric not stated.

quote: A cross-cutting challenge will be to ensure that foreseen solutions will keep the human in the middle.
location: Security fundamentals, '4. Talent and human capital'; p. 12
note: Human oversight of AI-based security solutions: 'humans will still need to understand the environments they assume responsibility for.' Holder unnamed; nearest: organisations using AI for defence.
basis: AI pass A; different cell in pass B

quote: This threat model demands detection and response strategies that go beyond perimeter-oriented defences and assume that adversaries may already be present within trusted environments.
location: page 10, Impact on Vulnerability & Patch Management, 'The Risk of Inside-Out Attacks'
note: Threat is that adversaries 'are increasingly compromising the AI and software supply chain to land inside infrastructure directly, for example by arriving through a trusted software update or a compromised open-source dependency'. Concerns the security of AI components an organisation brings in, including public bodies [inference]. Quote joins a line-end hyphen ('perimeter-' / 'oriented') without a space.

quote: verifying these AI-generated patches may become a major bottleneck. System managers may face challenges to build tools that can quickly check and approve these fixes without accidentally introducing new bugs into the code.
location: page 11, Security fundamentals matter more than ever, 1. Vulnerability management
obligation: ENISA analysis of a challenge; no requirement
note: Checking AI outputs (AI-generated patches). Trigger: before deployment [inference]; comparator: no new bugs or vulnerabilities; metric not stated. Page 9 ('The Verification Bottleneck'): technical teams face 'how to audit and validate AI-generated patches so that they do not introduce new vulnerabilities'. A challenge is named; no check or holder is prescribed.

quote: Embed structured threat modelling early and continuously, leveraging advanced AI models with precise context to uncover combinations of weaknesses
location: page 15, The way ahead, Recommendations, Defenders (bullet 2)
note: Defenders using AI models for testing: 'run continuous simulations against live architectures, effectively turning AI into an always-on support capability for red teaming and defensive validation'. Trigger: early and continuous.

quote: The training personal data to be fed to a specific AI system needs to be formatted, checked against applicable quality and legal requirements , and normalised before they can be used.
location: p.10, s.3.2 Lifecycle of an AI system (phase 2)
obligation: descriptive of the typical lifecycle (needs to)
note: Nearest named actor: EUIs developing an AI system. Trigger: before use in training. Comparator: 'applicable quality and legal requirements'. Metric not stated. Section 3.2 describes the typical lifecycle (after ISO/IEC 22989) rather than prescribing it.

quote: to ensure it meets the functional and non -functional requirements set in the inception stage. This involves checking the AI system's statistical accuracy, r obustness, and generalisability  using test and validation datasets
location: p.10, s.3.2 Lifecycle of an AI system (phase 4)
note: Verification and validation. Trigger: after development, before deployment. Comparator: functional and non-functional requirements set at inception. Metric: statistical accuracy, robustness, generalisability on test and validation datasets; issues addressed by retraining. For procured systems this phase sits in contract execution (p.12). Nearest named actor: EUIs or the external provider.

quote: Once deployed, the AI system is then operated by its users and needs continuous monitoring to ensure it operates as expected.
location: p.10, s.3.2 Lifecycle of an AI system (phase 6)
note: Operation and monitoring. Trigger: ongoing after deployment. Comparator: expected operation. Metric: 'tracking performance' (unspecified). Who monitors is not stated; 'users' operate the system.

quote: The system’s performance is regularly assessed using test data to e nsure proper functioning.
location: p.11, s.3.2 Lifecycle of an AI system (phase 7)
note: Continuous validation. Trigger: where the system uses continuous learning; regular. Test data 'may need to be updated periodically' to reflect production data.

quote: The operational results of the system should be thoroughly analysed and compared against the identified risks associated with the AI system to verify if the identified risks have been suitably mitigated.
location: p.11, s.3.2 Lifecycle of an AI system (phase 8)
note: Re-evaluation. Trigger: after operation and monitoring, when reassessment 'may become necessary'. Comparator: the identified risks. Newly identified risks go into the next risk management cycle (s.2).

quote: it is also important to acknowledge , already in the procurement cycle , making a risk evaluation before any budget is actually committed for a solution that would bring undesirable risks to the organisation.
location: p.11, s.3.3 Procuring an AI system
note: Nearest named actor: EUIs procuring AI systems. Trigger: during procurement, before budget is committed. Works as a pre-commitment check [inference]; whose decision it informs is not stated.

quote: The corresponding mitigating measures should be devised for each of the indicated phases, if relevant.
location: p.12, s.3.3 Procuring an AI system
note: Nearest named actor: the controller. Phases where each risk can materialise are flagged for each risk in Sections 4-5 ('blue boxes'). Applies to development and procurement.

quote: Under the accountability principle, it is up to the controller to perform checks with regards to the concerns listed in Sections 4 and 5.
location: p.12, s.3.3 Procuring an AI system (fn 21)
obligation: statutory duty restated ('it is up to the controller')
note: Footnote to the selection and award step. Trigger: selection and award of a procured AI system. Comparator: the concerns in Sections 4-5 (interpretability/explainability, fairness, accuracy, data minimisation, security, data subject rights).

quote: these are prerequisites for EUIs acting as controllers for the processing of personal data in the context of AI systems to ensure compliance with their obligations un der the EUDPR
location: p.13, s.4 Interpretability and explainability as sine qua non
note: Interpretability and explainability concern 'the extent to which the controller understands the functioning of its AI system'. Cross-cutting for procuring, developing and deploying. Distinguished from transparency (coded as Accountability).

quote: Proper documentation should be drafted, including:
location: p.14-15, s.4.1.1 Risk 1: Uninterpretable or unexplainable AI system (measure 1)
note: Passive. Nearest named actor: the controller, who reads it [inference: drafted by the developer or provider]. Contents: (a) AI architecture and why chosen; (b) source and suitability of training personal data; (c) how the system acts and 'how accurate it is across different groups'; (d) potential biases and measures taken; (e) limitations. Should be 'relevant, useful and understandable to the user'. Phases: selection (procurement), verification and validation, operation and monitoring, continuous validation, re-evaluation.

quote: Consideration of techniques for explainability such as LIME or SHAP (Shapley Additive Explanations)
note: Repeated at p.24 for interpretation bias ('Incorporating AI model explainability techniques such as SHAP, LIME and feature importance analysis'). Tools coded as Delivery/Resources.
basis: AI pass A; different cell in pass B

quote: Analyse the output of the AI statistically and explain the rationale of the results or lack thereof.
note: Check of outputs. Trigger: phases listed for Risk 1. Metric not stated. Fn 26 points to ICO guidance (coded as Resources).

quote: an assessment should be made of how the processing will affect the interests and fundamental rights of those concerned, as a group and individually
note: Nearest named actor: controllers. Fairness impact assessment. Trigger not stated. Comparator: whether effects are 'unjustified adverse'. Same paragraph: fairness 'also requires controller s to implement procedural safeguards'. Link to good administration (Charter Art. 41) is reported, not coded.

quote: should identify and measure these biases and implement technical and organisational measures to prevent or correct any form of discriminatory outcome
holder: controllers procuring, developing or deploying AI systems that involve the processing of personal data
note: Holder named on p.16, 'especially those used to take or assist when taking decisions about individuals'. p.16 also: 'the principle of fairness is understood as requiring controllers to identify, measure and mitigate these biases'. Fn 32: AI Act Art. 10 has similar requirements. Metric not stated here (see bias-audit entries).

quote: Define and implement a procedure for assessing the training personal dataset which, in accordance with the policy, samples the dataset, measures and assess es against the agreed quality threshold.
note: Comparator: the agreed quality threshold in the quality assurance policy. Metric: the policy's quality criteria. Trigger not stated.

quote: it is essential to ensure that the training personal datasets used in the data acquisition and preparation phase are diverse and representative of the population in which the AI system will be used
location: p.18, s.5.1.1 Risk 1: Bias caused by the lack of data quality
note: Comparator: the population in which the system will be used. Also: 'Regular  audits and updates of training personal datasets can help maintain their relevance and inclusivity'. Phases: data acquisition and preparation; verification and validation; re-evaluation.

quote: Conduct regular data quality audits of the AI system’s training personal data to check for data quality.
note: Trigger: regular. Grouped with measure 4 (statistical outlier detection, then manual or statistical correction or removal) and measure 6 (standardisation and consistency checks). 'Audit' here is an internal check, not answerability, so coded as Delivery.

quote: doing a human review by some individuals with domain expertise
note: Training data verification: reliable sources, checking against trusted similar sources, human review by domain experts, fuzzy matching, clustering to detect biases, and 'documenting the provenance of the training personal data , justifying its correctness,42 validity and traceability'.

quote: Subject matter experts should define key variables and test if the training personal data  encapsulates all relevant operational aspects.
note: Expert review and scenario checks. Also 'Reviewing for class imbalance or sampling biases is also crucial'. Whether experts are internal or external is not stated.

quote: Conduct regular audits of the AI system’s training personal data to check for biases.
note: Trigger: regular. Metric not stated. Fn 48 points to IBM AI Fairness 360 and Aequitas (coded as Resources). Internal check, not Accountability.

quote: Distribution matching: Examine if the statistical distributions of key features in both the training and intended input datasets are similar.
location: p.20, s.5.1.2 Risk 2: Bias in training personal data (measure 1a-c)
note: Applies 'When the organisation has access to the training personal data'. Comparator: intended input data. Tools/metrics: histograms, summary statistics, clustering; also diversity and coverage analysis, validation and cross-validation on data mimicking operational data.

quote: Avoid features that directly encode sensitive attributes like race, gender or socioeconomic status, unless their inclusion is justified and handled carefully.
note: Grouped: bias-free features (detect proxies such as postal code), feature engineering (reweighting or rescaling), bias mitigation techniques for data (re-weighting). Who justifies inclusion is not stated.

quote: Simplifying the AI model is also a practical approach to mitigate overfitting.
location: p.21-22, s.5.1.3 Risk 3: Overfitting to the training personal data
note: Grouped measures: early stopping on validation performance, simplification (fewer features, pruning), L1/L2/Elastic Net regularisation, dropout. Phases include operation and monitoring and continuous validation. Nearest actor: developer [inference].

quote: Conduct regular audits of the AI system to check for biases. This involves evaluating the algorithm's performance across different demographic groups and identifying and assessing any disparities.
note: Trigger: regular. Comparator: performance across demographic groups. Metric: disparities; fn 55: 'it is recommended to calculate multiple metrics'. Phases: verification and validation, continuous validation, re-evaluation. Internal check.

quote: Test the algorithm on diverse datasets that reflect the variety of real-world scenarios it will encounter.
note: Comparator: real-world scenarios. Trigger: phases for Risk 4.

quote: Choose algorithms that are designed with fairness constraints in mind.
note: Grouped: fairness-aware algorithms (e.g. Two Naive Bayes), choice of objective function accounting for fairness across groups, interpretable models. Phase: inception/analysis. Intro also lists 'regular audits, transparency, fairness metrics' and 'inclusive development practices'.

quote: Maintaining clear and comprehensive documentation of the data sources, feature selection, pre-processing steps and modelling decisions helps ensure that the analysis process is transparent.
note: Recording.

quote: Conduct regular audits of the interpretation of the output by analysts to check for biases.
note: Review of how human analysts interpret outputs. Trigger: regular. Example on p.24: reading a probability score as a definitive diagnosis.

quote: Accuracy under the EUDPR requires controllers to ensure that the personal data itself is not incorrect or misleading as to any matter of fact.
location: p.25, s.5.2.1 Legal meaning of accuracy in the EUDPR
note: Legal accuracy is distinguished from 'statistical accuracy' (an AI performance metric, s.5.2.2). Failing to assess statistical accuracy is a compliance risk where it leads to inaccurate personal data output, including hallucinations (s.5.2.3). Annex 1 gives metrics.

quote: The AI system should be verified and validated with edge cases (outliers) and adversarial examples to evaluate its resilience and reliability under unusual or challenging conditions.
location: p.26, s.5.2.3 Risk 1: Inaccurate personal data output (measure 2)
note: Trigger: verification and validation. Grouped with measures 1, 3-5: high quality, diverse and representative, balanced training data; hyperparameter optimisation.

quote: incorporating human review into the AI decision -making process ensures that the model's predictions are double -checked, reducing the chances of errors.
note: Human review of outputs. Form depends on context, complexity and risk. Fn 69 distinguishes pre-deployment review, HITL during operation and post-decision review. Who reviews is not stated. Also coded Decision-making (fn 69).

quote: Retraining can be done on a fixed schedule (e.g. weekly or monthly) or triggered by performance  drops or detected drift.
note: Trigger: schedule, or on change (performance drop or detected drift). Process ends by 'validating the new version to ensure improved performance'.

quote: Implement data drift detection methods that monitor changes in the distribution of data over time.
location: p.28, s.5.2.4 Inaccurate output due to data drift (measures 1-2)
note: Trigger: ongoing (operation and monitoring, continuous validation, re-evaluation). Also measure 2: data quality monitoring tracking completeness, statistical accuracy and consistency of incoming data, 'Regularly review these metrics'.

quote: organisations should focus on understanding the development processes employed by the AI provider.
location: p.28, s.5.2.5 Risk 2: Unclear information from the AI system provider
note: Due diligence on procured systems: 'asking questions' about how risks in inception, data, development and verification phases were managed. Phases: call for tenders; selection. What to request is coded under Coordination.

quote: The controllers would need to assess whether the demographics of training personal dataset are close or far from the demographics of the personal data that the AI system will ingest during its operation.
note: Comparator: demographics of the personal data the system will ingest in operation. Trigger: procurement (call for tenders, selection). Depends on the provider disclosing statistical properties of training data.

quote: the organisation should request from the provider a set of metrics that will allow for the evaluation of the AI system against the organisation’s objectives.
note: Evaluation of a procured system. Comparator: the organisation's objectives. Metrics suggested: False Positive Rate parity, False Negative Rate parity, calibration fairness, equality of opportunity (each 'should be similar' across groups); also task-specific benchmarks (Annex 1). The request is also a coordination step (see Coordination entry).
basis: AI pass A; different cell in pass B

quote: EUIs must also ensure compliance with the principle of data minimisation.
location: p.30, s.5.3 Principle of data minimisation
note: Requires a balance between enough personal data for accuracy and limiting it to what is necessary for the purpose.

quote: The AI system should be developed with anonymised data wherever possible. If personal data are necessary, pseudonymised data should be considered.
note: Also measure 2: data sampling of a representative subset.

quote: Validate the relevance of the planned training personal data types before full training and operation.
location: p.31, s.5.3.1 Risk 1: Indiscriminate collection and storage (measure 1)
note: Trigger: before full training and operation. Comparator: usefulness for the needed inferences, via a pre-assessment using existing information.

quote: it is necessary to protect the training personal data, the input data, the output data and the AI model itself.
note: Nearest named actor: EUIs as controllers. Covers AI-specific security risks only, not general IT security. Threats named: model inversion, data poisoning, model poisoning, model theft.

quote: Implement measure to prevent exact replication of training personal data when producing an output such as by using MEMFREE decoding.
location: p.33, s.5.4.1 Risk 1: AI system output disclosure of training personal data (measures 1-4)
note: Grouped with training data minimisation; perturbation (generalisation, aggregation, differential privacy); synthetic data 'with due care', combined with other measures. Phases: operation and monitoring, continuous validation, re-evaluation.

quote: Follow secure coding practices when developing AI models to prevent attackers from exploiting vulnerabilities in AI code or infrastructure.
location: p.34-35, s.5.4.2 Risk 2: Personal data storage and personal data breaches (measures 1-5)
note: Grouped: anonymisation/pseudonymisation, encryption at rest, synthetic training data, secure development, MFA for sensitive AI systems. Breach as defined in Art. 3(16) EUDPR.

quote: Implement logging and monitoring for API calls.
note: Logging. Trigger: ongoing. Plus SIEM systems 'to analyse and respond to potential threats in near real-time'.

quote: Implement strong authentication mechanisms, such as MFA, to ensure that only authorised users and systems can access the APIs.
location: p.35-36, s.5.4.3 Risk 3: Personal data leakage through APIs (measures 1, 3, 4, 7, 8)
note: Applies where systems use third-party models via API. Grouped: MFA, throttling, TLS encryption, secure API development (input validation), patching. RBAC, logging and security audits coded separately.

quote: Conduct regular security audits and penetration testing of APIs to identify and address vulnerabilities.
note: Trigger: regular. Should include code reviews, configuration checks, vulnerability scans and automated tools. Auditor not stated; internal check, not answerability.

quote: the controller must both identify whether and where personal data are used during the training phase, and assess whether the model, when answering certain prompts, might leak that data
location: p.36, s.5.5.1 Risk 1: Incomplete identification of the personal data processed
note: Trigger: on receiving a data subject's request to exercise their rights. Verb: must. The redress route itself is coded as Accountability/Design. Phases: development; operation and monitoring.
basis: AI pass B; different cell in pass A

quote: The training personal datasets should include metadata so that the relevant records or files including personal data can be more easily identified in case a data subject invokes their right to access their personal data.
note: Recording/traceability. Metadata should include sources, collection methods and pre-processing steps (cleaning, pseudonymisation, augmentation). Serves the access right (Accountability).
basis: AI pass B; different cell in pass A

quote: When machine un-learning is not viable, output filtering can be used. Output filtering involves real- time scanning of AI model responses to detect and block personal information before reaching users.
note: Output control; trigger: where machine unlearning (measure 2: exact or approximate) is not viable. Serves rectification/erasure requests. Phases: development; operation and monitoring.
basis: AI pass B; different cell in pass A

quote: This requires more than a one -off assessment: it demands a culture of accountability, continuous monitoring and adaptive improvement.
note: Holder named in the preceding sentence ('a central obligation for EUIs'). Trigger: throughout the AI lifecycle.

quote: it does not replace the necessary compliance assessment of each AI system to be done by the controller, who must ensure that the risks identified (with the support of this framework ) are managed
obligation: statutory duty restated in non-binding guidance (must)
note: Verb: must ensure. Trigger: each AI system (timing not stated). Comparator: 'all the obligations arising under the EUDPR'. Metric not stated. Same point in Executive summary (p.4: guidance does 'not exempt EUIs from conducting their own assessment') and Conclusion (p.39-40, coded as Accountability). 'Ensure ... managed' could be read as Decision-making; coded Delivery because the assessment is done by the controller itself. See also p.6 and p.8 entries.

quote: EUIs are responsible for identifying and mitigating risks to these rights and freedoms raised by their processing activities, and to demonstrate how they did so.
obligation: statutory duty restated in non-binding guidance
note: Body text; Executive summary (p.4) states the same citing Art. 4(2) and 71(4) (operational personal data). Trigger: 'for each of their processing activities' (p.6). The guidance limits its own scope to non-compliance risks under fairness, accuracy, data minimisation, security and certain data subject rights. Also coded as Accountability/Design (demonstrate).

quote: EUIs should perform a thorough analysis for each AI system they plan to use in order to also evaluate the likelihood and impact of the risks
note: Trigger: before use ('each AI system they plan to use'). Comparator: the organisation's own risk criteria. Metric: qualitative likelihood x impact (five-level scale and risk matrix, p.7-8), grading definitions left to the organisation. If risks cannot be mitigated by reasonable means, see p.9 entries.

quote: Execution (Article 175): Monitor implementation and ensure compliance.
note: Contract execution phase for a procured AI system; the document says it comprises verification and validation, deployment, operation and monitoring, continuous validation, re-evaluation and retirement. What is checked and against what: not stated at this point.

quote: The training personal data can be verified to confirm the validity of the information and minimise the risk of bias.
note: Verb: can. Includes getting data from reliable sources, checking against trusted similar sources, 'doing a human review by some individuals with domain expertise', fuzzy matching, cluster detection, and 'documenting the provenance of the training personal data'. Measure 4 (p18): statistical outlier detection with manual or statistical correction.

quote: Early stopping is a technique where the training process is halted as soon as the AI model's performance on the validation set starts to degrade
note: Technical development measures against overfitting: 1 early stopping (trigger: validation performance degrades), 2 simplification, 3 L1/L2 regularisation, 4 dropout. Phases include operation and monitoring and continuous validation. No holder named; nearest: developers.

quote: Implement MFA for access to sensitive AI systems to prevent unauthorised users from manipulating or stealing models.
location: p35, Section 5.4.2 Risk 2: Personal data storage and breaches, measure 5
note: Other measures in 5.4.2: anonymisation/pseudonymisation, encryption at rest, synthetic training data, secure development practices. A breach is defined by reference to Art. 3(16) EUDPR.

quote: AI models are likely to require a thorough evaluation of the likelihood of identification to reach a conclusion on their possible anonymous nature.
note: Nearest named actor: the controller. Check of claimed anonymity. Comparator: likelihood of extraction of training personal data and of obtaining it from queries should be 'insignificant' for any data subject, taking into account 'all the means reasonably likely to be used' and unintended (re)use or disclosure of the model.
basis: AI pass A; different cell in pass B

quote: the use of web scraping techniques to collect data f rom websites and their use for training purposes will have to comply with all relevant data protection principles
note: Nearest named actor: EUIs. 'publicly available' personal data remains subject to EU data protection law.

quote: If web scraping techniques are used for personal data collection, EUIs should put in place safeguards to minimise the impact such collection has on the rights and freedoms of individuals.
note: Example safeguard: limit collection to 'freely accessible data that were made manifestly public by the individual'. Fn 20 points to CNIL (coded as Resources).

quote: Regular monitoring and the implementation of controls at all stages can help verify that there is no personal data processing, in cases where the model is not intended for it.
location: PDF p.14 (printed p.13), s.4 (conclusion box [inference from layout])
note: Trigger: regular, all stages. Comparator: absence of personal data processing. Box content not stated in body.

quote: Developers and deployers may need to carry out their own risk assessments and document any mitigation action taken.
note: Value-chain actors addressed directly. Linked to data protection by design from the inception stage.

quote: a DPIA 24  must be carried out before any processing operation that is likely to result in a high risk25 to fundamental rights and freedoms of individuals
note: Nearest named actor: the controller. Trigger: before processing likely to result in high risk; especially new technologies 'in the case of generative AI systems for example'. Fn 25: AI Act high-risk classification 'does trigger a presumption of high-risk' under GDPR, EUDPR and LED. s.2 list: 'If required, conduct a DPIA and adopt data protection by design and by default measures'. Worked example (PDF p.31): a DPIA 'must also be carried out prior to the deployment' of a CV-screening system.

quote: regular monitoring and reviews of the risk assessments need to be carried out, since the functioning of the model may exacerbate identified risks or create new ones.
note: Trigger: regular/ongoing. Covers data protection and 'other fundamental rights and freedoms'. Also reviews of whether the DPIA 'is rightly implemented'. Repeated in s.15: 'regular monitoring and updates of the risk assessment are needed'; conclusion box (PDF p.18) adds monitoring whether identified risks are worsening or new risks appear.

quote: All the actors involved in the DPIA must ensure that any decision and action is properly documented, covering the entire generative AI system lifecycle
holder: All the actors involved in the DPIA
note: Recording, including 'actions taken to manage risks and the subsequent reviews to be carried out'.
basis: AI pass A; different cell in pass B

quote: appropriate technical and organisational measures must be taken to mitigate the identified risks
if_not_met: If following the DPIA, controllers are not sure whether risks are appropriately mitigated, they should proceed to a prior consultation with the EDPS (PDF p.18)
note: Nearest named actor: the controller. Trigger: result of the DPIA. Measures relative to 'the responsibilities the context and the ava ilable state -of-the-art measures'.

quote: Where necessary, the controller shall carry out a review to assess if the data processing is being performed in accordance with the data protection impact assessment, at least when there is a change to the risks
note: Trigger: on change to the risks. Comparator: the DPIA. In an information box rather than body text.

quote: to verify that the AI model that they are deploying has not been developed by unlawfully  processing personal data.
obligation: non-binding interpretation of a statutory duty ('specific responsibility')
note: Check on the provider's development of a deployed model (value chain). Trigger: before deployment [inference]. Linked to Accountability entry on demonstrating compliance (same sentence).

quote: Datasets and models must be accompanied by documentation on their structure, maintenance and intended use.
note: Passive. Nearest named actors: EUIs; for third-party datasets and models, the supplier or developer [inference]. Recording.

quote: When using systems designed or operated by third- party service providers, EUIs should include in their assessments considerations related to the principle of data minimisation.
note: Vendor assessment. Trigger: use of third-party systems.

quote: these datasets should be well labelled and curated, within the framework of appropriate data governance procedures, including periodic and systematic review of the content.
location: PDF p.25 (printed p.24), s.9 Data minimisation
note: Trigger: periodic. Comparator: data necessary for the purpose; high quality. Holder from the preceding sentence ('EUIs should develop and use models trained with high quality datasets').

quote: EUIs must also verify that the purpose in question cannot be achieved by processing other data, such as synthetic or anonymised data before deciding that personal data is necessary to process in the first place
location: PDF p.25 (printed p.24), s.9 Data minimisation
obligation: non-binding interpretation of a statutory duty (must)
note: Check before the decision to process personal data (gate). Obligation 'covers the entire lifecycle of the system, including testing, acceptance and release into production phases'.
basis: AI pass B; different cell in pass A

quote: data controllers have an obligation to limit the collection and otherwise processing of personal data to what is necessary for the purposes of the processing, avoiding indiscriminate processing of personal data.
location: PDF p.25 (printed p.24), s.9 Data minimisation
note: Covers the whole lifecycle, 'including testing, acceptance and release into production phases'.

quote: It is equally important to have control over the output data, including the inferences made by the model, which requires regular monitoring of that information, including human oversight.
note: Output checking with human oversight. Trigger: regular. Comparator and metric not stated; metrics on statistical accuracy 'when available, can offer an indicator'. Who carries out human oversight is not stated. A worked example (PDF p.28) shows a manual verification step for each AI-generated CV summary; example not coded.

quote: Developers should use validation sets46 during training and separate testing sets for final evaluation to obtain an estimation on how the system will perform.
note: Trigger: during training and at final evaluation (before deployment). Metric: statistical accuracy (when available).

quote: This implies verifying the structure and content of the datasets used for training models, including those sourced or obtained from third parties.
note: Check of training data. Trigger not stated. Includes third-party data (value chain).

quote: Data controllers must ensure data accuracy at all stages of the development and use of a generative AI system.
if_not_met: EUIs should 'reconsider the use of such systems if the accuracy cannot be maintained' (conclusion box, PDF p.27)
note: Continues: 'they must implement the necessary measures to integrate data protection by design'. Hallucinations named as a risk even with high quality data.

quote: EUIs know best their business case and should test and regularly monitor if the system output is biased by using input data tailored to their business needs.
note: Output testing for bias by the deployer, not left to providers ('Generative AI systems providers try to detect and mitigate bias'). Trigger: testing plus regular monitoring. Comparator: input data tailored to business needs. Metric not stated.

quote: EUIs, as public authorities, should put in place safeguards to avoid overreliance on the results provided by the systems that can lead to automation and confirmation biases.
note: Safeguards on human use of outputs. Also bears on Decision-making (keeping human judgement over outputs); safeguards not specified.

quote: implementing accountability and oversight mechanisms that allow for continuous monitoring to prevent the occurrence of biases that have an effect on individuals, as well as to correct those behaviours.
location: PDF p.32 (printed p.31), s.13 Fairness and bias
note: Nearest named actor: EUIs. Trigger: continuous. Also: datasets should give 'an adequate and fair representation of the real world'.

quote: Controllers are advised to only use datasets provided by trusted sources and carry out regularly verification and validation procedures, including for in-house datasets.
note: Trigger: regular. Comparator not stated.

quote: A possible way to deal with unknown risks is to use “red teaming 57” techniques to try to find and expose vulnerabilities.
note: Adversarial testing. Trigger not stated.

quote: it is necessary to test that the generative AI system is not leaking personal data that might be present in the system’s knowledge base.
note: Trigger: when using Retrieval Augmented Generation. Nearest named actor: the EUI as owner of the knowledge base (fn 58).

quote: Controllers should, in addition to the traditional security controls for IT systems, integrate specific controls tailored to the already known vulnerabilities of these systems
note: Vulnerabilities named: model inversion, prompt injection, jailbreaks; controls 'in a way that facilitates continuous monitoring and assessment of their effectiveness'. Trigger: ongoing.

quote: The Regulation requires EUIs to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security 53 appropriate to the risk for the rights and freedoms of natural persons.
location: PDF p.37 (printed p.36), s.15 Data security
note: Comparator: risk to rights and freedoms. Notes that a limited offer of models in critical sectors such as health can amplify vulnerabilities.

quote: Perform a comprehensive generative AI risk assessment in accordance with the EDPS’ Guidance for Risk Management for Artificial Intelligence system.
location: PDF p.8 (printed p.7), s.2 (recommendation 'Conduct a Generative AI Risk Assessment')
note: Comparator: the EDPS risk management guidance, cited here as '(forthcoming)' (fn 7). Trigger not stated (before deployment [inference]).

quote: As required under the Regulation, implement all data protection principles such as transparency, data minimisation, data retention and data security.
location: PDF p.9 (printed p.8), s.2 (recommendation 'Implement core data protection principles')
obligation: statutory duty restated ('As required under the Regulation')
note: Umbrella item; each principle is detailed in ss.8-15.

quote: In case EUIs use a generative AI model developed by another entity, they should thoroughly assess and ensure that the generative AI complies with all data protection requirements, and request all documentation to perform the verification.
location: PDF p.9 (printed p.8), s.2 (recommendation 'Perform Third Party Vendor Due Diligence')
holder: EUIs (using a generative AI model developed by another entity)
note: Vendor due diligence. Trigger: before use of a third-party model [inference]. Comparator: all data protection requirements. The documentation request is also a coordination step with the vendor.

quote: This likelihood should be assessed taking into account ‘all the means reasonably likely to be used’ by  the controller or another person, and should also consider unintended (re)use or disclosure of the model.
note: Check of whether a model is anonymous; metric: likelihood of identification, threshold 'insignificant'. Holder passive; nearest named actor: the controller/EUI. Related: when a provider claims no personal data, 'it is crucial to ask about the specific controls' (coded as Coordination/Design).

quote: EUIs should identify whether the request concern s i) training data, ii) post-training data, (including fine-tuning data and data from reinforcement learning from human feedback) iii) user inputs (prompts), and/or) iv) outputs of the generative AI model
note: Trigger: on receiving an individual rights request. For output requests (e.g. rectification of inaccurate generated data) see Accountability/Design. 'Keeping a traceable record of the processing of personal data ... may support the exercise of individual rights' (p35).

quote: integrate specific controls tailored to the already known vulnerabilities of these systems - model inversion attacks 54 , prompt injection 55 , jailbreaks 56  - in a way that facilitates continuous monitoring and assessment of their effectiveness
note: Verb: should, 'in addition to the traditional security controls for IT systems'. Ongoing monitoring of control effectiveness. Edge case: these attacks are by others against the body's system (malicious third parties).

quote: DPIAs are an important element of accountability, where the processing in the context of AI models is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons
obligation: statutory duty where processing is likely to result in high risk (recalled; not analysed in the Opinion)
note: Impact assessment. Passive; nearest actor: controllers (Art. 35, not quoted). Listed among provisions 'This Opinion does not analyse' but which may still play an important role. The document calls DPIAs 'an important element of accountability'; coded Delivery as an impact assessment per the coding frame. Trigger: likely high risk; timing not stated. Points to WP29 DPIA Guidelines (fn 15). Para 58(a): SAs should ideally check DPIA information, including decisions that a DPIA was not necessary.

quote: Data protection by design is an essential safeguard to be assessed by SAs in the context of the development and deployment of an AI model.
obligation: statutory duty (recalled; not analysed in the Opinion)
note: Passive for the duty-holder; nearest actor: controllers (Art. 25(1), not quoted). SAs are named as assessors, so this could also be read as Accountability. Listed among provisions not analysed by the Opinion.

quote: SAs should consider whether controllers have assessed the risk of identification by the controller and by different types of ‘ other persons’, including unintended third parties accessing the AI model
note: Risk assessment by the controller, considering whether others can reasonably gain access. Means assessed on objective factors (para 41): characteristics of training data, model and training procedure; release context; additional information available; cost and time; available technology. Also 'unintended (re)use or disclosure of the model' (para 43). Trigger: not stated.

quote: SAs should evaluate the approach es taken by controllers during the development phase. The application and effectiveness of four key areas (identified below) should be considered in this regard.
obligation: non-binding interpretation; non-prescriptive, non-exhaustive list (para 47); verb 'should' (addressed to SAs)
if_not_met: not stated here; see Accountability/Design entry (paras 45, 57)
note: Framed as what SAs should evaluate; the measures are the controller's [inference that controllers are expected to take them]. Four areas: selection of sources (criteria, relevance, exclusion of inappropriate sources, para 50); data preparation and minimisation (anonymous or pseudonymised data considered, reasons if not, minimisation, filtering, para 51); methodological choices (regularisation to reduce overfitting and, 'crucially', privacy-preserving techniques e.g. differential privacy, para 52); measures on model outputs lowering the likelihood of obtaining training personal data via queries (para 53). Trigger: development phase. 'The presence or absence of the elements listed below is not a conclusive criterion' (para 48).

quote: SAs should evaluate whether controllers have conducted  any document -based audits (internal or external) that include an evaluation of the chosen measures and of their impact to limit the likelihood of identification.
